# React: From Absolute Basics to Interviews

React explained from zero, in **five levels**: **Basic** (how web pages work, the JavaScript React relies on, why React exists, setting up a project; then components, JSX, props, purity, conditions, lists and keys) → **Easy** (events, state, rendering, snapshots, updating objects and arrays, forms; then thinking in React: state machines, state structure, lifting state, preserving and resetting state, composition, TypeScript and styling) → **Moderate** (refs, effects and when not to use them, data fetching, useReducer, context, custom hooks, how hooks work inside, debugging; how React works: reconciliation built from scratch, Fiber, re-renders, memoisation and the React Compiler, virtualisation, code splitting, error boundaries, accessibility; real apps: React Router, TanStack Query, React 19 actions, React Hook Form + Zod, global state, testing with Vitest, Testing Library, MSW and Playwright) → **Advanced** (CSR, SSR, SSG and ISR, hydration, streaming, Server Components, Next.js, transitions and Activity, real-time and AI chat interfaces; internationalisation, architecture, class components, production monitoring and deployment, what's new up to React 19.3) → **Interview Prep** (hooks and utilities from scratch, the machine-coding round, behaviour questions, what companies ask, a cheat sheet, the most asked questions and a glossary).

**Nothing is left for you to look up.** Every technical word is explained in plain language the first time it appears (look for the **Words to know** box at the top of each section), and Section [76](#76-glossary-every-term-in-these-notes) collects every term in one alphabetical glossary with a link back to where it's taught.

Every section has the same shape:

1. **Picture:** a diagram of the idea, or a real screenshot of what the code renders.
2. **Theory:** what it is, an everyday picture, how it works step by step (traced by hand where possible), when to use it, when *not* to, common mistakes, and where it's used in real software.
3. **Code:** working programs, first **from scratch** (plain JavaScript or a hand-made version, so you see the idea) and then **the React or library way** (how you'd do it at work). Every example is TypeScript (`.tsx`) and was run with **React 19.3.1** on **Node.js 24.5**, rendering into a simulated browser page (**jsdom 30**) and clicking and typing through **Testing Library** the way a user would, and type-checked with **TypeScript 7.0.2** (Section [6](#6-setting-up-node-npm-vite-and-how-these-examples-run) explains how). Results under **Output** are exactly what was printed; **Compiler output** is exactly what the TypeScript compiler reported. Library versions: React Router 8.4, TanStack Query 5.104, Zustand 5.0, Redux Toolkit 2.13, Jotai 3.0, React Hook Form 7.90, Zod 4.6, MSW 3.0, Vitest 5.0, Vite 8.3, Tailwind CSS 4.3, i18next 26, Vercel AI SDK 7, Next.js 16.4 and Playwright 1.64. Things jsdom can't do (layout, scrolling, View Transitions, Web Vitals, end-to-end flows) were run in real Google Chrome through Playwright; Next.js apps were really built and served; the few short answer sketches shown as plain text are marked as not run. Blocks within one section share their variables, like cells in a notebook.
4. **Practice:** exercises with hidden answers, plus graded problems (🟢 Easy, 🟡 Medium, 🔴 Hard, all free): the official **react.dev challenges**, React problems and quizzes from **BFE.dev**, JavaScript problems from **LeetCode**, and real designs to build from **Frontend Mentor**.

Each part ends with a ✅ **checkpoint**. Before this file you only need to be comfortable using a computer and typing code; `javascript.md` goes deeper into the language and `typescript.md` into types. After it, continue with `nodejs.md` (servers and APIs) and `llm-engineering.md` + `rag-and-agents.md` to build AI features behind your React UI.

# Part 1 — Basic: The Web and the JavaScript React Needs

> **Goal:** Understand how a web page is built and changed (HTML, CSS, the DOM, events), the modern JavaScript that React code is written in, why React exists at all, and how to create a React project and run the examples in these notes.  
> **You need:** Nothing beyond basic computer use. If you have never programmed, read `javascript.md` Part 1 alongside this part; every idea used here is still explained where it appears.

---

## 1. How to Use These Notes (and What a React Developer Does)

![The learning path through these notes: eleven parts from web basics to interview prep](images/react/00-roadmap.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** **React** is a JavaScript library for building **user interfaces** (the buttons, forms, lists and pages people click on) out of small reusable pieces called **components**. You describe what the screen should look like for the current data, and React keeps the real page in sync when the data changes. These notes take you from "what is a web page?" to building, testing, optimising and shipping React apps the way companies do, one small step at a time.

**Words to know:**

- **User interface (UI):** everything a person sees and interacts with in an app: text, buttons, inputs, menus, pages.
- **React:** an open-source JavaScript library for building UIs from components, created at Facebook (now Meta) and open-sourced in 2013; since February 2026 it is owned by the independent React Foundation, hosted by the Linux Foundation.
- **Component:** a reusable piece of UI, such as a button, a product card or a whole checkout page, written as a JavaScript function.
- **Library vs framework:** a **library** is code you call when you need it (React renders UI; you pick the rest); a **framework** calls *your* code and decides the structure of the whole app (Next.js decides routing, data loading and the server for you).
- **Frontend / backend:** the **frontend** is the part of an app that runs in the user's browser (the UI); the **backend** runs on servers (databases, business logic, APIs).
- **Full-stack developer:** someone who builds both the frontend and the backend.
- **React DOM:** the package that connects React to web pages. **React Native:** the sibling that connects React to iPhone and Android screens instead.
- **Next.js:** the most used **React framework**: React plus routing, server rendering and a server, made by Vercel (Part 9).
- **TypeScript:** JavaScript with **types** (labels such as "this is a number") that catch mistakes before the code runs; most React teams use it, and so do these notes (Section [26](#26-typescript-with-react-typing-props-state-events-and-children)).
- **Open source:** software whose code anyone can read, use and improve, usually for free.

**Everyday picture.** LEGO. Instead of carving a whole castle from one block of wood (and starting over to change a tower), you snap together small standard bricks. A React app is built the same way: small components (a button, a price tag) are snapped into bigger ones (a product card), which form pages. Change one brick and only that part of the castle changes.

**These notes climb level by level:**

| Part | Level | What you learn | Afterwards you can… |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Basic | How web pages work, the JavaScript React uses, why React, project setup | Read React code without getting lost in the syntax |
| 2 | Basic | Components, JSX, props, purity, conditions, lists and keys | Build static pages from components and data |
| 3 | Easy | Events, state, rendering, snapshots, objects and arrays in state, forms | Build interactive widgets: counters, carts, forms |
| 4 | Easy | Thinking in React: state machines, state structure, lifting state, keys, composition, TypeScript, styling | Design a small app's components and state like a professional |
| 5 | Moderate | Refs, effects, when not to use effects, data fetching | Talk to the browser and servers safely |
| 6 | Moderate | useReducer, context, custom hooks, how hooks work, debugging | Organise state in a growing app |
| 7 | Moderate | Reconciliation built from scratch, Fiber, re-renders, memoisation, the React Compiler, virtualisation, code splitting, error boundaries, accessibility | Make apps fast, robust and usable by everyone |
| 8 | Moderate | React Router, TanStack Query, React 19 actions, React Hook Form + Zod, global state, testing | Build and test a real multi-page app |
| 9 | Advanced | SSR, SSG, hydration, streaming, Server Components, Next.js, transitions, real-time and AI chat UIs | Build server-rendered and streaming apps |
| 10 | Advanced | Internationalisation, architecture, class components, production, what's new | Ship and maintain React in production |
| 11 | Interview Prep | Hooks from scratch, machine coding, behaviour questions, checklist, cheat sheet, theory questions, glossary | Revise quickly and check your coverage |

**What a React developer actually does.** Less time goes into clever code than people expect:

| Activity | Share of a typical week |
|---|---|
| building screens from designs (components, layout, styling) | **the largest part** |
| connecting screens to data (APIs, loading and error states, forms) | large |
| fixing bugs and reading other people's code | large |
| writing tests and reviewing pull requests | moderate |
| performance, accessibility and production issues | small, but what separates seniors |

**Roles you'll hear about (2026):**

| Role | Mostly does |
|---|---|
| **Frontend engineer** | builds web UIs, usually with React and TypeScript |
| **Full-stack engineer** | React on the frontend plus APIs and databases (Next.js, Node.js, `nodejs.md`) |
| **UI / design-systems engineer** | builds the shared component library that every team uses (Section [66](#66-architecture-project-structure-design-systems-and-monorepos)) |
| **Mobile engineer (React Native)** | iOS and Android apps with React Native and Expo |
| **AI product engineer** | builds chat, streaming and agent interfaces on top of LLM APIs (Section [64](#64-real-time-and-streaming-uis-websockets-sse-and-ai-chat)) |

**How to study each section:** look at the picture; read the theory slowly and trace the worked example by hand; **type** the code (don't paste it), run it, change one thing and predict the result before re-running; then try the practice before opening the answers. Section [6](#6-setting-up-node-npm-vite-and-how-these-examples-run) shows how to set up a project that runs every example.

**When NOT to reach for React:** a mostly static site (a blog, documentation, a landing page) is often better as plain HTML or a content-focused tool such as Astro; a tiny widget on an existing page may need only a few lines of plain JavaScript (Section [5](#5-why-react-updating-a-page-by-hand-vs-describing-it)).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Starting with a framework (Next.js) before understanding components, props and state.
- ❌ Copying code without running it; React's behaviour (re-renders, effects) only clicks when you watch it happen.
- ❌ Skipping the JavaScript basics: most "React bugs" beginners hit are JavaScript bugs (mutation, `this`, async timing).

**Used in real software:** React powers the web apps of Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp Web), Netflix, Airbnb, Discord, Notion, Shopify's admin, Atlassian products and much of the web; React Native powers apps such as Instagram, Discord and Shopify's mobile apps.

### Practice

1. Open three web apps you use daily. For each, sketch the screen on paper and draw boxes around the pieces that repeat (a message, a product, a notification). Each repeating box is a candidate **component**. Write a name for each.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

For a shopping site you might draw: `Header` (logo, `SearchBox`, `CartButton`), `ProductGrid` made of many `ProductCard`s (image, name, `PriceTag`, `AddToCartButton`), and `Footer`. For a chat app: `ConversationList` of `ConversationItem`s, `MessageList` of `Message`s, and a `Composer`. The habit of seeing screens as nested, repeating boxes is the first skill of a React developer (Section [20](#20-thinking-in-react-from-mockup-to-components)).

</details>

## 2. How a Web Page Works: HTML, CSS, the DOM and Events

![HTML text is parsed into a DOM tree, CSS styles it, the browser paints pixels; JavaScript changes the tree and listens for events that bubble up from the clicked element](images/react/02-dom-tree.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** a web page starts as **HTML** text. The browser reads it and builds a **tree of objects** in memory, the **DOM**, one object per element. **CSS** decides how each element looks, and the browser draws (paints) the tree on screen. **JavaScript** can change the tree (add, remove or edit elements) and react to **events** like clicks; whenever the tree changes, the browser redraws. React is, at heart, a smart way of changing the DOM for you.

**Words to know:**

- **Browser:** the program that downloads and shows web pages (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge).
- **HTML (HyperText Markup Language):** the text format that describes a page's content and structure: `<h1>Menu</h1><button>Order</button>`.
- **Tag / element:** `<p>` is an opening **tag** and `</p>` a closing tag; together with what's between them they form an **element**. Some elements have no content and no closing tag (`<img>`, `<input>`, `<br>`).
- **Attribute:** extra information on an element, written `name="value"`: `<img src="tea.png" alt="A cup of tea">`.
- **CSS (Cascading Style Sheets):** rules that style elements: `.price { color: green; }`.
- **Selector:** the part of a CSS rule (or a JavaScript query) that picks elements: `p`, `.price` (class), `#cart` (id), `ul > li`.
- **Class / id:** a **class** (`class="price"`) labels any number of elements for styling; an **id** (`id="cart"`) names exactly one element.
- **DOM (Document Object Model):** the tree of JavaScript objects the browser builds from HTML; JavaScript reads and changes the page through it.
- **Node:** one item in the DOM tree: an element node (`<li>`), a text node (the words inside it), and others.
- **Parent / child / sibling:** in `<ul><li>A</li><li>B</li></ul>` the `ul` is the **parent** of both `li`s, they are its **children**, and they are **siblings** of each other.
- **`document`:** the JavaScript object that represents the whole page; `document.body` is the `<body>` element.
- **`querySelector`:** finds the first element matching a selector: `document.querySelector(".price")`.
- **Event:** something that happened that code can react to: a click, a key press, a form submit, the page finishing loading.
- **Event listener (handler):** a function the browser calls when an event happens: `button.addEventListener("click", fn)`.
- **Event bubbling:** after an event fires on the clicked element, it travels **up** through each ancestor, so a listener on a parent also hears clicks on its children.
- **`event.target` vs `event.currentTarget`:** `target` is the element where the event started; `currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running right now.
- **Default action / `preventDefault()`:** what the browser does on its own after an event (a form submit reloads the page, a link navigates); `event.preventDefault()` cancels it.
- **Paint / render (browser):** the browser turning the DOM plus CSS into pixels; changing the DOM makes it redo part of that work.

**Everyday picture.** HTML is the **architect's drawing** of a house; the DOM is the **house itself** after it's built; CSS is the **paint and furniture**; JavaScript is a **builder** who can knock down a wall or add a window while people live inside; events are the **doorbell**, and bubbling is the sound travelling from the front door through the hall to every room on the way.

**How the browser builds a page, traced by hand** for this HTML:

```text
<body>
  <h1>Chai Point</h1>
  <ul id="menu">
    <li>Masala chai</li>
    <li>Ginger chai</li>
  </ul>
</body>
```

1. Read `<body>` → create an element node `body`.
2. Read `<h1>` → create `h1` as a child of `body`; the text "Chai Point" becomes a text node inside it.
3. Read `<ul id="menu">` → create `ul` (with attribute `id="menu"`) as `body`'s second child.
4. Each `<li>` becomes a child of `ul`, each with a text node.

The result is a tree: `body → [h1 → "Chai Point", ul → [li → "Masala chai", li → "Ginger chai"]]`. Clicking the second `li` fires a `click` event on the `li`, then it bubbles to `ul`, then `body`, then `html`, then `document`.

**When to change the DOM by hand:** a tiny script on a mostly static page (toggle a menu, copy a link). **When not to:** whenever many parts of the screen depend on the same changing data; keeping all of them correct by hand gets hard fast, which is the problem React solves (Section [5](#5-why-react-updating-a-page-by-hand-vs-describing-it)).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Confusing HTML (text you write) with the DOM (live objects the browser built); JavaScript changes the DOM, and the HTML file stays as it was.
- ❌ Forgetting that events bubble, so one click triggers listeners on several ancestors.
- ❌ Forgetting `preventDefault()` on a form submit, so the page reloads and loses everything.
- ❌ Using an `id` twice on one page; `querySelector("#x")` will only ever find the first.

**Used in real software:** every website and web app; every framework (React, Vue, Angular, Svelte) ultimately calls the same DOM functions shown below.

### Code

These examples run in a **simulated browser page** called jsdom (Section [6](#6-setting-up-node-npm-vite-and-how-these-examples-run) explains the setup), so `document` works exactly as in a browser.

**From scratch: build a tree from HTML and walk it.** `innerHTML` makes the browser parse HTML into DOM nodes; a small recursive function then prints the tree:

```tsx
document.body.innerHTML = `
  <div id="app">
    <h1>Chai Point</h1>
    <ul id="menu">
      <li class="item">Masala chai</li>
      <li class="item">Ginger chai</li>
    </ul>
  </div>`;

function printTree(node: Element, depth = 0) {
  const own = [...node.childNodes].filter((n) => n.nodeType === Node.TEXT_NODE).map((n) => n.textContent!.trim()).join("");
  const id = node.id ? `#${node.id}` : "";
  console.log(`${"  ".repeat(depth)}${node.tagName.toLowerCase()}${id}${own ? `  "${own}"` : ""}`);
  for (const child of node.children) printTree(child, depth + 1);
}
printTree(document.body);
```

**Output:**

```text
body
  div#app
    h1  "Chai Point"
    ul#menu
      li  "Masala chai"
      li  "Ginger chai"
```

`node.children` lists only element children; `childNodes` also includes the text nodes, which is where the words live. `nodeType === Node.TEXT_NODE` picks those out.

**Changing the DOM by hand:** find elements, create new ones, change text and classes:

```tsx
const menu = document.querySelector("#menu")!;
const extra = document.createElement("li");          // a new element, not yet on the page
extra.textContent = "Lemon tea";
extra.className = "item new";
menu.appendChild(extra);                             // now it is in the tree (and on screen)
document.querySelector("h1")!.textContent = "Chai Point (open)";
console.log(document.querySelectorAll(".item").length, "items");
console.log(menu.innerHTML.replace(/\s+</g, "<"));
```

**Output:**

```text
3 items
<li class="item">Masala chai</li><li class="item">Ginger chai</li><li class="item new">Lemon tea</li>
```

`querySelectorAll(".item")` returns every element with class `item`; the `!` after `querySelector(...)` tells TypeScript "I know this exists" (it would otherwise warn that it might be `null`, Section [26](#26-typescript-with-react-typing-props-state-events-and-children)).

**Events and bubbling:** one click on the `li` reaches listeners on the `li`, the `ul` and the wrapper `div`:

```tsx
const firstItem = document.querySelector("li")!;
for (const el of [firstItem, document.querySelector("ul")!, document.querySelector("#app")!]) {
  el.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
    const target = event.target as Element, current = event.currentTarget as Element;
    console.log(`listener on <${current.tagName.toLowerCase()}> heard a click that started on <${target.tagName.toLowerCase()}>`);
  });
}
firstItem.click();                                   // simulate a user's click
```

**Output:**

```text
listener on <li> heard a click that started on <li>
listener on <ul> heard a click that started on <li>
listener on <div> heard a click that started on <li>
```

**Default actions:** submitting a form normally reloads the page; `preventDefault()` stops that so your code can handle the data:

```tsx
document.body.innerHTML = `<form><input name="item" value="Masala chai"><button>Order</button></form>`;
const form = document.querySelector("form")!;
form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();                            // no page reload
  const data = new FormData(form);
  console.log("ordering:", data.get("item"), "| default prevented:", event.defaultPrevented);
});
document.querySelector("button")!.click();          // clicking a submit button submits the form
```

**Output:**

```text
ordering: Masala chai | default prevented: true
```

`FormData` reads every named input of a form; React 19's form actions use exactly this object (Section [53](#53-react-19-forms-actions-useactionstate-useformstatus-and-useoptimistic)).

### Practice

1. Write `countTags(root)` that returns an object counting elements by tag name below `root`, e.g. `{ h1: 1, ul: 1, li: 2 }`.
2. A listener on `<ul>` logs `event.target.tagName`. The user clicks the text inside the second `<li>`. What is logged, and why isn't it `UL`?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function countTags(root: Element): Record<string, number> {
  const counts: Record<string, number> = {};
  for (const el of root.querySelectorAll("*")) {
    const tag = el.tagName.toLowerCase();
    counts[tag] = (counts[tag] ?? 0) + 1;
  }
  return counts;
}
document.body.innerHTML = `<h1>Menu</h1><ul><li>A</li><li>B</li></ul>`;
console.log(countTags(document.body));
```

**Output:**

```text
{ h1: 1, ul: 1, li: 2 }
```

1. `querySelectorAll("*")` matches every descendant element; `?? 0` starts each count at zero (the `??` operator is explained in Section [3](#3-the-javascript-react-uses-arrow-functions-destructuring-spread-array-methods-and-modules)).
2. `LI`. The event **started** on the `li` (text nodes can't be targets, so the target is the element containing the text), and the `ul`'s listener hears it during bubbling. `event.currentTarget` would be the `ul`.

</details>

## 3. The JavaScript React Uses: Arrow Functions, Destructuring, Spread, Array Methods and Modules

![Each modern JavaScript feature and where React code uses it: destructuring for props, map for lists, spread for state updates, arrow functions for handlers, modules for component files](images/react/03-js-for-react.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** React code is ordinary modern JavaScript. A handful of features appear on almost every line: **arrow functions** (short functions), **destructuring** (pulling values out of objects), **spread** (copying objects and arrays with changes), **array methods** like `map` and `filter` (turning lists of data into lists of UI), the **ternary** and `&&` (choosing what to show), and **modules** (one component per file). Learn these well and React's syntax stops looking strange.

**Words to know:**

- **Variable (`const` / `let`):** a name for a value. `const` can't be reassigned (use it by default); `let` can. (Old `var` has confusing scoping; don't use it.)
- **Function / parameter / argument / return value:** a reusable block of code; **parameters** are the names in its definition, **arguments** the values passed in a call, and the **return value** what it hands back.
- **Arrow function:** a shorter function syntax: `(a, b) => a + b`. With braces you need `return`: `(a, b) => { return a + b; }`.
- **Object / property:** a group of named values `{ name: "Chai", price: 180 }`; each name–value pair is a **property**, read with `obj.name`.
- **Array:** an ordered list `[10, 20, 30]`; items are read by **index** from 0: `arr[0]`.
- **Template literal:** a string in backticks that can embed values: `` `₹${price}` ``.
- **Destructuring:** unpacking values into variables: `const { name, price } = item;` and `const [first, second] = list;`. React props and `useState` both use it.
- **Default value:** a fallback used when a value is `undefined`: `function f({ size = "md" }) {}`.
- **Spread syntax (`...`):** copies the items of an array or properties of an object into a new one: `[...list, 4]`, `{ ...user, age: 31 }`.
- **Rest syntax (`...`):** the reverse: gathers "everything else": `const { id, ...rest } = item;`.
- **Shallow copy:** a copy of the outer object only; nested objects inside are still **shared** with the original.
- **Reference vs value:** variables hold objects and arrays **by reference** (an arrow to the same object), so `a === b` is true only when both point to the **same** object, not when they merely look equal.
- **Mutation:** changing an object or array in place (`arr.push(x)`, `obj.n = 1`). React expects you **not** to mutate state; you create new objects instead (Section [17](#17-updating-objects-in-state)).
- **Immutability:** the habit of never changing existing data, only making changed copies.
- **`map` / `filter` / `find` / `some` / `reduce`:** array methods that return a **new** array of transformed items / a new array of items that pass a test / the first item that passes / whether any passes / one value accumulated from all items.
- **`toSorted` / `toReversed` / `with`:** newer (ES2023) array methods that return a changed **copy** instead of mutating, perfect for React state.
- **Ternary operator:** `condition ? a : b` (an `if/else` that produces a value).
- **Logical AND (`&&`) / nullish coalescing (`??`) / optional chaining (`?.`):** `a && b` gives `b` when `a` is truthy, else `a`; `a ?? b` gives `b` only when `a` is `null` or `undefined`; `user?.address?.city` gives `undefined` instead of crashing when something along the way is missing.
- **Truthy / falsy:** values treated as `true` or `false` in conditions. The falsy ones are `false`, `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`; everything else is truthy.
- **Module / `import` / `export`:** each file is a module; `export` makes a value available, `import` brings it into another file. A file has at most one **default export** (`export default App`, imported without braces) and any number of **named exports** (`export function Button`, imported as `{ Button }`).

**Everyday picture.** A recipe card. **Destructuring** is reading just the lines you need ("flour, sugar"); **spread** is photocopying the card and writing one change on the copy, so the original stays clean; **map** is "do this to every ingredient"; **filter** is "only the vegetarian ones"; a **module** is a recipe kept in its own folder so any kitchen can borrow it.

**Why references matter for React, traced by hand:**

```text
const cart = ["chai"];           cart ──► ["chai"]
const same = cart;               same ──┘            (same arrow, same array)
same.push("samosa");             the ONE array is now ["chai", "samosa"]
cart === same                    → true  (React can't tell anything changed!)

const next = [...cart, "vada"];  next ──► ["chai", "samosa", "vada"]   (a NEW array)
next === cart                    → false (React sees a new value and re-renders)
```

React decides whether state changed by comparing with `Object.is` (essentially `===`). Mutating keeps the same reference, so React thinks nothing happened; a new copy has a new reference. This one fact explains a whole family of React bugs.

**When to use which:** `map` to turn data into UI (every list), `filter` to remove an item, spread to change one property, `find` to look one item up, `reduce` for totals. **When not:** don't use `forEach` + `push` to build lists in components (it mutates and returns nothing), and don't reach for `reduce` when a `for` loop or a `map` + sum reads more clearly.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ `arr.sort()` or `arr.reverse()` on state: both **mutate** the original. ✅ `arr.toSorted()`, `[...arr].reverse()`.
- ❌ Arrow function with braces but no `return`: `items.map((x) => { x * 2 })` gives `[undefined, …]`.
- ❌ Thinking spread copies deeply: `{ ...user }` still shares `user.address`.
- ❌ `count && <p>…</p>` when `count` can be `0`: `0` is falsy but still a value, so `0` is what you get (and React shows it, Section [11](#11-conditional-rendering)).
- ❌ Mixing up default and named imports: `import Button from "./Button"` when the file did `export function Button`.

**Used in real software:** every React codebase; these exact patterns (`map` for lists, spread for updates, destructured props) are on almost every line.

### Code

**Arrow functions, template literals and destructuring:**

```tsx
const formatRupees = (paise: number) => `₹${(paise / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
const item = { name: "Masala chai", pricePaise: 18000, tags: ["tea", "spiced"] };

const { name, pricePaise, rating = 4.5 } = item as typeof item & { rating?: number };   // rating has a default
const [firstTag, ...otherTags] = item.tags;                                             // array destructuring + rest
console.log(name, formatRupees(pricePaise), rating, firstTag, otherTags);

function describe({ name, tags }: { name: string; tags: string[] }) {   // destructuring right in the parameter
  return `${name} (${tags.join(", ")})`;
}
console.log(describe(item));
```

**Output:**

```text
Masala chai ₹180.00 4.5 tea [ 'spiced' ]
Masala chai (tea, spiced)
```

`toFixed(2)` formats a number with exactly two decimals; prices are kept in **paise** (whole numbers) because decimal fractions like 0.1 can't be stored exactly in binary.

**Spread makes copies; mutation changes the original.** This is the single most important JavaScript fact for React:

```tsx
const cart = ["chai"];
const same = cart;
same.push("samosa");                                 // mutation through another name
console.log(cart, "| same object?", cart === same);

const next = [...cart, "vada pav"];                  // a new array
console.log(next, "| same object?", next === cart);

const user = { name: "Asha", address: { city: "Pune" } };
const copy = { ...user, name: "Ravi" };              // shallow copy with one change
copy.address.city = "Mumbai";                        // nested object is SHARED
console.log(user.address.city, "| deep-copied?", copy.address !== user.address);

const safe = { ...user, address: { ...user.address, city: "Delhi" } };   // copy every level you change
console.log(user.address.city, safe.address.city);
```

**Output:**

```text
[ 'chai', 'samosa' ] | same object? true
[ 'chai', 'samosa', 'vada pav' ] | same object? false
Mumbai | deep-copied? false
Mumbai Delhi
```

The third line of output is the classic trap: changing the copy's address also changed the original, because spread only copies one level.

**Array methods: the tools for turning data into UI:**

```tsx
const menu = [
  { id: 1, name: "Masala chai", pricePaise: 18000, veg: true },
  { id: 2, name: "Chicken roll", pricePaise: 22000, veg: false },
  { id: 3, name: "Samosa", pricePaise: 6000, veg: true },
];
console.log(menu.map((m) => m.name));                              // transform each
console.log(menu.filter((m) => m.veg).map((m) => m.id));            // keep some
console.log(menu.find((m) => m.id === 3)?.name);                    // look one up
console.log(menu.some((m) => !m.veg), menu.every((m) => m.pricePaise > 5000));
console.log(menu.reduce((sum, m) => sum + m.pricePaise, 0));        // total
const byPrice = menu.toSorted((a, b) => a.pricePaise - b.pricePaise);   // sorted COPY
console.log(byPrice.map((m) => m.name), "| original first:", menu[0].name);
console.log(menu.with(1, { ...menu[1], pricePaise: 20000 })[1].pricePaise, menu[1].pricePaise);
```

**Output:**

```text
[ 'Masala chai', 'Chicken roll', 'Samosa' ]
[ 1, 3 ]
Samosa
true true
46000
[ 'Samosa', 'Masala chai', 'Chicken roll' ] | original first: Masala chai
20000 22000
```

`toSorted` and `with(index, value)` return new arrays and leave `menu` untouched; the comparison function `(a, b) => a - b` sorts numbers ascending (a negative result puts `a` first).

**Choosing values: ternary, `&&`, `??` and `?.`:**

```tsx
const order = { items: 0, coupon: null as string | null, user: { address: undefined as { city: string } | undefined } };
console.log(order.items > 0 ? "Checkout" : "Cart is empty");
console.log(order.items && "has items");             // 0 && ... → 0  (not false!)
console.log(order.coupon ?? "no coupon");            // null → fallback
const zero = 0 as number | null;
console.log(zero ?? 5, zero || 5);                    // ?? keeps 0; || does not
console.log(order.user.address?.city);               // undefined instead of a crash
```

**Output:**

```text
Cart is empty
0
no coupon
0 5
undefined
```

**Modules:** a component library file exports, and another file imports. Here a file is written next to the example and then imported:

```tsx
export const formatRupees = (paise: number) => `₹${(paise / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
export default function total(prices: number[]) {
  return prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0);
}
```

```tsx
import total, { formatRupees as fmt } from "./money.ts";
console.log(fmt(total([18000, 6000])));
```

**Output:**

```text
₹240.00
```

`total` (no braces) is the default export; `{ formatRupees as fmt }` is a named export renamed on import. Real projects usually leave out the `.ts` extension (`"./money"`); the bundler finds the file.

### Practice

1. Given `const cart = [{ id: 1, qty: 2 }, { id: 2, qty: 1 }]`, write one expression that returns a **new** cart where item 2 has `qty: 5`, without mutating `cart`.
2. What does `[1, 2, 3].map((n) => { n * 2 })` return, and how do you fix it?
3. Remove the item with `id: 1` from `cart` immutably, and compute the total quantity of the original cart.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
const cart2 = [{ id: 1, qty: 2 }, { id: 2, qty: 1 }];
const updated = cart2.map((line) => (line.id === 2 ? { ...line, qty: 5 } : line));
console.log(updated, cart2[1].qty);
console.log([1, 2, 3].map((n) => { n * 2; }), [1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2));
console.log(cart2.filter((line) => line.id !== 1), cart2.reduce((sum, line) => sum + line.qty, 0));
```

**Output:**

```text
[ { id: 1, qty: 2 }, { id: 2, qty: 5 } ] 1
[ undefined, undefined, undefined ] [ 2, 4, 6 ]
[ { id: 2, qty: 1 } ] 3
```

1. `map` + spread: copy only the line you change, keep the others as they are. This is the standard "update one item" pattern (Section [18](#18-updating-arrays-in-state)).
2. `[undefined, undefined, undefined]`: braces start a function body, which needs `return`. Drop the braces (or add `return`).
3. `filter` keeps everything except id 1; `reduce` sums from a starting value of 0.

</details>

## 4. Asynchronous JavaScript for React: Promises, async/await and fetch

![The event loop: synchronous code runs first on the call stack, then promise callbacks (microtasks), then timers and network callbacks (tasks); fetch returns a promise that settles later](images/react/04-event-loop.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** some work takes time: waiting for a server, a timer, a file. JavaScript doesn't stop and wait; it **starts** the work, carries on, and runs your code **later** when the result is ready. A **promise** is an IOU for that future result, and `async`/`await` lets you write "wait for this, then continue" in normal top-to-bottom style. React apps use this constantly to load data, so understanding *when* code runs prevents a whole class of bugs.

**Words to know:**

- **Synchronous / asynchronous:** synchronous code runs line by line, each line finishing before the next; asynchronous work finishes **later**, while other code keeps running.
- **Callback:** a function you hand to something else to be called later: `setTimeout(callback, 1000)`.
- **Call stack:** the list of functions currently running; JavaScript runs one thing at a time on a single thread.
- **Event loop:** the mechanism that, whenever the call stack is empty, picks the next waiting callback and runs it.
- **Task (macrotask) / microtask:** two queues of waiting callbacks. Timers, clicks and network events are **tasks**; promise callbacks (`then`, code after `await`) are **microtasks**, and all waiting microtasks run before the next task.
- **Promise:** an object representing a value that isn't ready yet; it is **pending**, then either **fulfilled** (with a value) or **rejected** (with an error). Fulfilled or rejected = **settled**.
- **`then` / `catch` / `finally`:** methods that register callbacks for when a promise fulfils, rejects, or settles either way.
- **`async` function:** a function that always returns a promise and may use `await` inside.
- **`await`:** pauses the `async` function until a promise settles, then gives its value (or throws its error) so you can use `try/catch`.
- **`fetch`:** the built-in function for HTTP requests; returns a promise of a **Response**.
- **HTTP request / response / status code:** a request asks a server for something (`GET /api/menu`); the response carries a status code (`200` OK, `404` Not Found, `500` Server Error) and a body.
- **API (application programming interface):** a defined way for programs to talk; for web apps, usually URLs that return JSON.
- **JSON (JavaScript Object Notation):** the text format APIs use for data: `{"name":"Chai","price":180}`. `JSON.parse` turns text into objects; `JSON.stringify` the reverse; `response.json()` reads and parses a response body.
- **`response.ok`:** `true` for statuses 200–299. `fetch` does **not** reject on 404 or 500, so you must check it.
- **`Promise.all`:** waits for several promises **in parallel** and gives all results (or the first error).
- **`AbortController` / `AbortSignal`:** a way to cancel a `fetch` (or other work): pass `controller.signal`, then call `controller.abort()`.
- **Race condition:** a bug where the result depends on which of several async operations finishes first, e.g. an old, slow search response overwriting a newer one.

**Everyday picture.** Ordering at a busy chai stall: you pay and get a **token** (the promise). You don't stand frozen at the counter; you chat with friends (other code keeps running). When your number is called (the promise fulfils), you collect your chai (the value). If they've run out, they call your number and say so (the promise rejects). `await` is deciding to stand by the counter until your number comes up.

**Predicting the order, traced by hand:**

```text
console.log("1 sync");
setTimeout(() => console.log("4 timer (task)"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3 promise (microtask)"));
console.log("2 sync");
```

1. Line 1 runs immediately → `1 sync`.
2. `setTimeout(…, 0)` puts its callback in the **task** queue; it does not run yet.
3. `then` puts its callback in the **microtask** queue.
4. Line 4 runs → `2 sync`. The stack is now empty.
5. The event loop runs **all microtasks first** → `3 promise`.
6. Then the next task → `4 timer`. A delay of 0 means "as soon as possible after everything else", never "now".

**When to use what:** `async`/`await` with `try/catch` for readable sequential steps; `Promise.all` when requests don't depend on each other (much faster than awaiting one by one); `AbortController` when a request may become irrelevant (the user typed again, the component disappeared). **When not:** don't `await` inside a loop for independent requests (it serialises them), and don't fire requests without handling the error case.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Assuming `fetch` throws on 404/500. ✅ Check `response.ok`.
- ❌ Forgetting `await` (`const data = response.json()` gives a promise, not data).
- ❌ Awaiting independent requests one after another. ✅ `Promise.all`.
- ❌ Ignoring out-of-order responses: the last request **sent** is not always the last to **arrive** (Section [34](#34-fetching-data-in-effects-loading-errors-race-conditions-and-abortcontroller)).

**Used in real software:** every React app that loads data; libraries such as TanStack Query (Section [52](#52-server-state-with-tanstack-query)) and React's `use` and Suspense (Section [47](#47-code-splitting-lazy-suspense-and-bundle-size)) are built on promises.

### Code

**The event loop order** from the trace above, run for real:

```tsx
console.log("1 sync");
setTimeout(() => console.log("4 timer (task)"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3 promise (microtask)"));
console.log("2 sync");
await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 10));   // wait so the timer prints before the next block
```

**Output:**

```text
1 sync
2 sync
3 promise (microtask)
4 timer (task)
```

`await` at the top level of a module (outside any function) is allowed in modern JavaScript modules, which is what these examples are.

**From scratch: a fake API with promises and `setTimeout`.** This is how you test loading states before a real server exists:

```tsx
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function fakeMenuApi(shouldFail = false) {
  await sleep(50);                                    // pretend the network takes 50 ms
  if (shouldFail) throw new Error("Server is down");
  return [{ id: 1, name: "Masala chai" }, { id: 2, name: "Samosa" }];
}

const started = Date.now();
const menu = await fakeMenuApi();
console.log(menu.map((m) => m.name), `after ~${Math.round((Date.now() - started) / 10) * 10} ms`);
try {
  await fakeMenuApi(true);
} catch (error) {
  console.log("caught:", (error as Error).message);
}
```

**Output:**

```text
[ 'Masala chai', 'Samosa' ] after ~50 ms
caught: Server is down
```

**The real way: `fetch` against an HTTP server.** To keep the example self-contained, it starts a tiny local server with Node's built-in `http` module (the kind of server `nodejs.md` teaches) and then calls it exactly as a browser would:

```tsx
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  if (req.url === "/api/menu") {
    res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    res.end(JSON.stringify([{ id: 1, name: "Masala chai", pricePaise: 18000 }]));
  } else {
    res.writeHead(404).end("Not found");
  }
});
await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.listen(4401, resolve));

const ok = await fetch("http://localhost:4401/api/menu");
console.log(ok.status, ok.ok, await ok.json());

const missing = await fetch("http://localhost:4401/api/nope");
console.log(missing.status, missing.ok, "← fetch did NOT throw");
```

**Output:**

```text
200 true [ { id: 1, name: 'Masala chai', pricePaise: 18000 } ]
404 false ← fetch did NOT throw
```

**Parallel requests and cancelling:**

```tsx
async function getJson(path: string, signal?: AbortSignal) {
  const response = await fetch(`http://localhost:4401${path}`, { signal });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status} for ${path}`);
  return response.json();
}

const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getJson("/api/menu"), getJson("/api/menu")]);   // both at once
console.log("parallel:", a.length + b.length, "items");

try {
  await getJson("/api/nope");
} catch (error) {
  console.log("error:", (error as Error).message);
}

const controller = new AbortController();
const pending = getJson("/api/menu", controller.signal);
controller.abort();                                   // the user navigated away, say
try {
  await pending;
} catch (error) {
  console.log("aborted:", (error as Error).name);
}
server.close();
```

**Output:**

```text
parallel: 2 items
error: HTTP 404 for /api/nope
aborted: AbortError
```

A cancelled `fetch` rejects with an error named `AbortError`; code that cancels on purpose usually ignores exactly that error.

**A race condition in miniature:** two searches are sent; the first is slow and arrives **last**, overwriting the newer result:

```tsx
let shown = "";
async function search(query: string, delayMs: number) {
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  shown = `results for "${query}"`;                   // whoever finishes last wins
}
await Promise.all([search("ch", 80), search("chai", 20)]);   // user typed "ch", then "chai"
console.log(shown, "← stale: the user asked for chai");
```

**Output:**

```text
results for "ch" ← stale: the user asked for chai
```

React apps meet this bug when loading data as the user types; Section [34](#34-fetching-data-in-effects-loading-errors-race-conditions-and-abortcontroller) fixes it with an "ignore stale results" flag and `AbortController`.

### Practice

1. Predict the output order: `console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B")); queueMicrotask(() => console.log("C")); (async () => { console.log("D"); await null; console.log("E"); })(); console.log("F");`
2. Write `withTimeout(promise, ms)` that rejects with `Error("timeout")` if `promise` hasn't settled within `ms`.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B")); queueMicrotask(() => console.log("C"));
(async () => { console.log("D"); await null; console.log("E"); })();
console.log("F");
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 5));

function withTimeout<T>(promise: Promise<T>, ms: number): Promise<T> {
  return Promise.race([promise, new Promise<T>((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error("timeout")), ms))]);
}
console.log(await withTimeout(Promise.resolve("fast"), 50));
try { await withTimeout(new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100)), 20); } catch (e) { console.log((e as Error).message); }
```

**Output:**

```text
A
D
F
C
E
B
fast
timeout
```

1. `A D F C E B`: `A`, `D` (an async function runs synchronously until its first `await`) and `F` are synchronous; then microtasks in the order they were queued (`C`, then the rest of the async function, `E`); then the timer task `B`.
2. `Promise.race` settles with whichever promise settles first: the real one or the timer that rejects. (`<T>` makes the function generic, so it keeps the promise's type; Section [26](#26-typescript-with-react-typing-props-state-events-and-children).)

</details>

## 5. Why React? Updating a Page by Hand vs Describing It

![Imperative code lists the steps to change the page; declarative code describes the page for the current state and lets React work out the steps: UI = f(state)](images/react/05-imperative-declarative.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** without React you write **step-by-step instructions** to change the page ("find the counter, change its text, if it's 0 hide the badge, add a row to the list…"). With React you write **one function that describes the whole UI for the current data**, and when the data changes React works out which DOM changes are needed. The first style is **imperative**, the second **declarative**, and declarative code stays correct as apps grow.

**Words to know:**

- **Imperative:** code that says **how**, step by step: "create an `li`, set its text, append it".
- **Declarative:** code that says **what** the result should be: "the list shows one `li` per item".
- **State:** data that changes while the app runs (the cart's items, the text in a search box, whether a menu is open).
- **UI = f(state):** React's core idea: the screen is the output of a function of the state. Same state in, same UI out.
- **Re-render:** calling the component function again after state changes to get the new description of the UI.
- **Virtual DOM:** React's lightweight description of the UI (plain JavaScript objects). React compares the new description with the previous one and changes only the real DOM nodes that differ (Section [42](#42-the-virtual-dom-and-reconciliation-build-a-mini-react-from-scratch)).
- **Reconciliation:** that comparing-and-updating process.
- **Single-page application (SPA):** a site that loads one HTML page and then updates it with JavaScript instead of loading new pages from the server.
- **Ecosystem:** the libraries, tools, frameworks, tutorials and jobs around a technology; React's is the largest of any UI library.

**Everyday picture.** A **satellite navigator** vs **turn-by-turn directions written on paper**. With paper directions (imperative), one wrong turn or road closure and every later instruction is wrong. With a navigator (declarative), you state the **destination**; it recalculates the route from wherever you are. In React you state the destination screen for the current data, and React recalculates the DOM changes.

**The problem, traced by hand.** A "cart" widget shows a count, a list, and a "Checkout" button that should be disabled when empty. With imperative code, adding an item needs **three** separate DOM updates (count text, new `li`, button state) and removing an item needs three different ones. Add a total, a "free delivery over ₹500" banner and a badge in the header, and every new feature multiplies the places you must remember to update. Forget one and the screen **contradicts itself** (the badge says 2, the list shows 3).

The obvious fix is to **redraw everything from the data** on every change (`container.innerHTML = renderPage(state)`). That's declarative, but rebuilding the DOM throws away things the DOM was holding: what's typed in inputs, focus, scroll position, and it's slow for big pages. The code below shows the typed text being lost.

React gives you the **best of both**: you write the "redraw everything" style, and React's reconciliation applies only the minimal changes, so inputs keep their text and focus.

**When React fits:** interactive UIs where many parts depend on shared, changing data (dashboards, editors, shops, chat apps), teams that want reusable components, and apps that also need mobile (React Native). **When it doesn't:** mostly static content (use plain HTML or a static-site tool), a tiny enhancement to a server-rendered page (a few lines of plain JavaScript), or when page weight must be minimal (React DOM adds tens of kilobytes; Section [47](#47-code-splitting-lazy-suspense-and-bundle-size)).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Mixing styles: changing the DOM by hand **inside** a React app (React will overwrite or fight your changes).
- ❌ Thinking React is "fast because of the virtual DOM". It's **predictable** because of it; raw hand-written DOM updates can be faster, but are much harder to keep correct.
- ❌ Choosing React for a five-page brochure site.

**Used in real software:** the declarative "UI = f(state)" model, made popular by React, is now used by Vue, Svelte, SolidJS, Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose.

### Code

**From scratch, imperative:** every change needs its own DOM steps, and the parts must be kept in sync by hand:

```tsx
document.body.innerHTML = `<p id="count">0 items</p><ul id="list"></ul><button id="checkout" disabled>Checkout</button>`;
const items: string[] = [];

function addItemImperative(name: string) {
  items.push(name);
  const li = document.createElement("li");                                   // step 1: new row
  li.textContent = name;
  document.querySelector("#list")!.appendChild(li);
  document.querySelector("#count")!.textContent = `${items.length} items`;   // step 2: count
  (document.querySelector("#checkout") as HTMLButtonElement).disabled = false;   // step 3: button
}
addItemImperative("Masala chai");
addItemImperative("Samosa");
console.log(document.body.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<p id="count">2 items</p><ul id="list"><li>Masala chai</li><li>Samosa</li></ul><button id="checkout">Checkout</button>
```

**From scratch, declarative:** one `render` function builds the whole UI from the state. Simple and always consistent, but watch what happens to text the user has typed:

```tsx
const state = { items: ["Masala chai"], note: "" };
const renderPage = () => `
  <p>${state.items.length} items</p>
  <input id="note" placeholder="Delivery note">
  <ul>${state.items.map((i) => `<li>${i}</li>`).join("")}</ul>`;

document.body.innerHTML = renderPage();
const note = document.querySelector("#note") as HTMLInputElement;
note.value = "Ring the bell twice";                 // the user types a note…
state.items.push("Samosa");                         // …then adds an item, and we redraw everything
document.body.innerHTML = renderPage();
const noteAfter = document.querySelector("#note") as HTMLInputElement;
console.log(`note after redraw: "${noteAfter.value}" | same input element? ${noteAfter === note}`);
```

**Output:**

```text
note after redraw: "" | same input element? false
```

The redraw created a **brand-new** input, so the user's note vanished (and in a real browser, focus too).

**The React way:** the same "describe everything" code, but React updates only what changed, so the input survives:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function Cart() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState(["Masala chai"]);
  return (
    <div>
      <p>{items.length} items</p>
      <input placeholder="Delivery note" />
      <ul>{items.map((item) => <li key={item}>{item}</li>)}</ul>
      <button onClick={() => setItems([...items, "Samosa"])}>Add samosa</button>
      <button disabled={items.length === 0}>Checkout</button>
    </div>
  );
}

render(<Cart />);
const input = screen.getByPlaceholderText("Delivery note") as HTMLInputElement;
fireEvent.change(input, { target: { value: "Ring the bell twice" } });   // the user types
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Add samosa"));                           // state changes, React re-renders
const inputAfter = screen.getByPlaceholderText("Delivery note") as HTMLInputElement;
console.log(`note: "${inputAfter.value}" | same input element? ${inputAfter === input}`);
console.log(screen.getAllByRole("listitem").map((li) => li.textContent), "|", screen.getByText(/items$/).textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
note: "Ring the bell twice" | same input element? true
[ 'Masala chai', 'Samosa' ] | 2 items
```

Every piece of this (`useState`, `onClick`, `key`, `render`, `screen`, `fireEvent`) is explained in the coming sections; for now notice the result: we described the whole UI, yet React kept the **same** input element and the typed note.

### Practice

1. In the imperative example, add a `removeItemImperative(name)` function. List every DOM update it must make. Which one is easiest to forget?
2. Name one thing besides typed text that a full `innerHTML` redraw destroys.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. Remove the matching `li`, update the count text, and **disable the button when the cart becomes empty**: the last one is the classic forgotten step, leaving an enabled Checkout on an empty cart.
2. Any of: keyboard focus, text selection, scroll position inside a list, a playing video's position, CSS transitions in progress, and event listeners attached directly to old elements.

</details>

## 6. Setting Up: Node, npm, Vite and How These Examples Run

![Anatomy of a Vite React project: index.html loads main.tsx, which mounts App into the root div; the dev server serves files with hot reload, and the build bundles everything into dist](images/react/06-project-anatomy.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** to build React apps you need **Node.js** (runs JavaScript tools on your computer), **npm** (downloads libraries), and a build tool, usually **Vite** (serves your app while you work and bundles it for production). `npm create vite@latest` makes a ready-to-run project. These notes run every example in Node instead of a browser, using a simulated page (jsdom) and **Testing Library** to look at what React rendered and to click buttons like a user.

**Words to know:**

- **Node.js:** a program that runs JavaScript outside the browser; development tools (Vite, TypeScript, test runners) run on it.
- **npm (Node Package Manager):** the tool and online registry for JavaScript libraries (**packages**). `npm install react` downloads React into your project.
- **`package.json`:** the project's manifest: its name, **scripts** (`npm run dev`) and **dependencies**.
- **Dependency / devDependency:** a package the app needs at runtime (React) / a package only needed while developing or building (Vite, TypeScript, test tools).
- **`node_modules`:** the folder where npm puts installed packages (never edit it, never commit it).
- **Lock file (`package-lock.json`):** records the exact version of every installed package so every machine installs the same ones.
- **Semantic versioning (semver):** versions written `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` (19.3.1); `^19.2.8` in `package.json` means "19.2.8 or any later 19.x".
- **npx / `npm create`:** run a package's command without installing it permanently; `npm create vite@latest` runs Vite's project generator.
- **Vite:** the standard build tool for React apps: a **dev server** with instant reloads, and a production **build**.
- **Dev server:** a local web server (`http://localhost:5173`) that serves your app while you develop.
- **Hot module replacement (HMR) / Fast Refresh:** when you save a file, only that module is swapped in the running page, and React keeps component state.
- **Bundler / build:** combines your many source files and libraries into a few optimised files (`dist/`), transforming TypeScript and JSX into plain JavaScript.
- **Entry point:** the first file that runs (`src/main.tsx`), which starts the app.
- **Root element / `createRoot`:** the empty `<div id="root">` in `index.html`; `createRoot(element).render(<App />)` tells React to manage everything inside it.
- **`StrictMode`:** a development-only wrapper that runs extra checks (it renders components twice and runs effects twice to expose bugs; Section [31](#31-the-lifecycle-of-an-effect-dependencies-cleanup-and-strict-mode)).
- **`.tsx` file:** a TypeScript file that may contain JSX.
- **Linter (oxlint / ESLint):** a tool that reads code and warns about likely bugs and style problems; the React Hooks lint rules catch many React mistakes (Section [39](#39-how-hooks-work-inside-build-usestate-from-scratch-and-the-rules-of-hooks)).
- **jsdom:** a JavaScript implementation of the browser DOM that runs in Node; tests and these notes render React into it.
- **Testing Library (`render`, `screen`, `fireEvent`):** helpers to render a component into jsdom (`render`), find things on the page as a user would (`screen.getByRole("button")`, `screen.getByText(...)`), and fire events (`fireEvent.click(button)`). Section [56](#56-testing-components-vitest-testing-library-and-user-event) covers it properly.
- **`act`:** React's testing helper that runs updates and effects to completion before you look at the page; Testing Library calls it for you.

**Everyday picture.** A restaurant kitchen. **Node** is the kitchen itself (where the work happens), **npm** is the supplier who delivers ingredients (packages) listed on your order sheet (`package.json`), **Vite's dev server** is tasting as you cook (instant feedback), and **the build** is plating the final dishes neatly for customers (`dist/`).

**What happens when the page loads, traced:**

1. The browser requests `index.html`, which contains `<div id="root"></div>` and `<script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx">`.
2. Vite transforms `main.tsx` (TypeScript + JSX → JavaScript) on the fly and sends it.
3. `main.tsx` calls `createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!)` and `.render(<StrictMode><App /></StrictMode>)`.
4. React calls `App()`, gets its description of the UI, and creates the real DOM nodes inside `#root`.
5. You save `App.tsx` → Vite sends just that module → Fast Refresh re-renders `App`, keeping state.

**Which starter to use (2026):**

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| to learn React, or a client-side app (dashboards, internal tools) | **Vite**: `npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts` |
| a full product with server rendering, SEO, API routes | **Next.js** (`npx create-next-app@latest`, Part 9) or **React Router** framework mode |
| mobile apps | **Expo** (React Native) |

Create React App (the old official starter) was deprecated in February 2025; don't start new projects with it.

**How the examples in these notes run.** Every `tsx` block is run with Node.js 24 through a small loader (`tsx`) that understands TypeScript and JSX, after this setup file, which creates the simulated page:

```text
// setup.ts: loaded before every example
import "global-jsdom/register";                      // a fake browser page: document, window, events
import { format } from "node:util";
(globalThis as any).IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true; // tells React updates are wrapped in act()
for (const name of ["FormData", "Event", "CustomEvent", "navigator"])  // Node has its own versions;
  Object.defineProperty(globalThis, name, { value: window[name], configurable: true, writable: true });  // use the page's
for (const level of ["error", "warn"] as const)      // show warnings in the output, one line each
  console[level] = (...args) => process.stdout.write(`console.${level}: ${format(...args).split("\n")[0]}\n`);
```

Blocks in one section form one file (so they share variables, like notebook cells); before each block the page is emptied (Testing Library's `cleanup()` unmounts what was rendered and `document.body` is cleared), the way a test runner resets between tests, unless a block continues the previous one. To run an example yourself: `npm install react react-dom` and `npm install -D typescript tsx global-jsdom jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/dom @types/react @types/react-dom`, save the code (plus the setup file) and run `node --import tsx --import ./setup.ts example.tsx`.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Starting with Create React App (deprecated).
- ❌ Committing `node_modules` (huge, machine-specific). ✅ Commit `package.json` and the lock file.
- ❌ Opening `index.html` directly from disk instead of running the dev server; modules and JSX need Vite.
- ❌ Deleting `StrictMode` to "fix" double logs; the double run is a development check, not a bug (Section [31](#31-the-lifecycle-of-an-effect-dependencies-cleanup-and-strict-mode)).

**Used in real software:** Vite is the default for new client-side React apps and is used under the hood by React Router's framework mode, Vitest, Storybook and Astro; Next.js uses its own bundler, Turbopack.

### Code

**Creating a project for real.** This shell block scaffolds a Vite + React + TypeScript project with Vite's official generator, then lists what it made:

```bash
npm create vite@9.2.1 shop -- --template react-ts --no-interactive < /dev/null > /dev/null 2>&1
cd shop && find . -type f -not -path "./src/assets/*" -not -path "./public/*" | sort
node -e "const p = require('./package.json'); console.log('scripts:', p.scripts); console.log('dependencies:', p.dependencies)"
```

**Output:**

```text
./.gitignore
./.oxlintrc.json
./index.html
./package.json
./README.md
./src/App.css
./src/App.tsx
./src/index.css
./src/main.tsx
./tsconfig.app.json
./tsconfig.json
./tsconfig.node.json
./vite.config.ts
scripts: {
  dev: 'vite',
  build: 'tsc -b && vite build',
  lint: 'oxlint',
  preview: 'vite preview'
}
dependencies: { react: '^19.2.8', 'react-dom': '^19.2.8' }
```

`--no-interactive` skips the questions the generator normally asks. Two choices in today's template are worth noticing: it lints with **oxlint** (a very fast linter written in Rust) instead of ESLint, and its `build` script runs the TypeScript compiler (`tsc -b`) before `vite build`, so a type error fails the build.

**The entry point** it generated (`src/main.tsx`) is the four-step trace above in code:

```bash
cat shop/src/main.tsx
```

**Output:**

```text
import { StrictMode } from 'react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'
import './index.css'
import App from './App.tsx'

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <App />
  </StrictMode>,
)
```

**Installing and building:**

```bash
cd shop && npm install --no-audit --no-fund > /dev/null 2>&1 && npm run build 2>&1 | grep -v "^$" | sed -E 's/ in [0-9.]+m?s/ in (time)/'
```

**Output:**

```text
> shop@0.0.0 build
> tsc -b && vite build
vite v8.3.4 building client environment for production...
transforming...
✓ 20 modules transformed.
rendering chunks...
computing gzip size...
dist/index.html                   0.45 kB │ gzip:  0.29 kB
dist/assets/react-CHdo91hT.svg    4.12 kB │ gzip:  2.06 kB
dist/assets/vite-BF8QNONU.svg     8.70 kB │ gzip:  1.60 kB
dist/assets/hero-CLDdwZDr.png    13.05 kB
dist/assets/index-D64VDMd1.css    4.10 kB │ gzip:  1.47 kB
dist/assets/index-Cl6Bt99l.js   222.45 kB │ gzip: 69.28 kB
✓ built in (time)
```

The build produced an HTML file, one CSS file, the template's images and **one JavaScript bundle** of about 222 kB (69 kB after gzip compression, roughly what users download), most of which is React and React DOM themselves. (Timings vary per machine, so they're replaced with "(time)".)

**From scratch: mounting React by hand** into the simulated page, exactly what `main.tsx` does, with `act` making React finish its work before we look:

```tsx
import { act } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";

function App() {
  return <h1>Welcome to Chai Point ☕</h1>;
}

document.body.innerHTML = `<div id="root"></div>`;
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!);
await act(async () => root.render(<App />));
console.log(document.body.innerHTML);
await act(async () => root.unmount());              // remove the app again
console.log(document.body.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<div id="root"><h1>Welcome to Chai Point ☕</h1></div>
<div id="root"></div>
```

**The Testing Library way,** used in the rest of these notes: `render` does the mounting and `act` for you, and `screen` finds elements as a user would:

```tsx
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function Hello() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Welcome</h1>
      <button onClick={() => console.log("clicked!")}>Order chai</button>
    </main>
  );
}

const { container } = render(<Hello />);
console.log(container.innerHTML);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Order chai" }));
```

**Output:**

```text
<main><h1>Welcome</h1><button>Order chai</button></main>
clicked!
```

`container` is the `div` Testing Library rendered into; `getByRole("button", { name: … })` finds a button by its accessible name (its visible text here); `fireEvent.click` dispatches a real DOM click event.

import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import Shop from "./Shop";
createRoot(document.getElementById("app")!).render(<Shop />);

# Part 2 — Basic: Your First Components

> **Goal:** Write components, understand what JSX really is, pass data with props, keep components pure, show things conditionally, and render lists with correct keys. By the end you can turn any static design plus some data into a tree of React components.  
> **You need:** Part 1 (the DOM, arrow functions, destructuring, `map`, modules, and how the examples run).

## 7. Your First Component

![A component is a function that returns a description of UI; App uses Header and ProductCard, and React calls each function and builds the DOM from the results](images/react/07-component-tree.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** a **component** is a JavaScript function whose name starts with a **capital letter** and which **returns markup** (JSX). You use it like an HTML tag: `<Welcome />`. React calls your function and puts what it returns on the page. Components can use other components, so a whole app is a **tree** of them, and each one can be reused as many times as you like.

**Words to know:**

- **Function component:** a function that returns JSX (or `null`); the only kind of component new code uses (older **class components** are covered in Section [67](#67-legacy-react-class-components-lifecycles-hocs-and-render-props)).
- **JSX:** the HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript (`<h1>Hi</h1>`) that describes UI; Section [8](#8-jsx-markup-inside-javascript-and-what-it-compiles-to) shows what it turns into.
- **Rendering a component:** React calling your component function to find out what it should show.
- **Component tree:** the nesting of components: `App` renders `Header` and `ProductCard`, and so on down to plain HTML elements.
- **Parent / child component:** a component that renders another is its **parent**; the one rendered is the **child**.
- **Root component:** the top of the tree, usually `App`, passed to `createRoot(...).render(...)`.
- **PascalCase:** `ProductCard`: every word capitalised. React treats `<productCard>` (lowercase first letter) as an HTML tag, so components **must** start with a capital.
- **Default export / named export:** a file's one main export (`export default function App`) vs extra ones (`export function Button`); you can use either for components (Section [3](#3-the-javascript-react-uses-arrow-functions-destructuring-spread-array-methods-and-modules)).
- **Built-in (host) component:** a lowercase tag such as `<div>` or `<button>`, which React turns into a real DOM element.
- **Nesting vs defining inside:** you **use** components inside other components, but you **define** each one at the top level of a file, never inside another component's body.

**Everyday picture.** A restaurant menu card is printed from a template: the template (the component) has slots for the dish name and price; the printer (React) runs the template once per dish. You never redraw the card by hand; you change the template once and every card updates.

**How React renders a small tree, traced by hand:**

```text
function Price()  { return <strong>₹180</strong>; }
function Card()   { return <article><h2>Masala chai</h2><Price /></article>; }
function App()    { return <main><Card /><Card /></main>; }
```

1. React calls `App()` → gets a `main` containing two `Card` elements.
2. For the first `<Card />` it calls `Card()` → `article` with an `h2` and a `<Price />`.
3. It calls `Price()` → `strong` with "₹180". No more components, only HTML elements: done with this branch.
4. Same again for the second `<Card />`. React now has a full description made only of HTML elements and creates the DOM: `<main><article><h2>…</h2><strong>₹180</strong></article><article>…</article></main>`.

**When to make something a component:** when a piece of UI repeats (a card, a row), has its own job (a search box), or makes the parent hard to read. **When not:** don't wrap every single `<div>` in its own component; a component should be a meaningful, reusable piece.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Lowercase component names: `<welcome />` renders an unknown HTML tag called `welcome`.
- ❌ Forgetting `return`, or returning on the next line after a bare `return` (JavaScript inserts a semicolon after `return`, so nothing is returned). ✅ Put `(` on the same line: `return (`.
- ❌ Defining a component **inside** another component: it becomes a brand-new component on every render, so React throws away its DOM and state each time (Section [24](#24-preserving-and-resetting-state-tree-position-and-keys)).
- ❌ Returning two sibling elements without a wrapper (Section [8](#8-jsx-markup-inside-javascript-and-what-it-compiles-to) shows fragments).

**Used in real software:** every screen of every React app is a component tree; large apps have thousands of components, from tiny `Icon`s to whole `CheckoutPage`s, many coming from a shared design system (Section [66](#66-architecture-project-structure-design-systems-and-monorepos)).

### Code

**From scratch: a component is just a function.** You can call it yourself; what it returns is a plain object describing UI (an **element**), not DOM:

```tsx
function Welcome() {
  return <h1 className="title">Welcome to Chai Point ☕</h1>;
}

const element = Welcome();                            // call it like any function
console.log(typeof element, "| type:", element.type, "| props:", element.props);
```

**Output:**

```text
object | type: h1 | props: { className: 'title', children: 'Welcome to Chai Point ☕' }
```

The result is a small object: the tag (`type`) and its `props`, with the text inside as `children`. Nothing appears on any page until React **renders** it into a DOM.

**The React way: use components as tags, nest and reuse them:**

```tsx
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";

function Price() {
  return <strong>₹180</strong>;
}

function Card() {
  return (
    <article>
      <h2>Masala chai</h2>
      <Price />
    </article>
  );
}

function App() {
  return (
    <main>
      <Welcome />
      <Card />
      <Card />
    </main>
  );
}

const { container } = render(<App />);
console.log(container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<main><h1 class="title">Welcome to Chai Point ☕</h1><article><h2>Masala chai</h2><strong>₹180</strong></article><article><h2>Masala chai</h2><strong>₹180</strong></article></main>
```

Only HTML elements reach the page: `App`, `Card`, `Price` and `Welcome` disappear into what they return. The two cards are identical because `Card` has no inputs yet; props (Section [9](#9-props-passing-data-to-components)) fix that.

**Components in their own files.** Real projects put each component in a file and import it:

```tsx
export default function Badge() {
  return <span className="badge">Bestseller</span>;
}

export function NewBadge() {
  return <span className="badge new">New</span>;
}
```

```tsx
import Badge, { NewBadge } from "./Badge.tsx";

function Labels() {
  return (
    <p>
      <Badge /> <NewBadge />
    </p>
  );
}
console.log(render(<Labels />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<p><span class="badge">Bestseller</span> <span class="badge new">New</span></p>
```

Notice the space between the two badges survived: a space between two tags on the **same line** is kept, while line breaks and indentation between tags are removed.

**The mistake of the bare `return`:**

```tsx
function Broken() {
  return
    <p>never shown</p>;
}
console.log("Broken() returned:", Broken());
```

**Output:**

```text
Broken() returned: undefined
```

JavaScript ends the statement after a bare `return`, so the function returns `undefined` and the JSX below is never reached. (TypeScript would also flag the unreachable line in a normal project.)

### Practice

1. Write a `Header` component (an `h1` with your shop's name and a `p` tagline) and a `Footer` (a `small` with "© 2026"), and an `App` that renders `Header`, two `Card`s and `Footer`. Print the HTML.
2. What does React do with `<card />` written in lowercase?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function Header() {
  return (
    <header>
      <h1>Chai Point</h1>
      <p>Fresh chai in 20 minutes</p>
    </header>
  );
}
function Footer() {
  return <small>© 2026</small>;
}
function Shop() {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />
      <Card />
      <Card />
      <Footer />
    </>
  );
}
console.log(render(<Shop />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<header><h1>Chai Point</h1><p>Fresh chai in 20 minutes</p></header><article><h2>Masala chai</h2><strong>₹180</strong></article><article><h2>Masala chai</h2><strong>₹180</strong></article><small>© 2026</small>
```

1. `<>…</>` is a **fragment**: it groups elements without adding a wrapper element (Section [8](#8-jsx-markup-inside-javascript-and-what-it-compiles-to)).
2. It treats `card` as an HTML tag name and creates an unknown `<card>` element; your `Card` function is never called. (TypeScript also rejects `<card />` because it isn't a known HTML element.)

</details>
