## 8. JSX: Markup Inside JavaScript (and What It Compiles To)

![JSX is compiled into jsx() calls that build plain element objects; React reads those objects to create DOM nodes](images/react/08-jsx-compile.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** **JSX** looks like HTML but lives inside JavaScript. A build tool turns every JSX tag into a **function call** (`jsx("h1", { children: "Hi" })`) that returns a plain object describing the element. Anything inside **curly braces `{}`** is ordinary JavaScript: a variable, a calculation, a function call. JSX has a few differences from HTML (`className`, `htmlFor`, camelCase attributes, closing every tag), all because it is JavaScript underneath.

**Words to know:**

- **JSX (JavaScript XML):** a syntax extension that lets you write markup in JavaScript; it is not valid JavaScript until a compiler transforms it.
- **Compiler / transpiler:** a tool that rewrites code into another form; esbuild, SWC, Babel and TypeScript all compile JSX into function calls.
- **`jsx()` / `jsxs()` (the automatic runtime):** the functions JSX compiles into, imported automatically from `react/jsx-runtime` (`jsxs` is used when there are several static children). Older setups compiled to `React.createElement`, which is why old files start with `import React from "react"`.
- **React element:** the plain object a JSX expression produces: `{ type: "h1", props: { children: "Hi" }, key: null }`. Cheap to create and thrown away after each render.
- **`children`:** the special prop holding whatever is written between an element's opening and closing tags.
- **Expression vs statement:** an **expression** produces a value (`price * qty`, `a ? b : c`, `items.map(...)`) and can go inside `{}`; a **statement** does something (`if`, `for`, `const x = 1`) and cannot.
- **Fragment (`<>…</>` or `<Fragment>`):** groups several elements without adding a wrapper to the DOM. Use `<Fragment key={…}>` when it needs a key (Section [12](#12-rendering-lists-and-keys)).
- **`className` / `htmlFor`:** JSX names for HTML's `class` and `for`, because `class` and `for` are reserved words in JavaScript.
- **camelCase attributes:** event and most multi-word attributes are camelCase in JSX: `onClick`, `tabIndex`, `maxLength`, `autoFocus`. Exceptions: `aria-*` and `data-*` keep their dashes.
- **`style` object:** inline styles are objects with camelCase CSS properties: `style={{ fontSize: 14, backgroundColor: "teal" }}` (numbers become pixels for most properties).
- **Escaping:** turning special characters into safe text (`<` → `&lt;`), so text from users can never become markup. JSX escapes everything in `{}` automatically.
- **`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`:** the deliberately scary escape hatch that inserts raw HTML; only for trusted or sanitised HTML (`javascript.md`, [Frontend Security](javascript.md#35-frontend-security-xss-csrf-csp-prototype-pollution-and-the-supply-chain)).

**Everyday picture.** A **form letter** with blanks: "Dear {name}, your order #{orderId} of {total} has shipped." The fixed text is the markup; the `{}` blanks are filled from your data. The mail-merge program that turns the template into finished letters is the compiler plus React.

**JSX rules (the differences from HTML):**

| Rule | HTML | JSX |
|---|---|---|
| return **one** root (or a fragment) | many siblings fine | `return <><h1 /><p /></>` |
| close every tag | `<img>`, `<br>` | `<img />`, `<br />` |
| `class` is reserved | `class="btn"` | `className="btn"` |
| label's `for` is reserved | `for="email"` | `htmlFor="email"` |
| camelCase attributes | `onclick`, `tabindex` | `onClick`, `tabIndex` (`aria-*`, `data-*` stay dashed) |
| inline styles | `style="color: red"` | `style={{ color: "red" }}` |
| comments | `<!-- -->` | `{/* comment */}` |
| JavaScript values | not possible | `{price * qty}`, `{user.name}` |

**What renders and what doesn't:** strings and numbers become text; `null`, `undefined`, `true` and `false` render **nothing**; arrays render item by item; elements render as elements. A plain object can't be rendered (React throws). And `0` **does** render, which matters for `count && …` (Section [11](#11-conditional-rendering)).

**What the compiler does, traced by hand:**

```text
<p className="price">Total: {qty * 90}</p>
→ jsxs("p", { className: "price", children: ["Total: ", qty * 90] })
→ { type: "p", props: { className: "price", children: ["Total: ", 270] } }      (when qty = 3)
→ <p class="price">Total: 270</p>                                                 (React DOM creates this)
```

**When to use JSX:** always, for React UI; it's far more readable than nested function calls. **When not:** logic. Keep calculations and `if`s above the `return`, and keep JSX for structure.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ `class=`, `for=`, `onclick=`, `style="..."` from HTML habit.
- ❌ An `if` statement inside `{}`. ✅ A ternary, `&&`, or compute a variable above `return`.
- ❌ Rendering an object (`{user}`). ✅ `{user.name}`.
- ❌ Two root elements returned side by side. ✅ Wrap in `<>…</>`.

**Used in real software:** JSX (or its TypeScript form, TSX) is how virtually all React code is written; Preact, SolidJS and Qwik use JSX too, with different runtimes.

### Code

**From scratch: build elements without JSX.** A hand-written `h` function makes the same kind of objects JSX makes, and a tiny `toHTML` function turns them into an HTML string (with escaping), which is the essence of what React DOM's server renderer does:

```tsx
type El = { type: string; props: Record<string, any> };
const h = (type: string, props: Record<string, any> | null, ...children: any[]): El =>
  ({ type, props: { ...props, children } });

const escapeHtml = (s: string) => s.replace(/&/g, "&amp;").replace(/</g, "&lt;").replace(/>/g, "&gt;");

function toHTML(node: any): string {
  if (node === null || node === undefined || typeof node === "boolean") return "";   // render nothing
  if (typeof node === "string" || typeof node === "number") return escapeHtml(String(node));
  if (Array.isArray(node)) return node.map(toHTML).join("");
  const { children, className, ...attrs } = node.props;
  const attrText = Object.entries({ class: className, ...attrs })
    .filter(([, v]) => v !== undefined).map(([k, v]) => ` ${k}="${escapeHtml(String(v))}"`).join("");
  return `<${node.type}${attrText}>${toHTML(children)}</${node.type}>`;
}

const qty = 3;
const tree = h("div", { className: "card" },
  h("h2", null, "Masala chai"),
  h("p", { className: "price" }, "Total: ", qty * 90),
  qty > 5 && h("span", null, "bulk discount"),           // false → renders nothing
  h("p", null, "<script>alert('hi')</script>"));          // escaped, harmless
console.log(toHTML(tree));
```

**Output:**

```text
<div class="card"><h2>Masala chai</h2><p class="price">Total: 270</p><p>&lt;script&gt;alert('hi')&lt;/script&gt;</p></div>
```

**The real thing: JSX compiles to `jsx()` calls.** This shell block asks esbuild (the compiler Vite and `tsx` use) to transform a line of JSX:

```bash
echo 'const el = <p className="price">Total: {qty * 90}</p>;' | npx esbuild --loader=tsx --jsx=automatic
```

**Output:**

```text
import { jsxs } from "react/jsx-runtime";
const el = /* @__PURE__ */ jsxs("p", { className: "price", children: [
  "Total: ",
  qty * 90
] });
```

`jsxs` (with an "s") is used because the `p` has more than one child: the text and the expression. The object it returns is the same shape as ours:

```tsx
const real = <p className="price">Total: {qty * 90}</p>;
console.log(real.type, real.props, "| key:", real.key);
```

**Output:**

```text
p { className: 'price', children: [ 'Total: ', 270 ] } | key: null
```

**JSX in practice: expressions, attributes, styles and fragments:**

```tsx
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";

const product = { name: "Masala chai", pricePaise: 18000, tags: ["tea", "spiced"], inStock: true };
const formatRupees = (paise: number) => `₹${(paise / 100).toFixed(2)}`;

function ProductCard() {
  const discountPercent = 10;                              // statements go above the return
  const final = product.pricePaise * (1 - discountPercent / 100);
  return (
    <article className="card" data-sku="TEA-250">
      {/* any expression goes inside braces */}
      <h2>{product.name.toUpperCase()}</h2>
      <p style={{ color: "green", fontWeight: 700 }}>
        {formatRupees(final)} <s>{formatRupees(product.pricePaise)}</s>
      </p>
      <p>{product.inStock ? "In stock" : "Sold out"}</p>
      <label htmlFor="qty">Qty</label>
      <input id="qty" type="number" defaultValue={1} />
      <small>Tags: {product.tags.join(", ")}</small>
    </article>
  );
}
console.log(render(<ProductCard />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<article class="card" data-sku="TEA-250"><h2>MASALA CHAI</h2><p style="color: green; font-weight: 700;">₹162.00 <s>₹180.00</s></p><p>In stock</p><label for="qty">Qty</label><input id="qty" type="number" value="1"><small>Tags: tea, spiced</small></article>
```

`className` became `class`, `htmlFor` became `for`, and the style object became a CSS string. `defaultValue` sets an input's starting value (Section [19](#19-forms-controlled-and-uncontrolled-inputs)).

**What renders and what doesn't, and why user text is safe:**

```tsx
function Values() {
  const userInput = "<script>alert('hacked')</script>";
  return (
    <ul>
      <li>string: {"hello"}</li>
      <li>number: {42}</li>
      <li>zero: {0}</li>
      <li>true/false/null/undefined: [{true}{false}{null}{undefined}]</li>
      <li>array: {["a", "b", "c"]}</li>
      <li>user input: {userInput}</li>
    </ul>
  );
}
console.log(render(<Values />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<ul><li>string: hello</li><li>number: 42</li><li>zero: 0</li><li>true/false/null/undefined: []</li><li>array: abc</li><li>user input: &lt;script&gt;alert('hacked')&lt;/script&gt;</li></ul>
```

`0` renders, booleans and `null` don't, and the "script" is harmless text (`&lt;` is the escaped `<`).

**Rendering an object is an error:**

```tsx
const user = { name: "Asha" };
render(<p>{user as any}</p>);
```

**Output:**

```text
Error: Objects are not valid as a React child (found: object with keys {name}). If you meant to render a collection of children, use an array instead.
```

(The `as any` silences TypeScript, which would otherwise reject this at compile time, so we can see React's own runtime error.)

**Fragments** return several elements without an extra wrapper:

```tsx
function PriceRow() {
  return (
    <>
      <dt>Price</dt>
      <dd>₹180</dd>
    </>
  );
}
console.log(render(<dl><PriceRow /></dl>).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<dl><dt>Price</dt><dd>₹180</dd></dl>
```

**TypeScript catches HTML habits.** Writing `class` instead of `className`:

```tsx
const a = <div class="x">Hi</div>;
```

**Compiler output:**

```text
example.tsx(1,16): error TS2322: Type '{ class: string; children: string; }' is not assignable to type 'DetailedHTMLProps<HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>, HTMLDivElement>'.
  Property 'class' does not exist on type 'DetailedHTMLProps<HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>, HTMLDivElement>'. Did you mean 'className'?
```

### Practice

1. Convert this HTML to JSX: `<label for="q" class="lbl">Search</label><input id="q" tabindex="1" style="width: 200px; margin-top: 4px">`.
2. Write `OrderSummary` for `const order = { id: 90312, items: 3, totalPaise: 149950, express: true }` showing `Order #90312`, `3 items · ₹1499.50`, and "⚡ Express" only when `express` is true.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function SearchField() {
  return (
    <>
      <label htmlFor="q" className="lbl">Search</label>
      <input id="q" tabIndex={1} style={{ width: 200, marginTop: 4 }} />
    </>
  );
}
const order = { id: 90312, items: 3, totalPaise: 149950, express: true };
function OrderSummary() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h3>Order #{order.id}</h3>
      <p>{order.items} items · {formatRupees(order.totalPaise)}</p>
      {order.express && <span>⚡ Express</span>}
    </div>
  );
}
console.log(render(<SearchField />).container.innerHTML);
console.log(render(<OrderSummary />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<label for="q" class="lbl">Search</label><input id="q" tabindex="1" style="width: 200px; margin-top: 4px;">
<div><h3>Order #90312</h3><p>3 items · ₹1499.50</p><span>⚡ Express</span></div>
```

`tabIndex={1}` passes a number (a string `"1"` would also work); `width: 200` becomes `200px`. `order.express && …` is safe here because `express` is a boolean, never `0`.

</details>

## 9. Props: Passing Data to Components

![Props flow down from parent to child like function arguments; the child cannot change them; to change data, the parent passes a callback that the child calls](images/react/01-props-flow.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** **props** (properties) are how a parent passes information to a child, exactly like arguments to a function. `<ProductCard name="Masala chai" price={180} />` makes React call `ProductCard({ name: "Masala chai", price: 180 })`. Props let one component show different data each time it is used. They are **read-only**: a component must never change its own props. To let a child change something, the parent passes a **function** as a prop that the child calls.

**Words to know:**

- **Prop:** one named input to a component, written like an HTML attribute: `name="Masala chai"`, `price={180}`.
- **Props object:** all of a component's props gathered into one object, the function's first (and only) parameter.
- **String vs expression prop:** `name="Chai"` passes a string; anything else (numbers, booleans, objects, functions, JSX) goes in braces: `price={180}`, `tags={["tea"]}`, `onAdd={handleAdd}`.
- **Boolean shorthand:** `<Button disabled />` is the same as `disabled={true}`.
- **Default prop value:** a fallback in the destructuring: `function Avatar({ size = 48 })`.
- **`children` prop:** whatever is nested between a component's tags: in `<Card><p>Hi</p></Card>`, `Card` receives the `p` as `children` (more in Section [25](#25-composition-children-slots-and-layout-components)).
- **Spreading props:** `<Avatar {...person} />` passes every property of `person` as a prop; handy but hides what's passed.
- **Callback prop:** a function passed down so the child can tell the parent something happened: `onAdd`, `onChange`. By convention prop names start with `on` and handler functions with `handle`.
- **One-way data flow:** data moves **down** the tree through props; requests to change it move **up** through callbacks.
- **Read-only (immutable) props:** React freezes the props object in development, so assigning to it throws.
- **Prop types (TypeScript):** describing each prop's type, e.g. `{ name: string; price: number; onAdd?: () => void }`; the `?` marks an optional prop (Section [26](#26-typescript-with-react-typing-props-state-events-and-children)).

**Everyday picture.** Props are the **order slip** a waiter hands to the kitchen: "masala chai, less sugar, table 4". The cook (child component) follows the slip but never edits it. If the cook needs to tell the waiter something ("we're out of ginger"), they ring a bell the waiter installed (a callback prop).

**Props through a tree, traced by hand:**

```text
<Menu items={[{ id: 1, name: "Masala chai", price: 180 }]} />
  Menu({ items })                         → items.map(item => <MenuItem key={item.id} {...item} onAdd={add} />)
    MenuItem({ id: 1, name: "Masala chai", price: 180, onAdd })
      → <li>Masala chai ₹180 <button onClick={() => onAdd(1)}>Add</button></li>
  user clicks "Add" → MenuItem calls onAdd(1) → Menu's add(1) runs (Menu owns the data)
```

**When to use props:** for every piece of data a component needs from its parent. **When not:** when the same data must pass through many layers that don't use it ("prop drilling"); composition (Section [25](#25-composition-children-slots-and-layout-components)) or context (Section [36](#36-context-passing-data-deeply)) fit better.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Changing props (`props.price = 0`) to "update" them. ✅ The parent owns the data; ask it via a callback.
- ❌ `price="180"` when a number is meant (a string). ✅ `price={180}`.
- ❌ Calling the function while passing it: `onAdd={handleAdd()}` runs it during render. ✅ `onAdd={handleAdd}` or `onAdd={() => handleAdd(id)}`.
- ❌ Copying a prop into state "so it can change" (`useState(props.price)`); the state then ignores later prop changes (Section [22](#22-choosing-the-state-structure)).

**Used in real software:** every reusable component (buttons, inputs, cards, tables) is configured entirely through props; design systems document each component's props as its public interface.

### Code

**From scratch: props are just the function's argument object.** React gathers the attributes into one object and calls your function with it:

```tsx
function PriceTag(props: { label: string; paise: number }) {
  return <span>{props.label}: ₹{props.paise / 100}</span>;
}
const el = <PriceTag label="Masala chai" paise={18000} />;
console.log("element props:", el.props);
console.log("calling it ourselves:", PriceTag(el.props).props.children);
```

**Output:**

```text
element props: { label: 'Masala chai', paise: 18000 }
calling it ourselves: [ 'Masala chai', ': ₹', 180 ]
```

The `span`'s children are three pieces, exactly the parts between its tags: the label, the literal text ": ₹", and the computed number.

**The React way: destructured props, defaults, and reuse:**

```tsx
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";

type ProductCardProps = { name: string; pricePaise: number; tags?: string[]; bestseller?: boolean };

function ProductCard({ name, pricePaise, tags = [], bestseller = false }: ProductCardProps) {
  return (
    <article>
      <h2>{name}{bestseller && " ⭐"}</h2>
      <p>₹{(pricePaise / 100).toFixed(2)}</p>
      {tags.length > 0 && <small>{tags.join(" · ")}</small>}
    </article>
  );
}

function Menu() {
  return (
    <section>
      <ProductCard name="Masala chai" pricePaise={18000} tags={["tea", "spiced"]} bestseller />
      <ProductCard name="Samosa" pricePaise={6000} />
    </section>
  );
}
console.log(render(<Menu />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<section><article><h2>Masala chai ⭐</h2><p>₹180.00</p><small>tea · spiced</small></article><article><h2>Samosa</h2><p>₹60.00</p></article></section>
```

One component, two different results. `bestseller` alone means `true`; `tags` falls back to `[]` for the samosa, so its `<small>` isn't rendered.

**Callbacks: the child asks, the parent decides.** The parent passes a function; the child calls it with the item's id:

```tsx
import { screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function AddButton({ itemId, onAdd }: { itemId: number; onAdd: (id: number) => void }) {
  return <button onClick={() => onAdd(itemId)}>Add #{itemId}</button>;
}

function Shop() {
  function handleAdd(id: number) {
    console.log("parent was asked to add item", id);
  }
  return (
    <>
      <AddButton itemId={1} onAdd={handleAdd} />
      <AddButton itemId={2} onAdd={handleAdd} />
    </>
  );
}
render(<Shop />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Add #2"));
```

**Output:**

```text
parent was asked to add item 2
```

**Props are read-only.** In development React freezes the props object, so a component that tries to change one fails loudly:

```tsx
function Sneaky(props: { price: number }) {
  (props as any).price = 0;                    // ❌ trying to change a prop
  return <p>{props.price}</p>;
}
render(<Sneaky price={180} />);
```

**Output:**

```text
TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'price' of object '#<Object>'
```

**Spreading props** passes every field of an object; `{ id, ...rest }` (rest syntax) takes one out first:

```tsx
const chai = { id: 7, name: "Ginger chai", pricePaise: 16000 };
const { id, ...cardProps } = chai;
console.log(render(<ProductCard {...cardProps} />).container.innerHTML, "| id kept aside:", id);
```

**Output:**

```text
<article><h2>Ginger chai</h2><p>₹160.00</p></article> | id kept aside: 7
```

### Practice

1. Write `Avatar({ name, size = 48 })` that renders `<img alt={name} width={size} height={size} src={...}>` with `src` built as `` `https://i.pravatar.cc/${size}?u=${name}` ``, and render it twice with different names and sizes.
2. A child calls `onSelect(item.id)`, but the parent wrote `<Row onSelect={select(item.id)} />`. What happens, and what's the fix?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function Avatar({ name, size = 48 }: { name: string; size?: number }) {
  return <img alt={name} width={size} height={size} src={`https://i.pravatar.cc/${size}?u=${name}`} />;
}
console.log(render(<><Avatar name="Asha" /><Avatar name="Ravi" size={96} /></>).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<img alt="Asha" width="48" height="48" src="https://i.pravatar.cc/48?u=Asha"><img alt="Ravi" width="96" height="96" src="https://i.pravatar.cc/96?u=Ravi">
```

1. The default `size` of 48 applies to Asha; Ravi gets 96.
2. `select(item.id)` runs **during render** (every render!), and its return value (probably `undefined`) is passed as `onSelect`, so clicking does nothing. Fix: `onSelect={select}` (the child supplies the id) or `onSelect={() => select(item.id)}`.

</details>

## 10. Keeping Components Pure

![A pure component returns the same JSX for the same props and changes nothing outside itself; side effects belong in event handlers and effects](images/react/10-pure.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** React expects every component to behave like a **pure function**, like a maths formula: **the same inputs (props, state) always give the same JSX**, and rendering **changes nothing outside** the component. React may call your component more often than you expect (twice in development, again whenever a parent re-renders, or partway and then restart), so a component that changes outside variables during render gives wrong, unpredictable results.

**Words to know:**

- **Pure function:** a function that (1) returns the same output for the same input and (2) has no side effects. `double(x) = x * 2` is pure.
- **Side effect:** anything a function does besides returning a value: changing a variable outside it, writing to the DOM, `fetch`, `console.log`, timers, `localStorage`.
- **Render phase:** the moment React calls your component to compute JSX; it must be pure.
- **Local mutation:** changing a variable or array **you created during this render**: perfectly fine (`const rows = []; rows.push(...)`).
- **Idempotent:** doing it twice has the same result as doing it once; pure rendering is idempotent.
- **`StrictMode` double render:** in development, React renders each component **twice** and compares, to surface impure components; production renders once.
- **Where side effects go:** in **event handlers** (Section [13](#13-responding-to-events)) for things caused by a user action, or in **effects** (Section [30](#30-effects-synchronising-with-systems-outside-react)) for synchronising with outside systems after rendering.

**Everyday picture.** A **recipe**: follow it twice with the same ingredients and you get the same dish, and following it doesn't secretly reorder your pantry. A recipe that said "and also eat one biscuit from the jar each time you read this" would leave a different jar every time someone merely *read* it, which is what an impure component does to your app.

**Why impurity breaks, traced by hand:** a component increments an outside counter while rendering:

```text
let guest = 0;
function Cup() { guest = guest + 1; return <h2>Tea cup for guest #{guest}</h2>; }
<><Cup /><Cup /><Cup /></>

Without StrictMode: renders Cup three times → guest 1, 2, 3   (looks fine!)
With StrictMode:    each Cup renders twice  → guest 2, 4, 6   (React keeps the second result)
Any later re-render: numbers keep climbing  → 7, 8, 9 … for the SAME three cups
```

The bug was there all along; StrictMode simply made it visible immediately. The fix is to pass the number in as a prop: `<Cup guest={1} />`. Same input, same output, every time.

**When purity matters:** always, for the render phase. **When it doesn't apply:** event handlers and effects are *supposed* to have side effects; they don't run during rendering.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Changing an outside variable, a prop, or an object received from a parent during render.
- ❌ Reading something that changes on its own during render (`Math.random()`, `Date.now()`) and expecting stable results; read it in an event handler or store it in state.
- ❌ Fetching data or setting timers directly in the component body (they run on every render).
- ❌ "Fixing" double logs by removing StrictMode instead of fixing the impurity.

**Used in real software:** purity is what lets React render in the background, pause and resume rendering (Section [43](#43-fiber-scheduling-and-concurrent-rendering)), skip work (Section [45](#45-memo-usememo-usecallback-and-the-react-compiler)) and render on the server (Part 9). The React Compiler (Section [45](#45-memo-usememo-usecallback-and-the-react-compiler)) assumes components are pure.

### Code

**From scratch: pure vs impure functions**, before React:

```tsx
const pureTotal = (prices: number[]) => prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0);
let runningTotal = 0;
const impureTotal = (prices: number[]) => { for (const p of prices) runningTotal += p; return runningTotal; };

console.log("pure:", pureTotal([10, 20]), pureTotal([10, 20]));
console.log("impure:", impureTotal([10, 20]), impureTotal([10, 20]), "← same input, different output");
```

**Output:**

```text
pure: 30 30
impure: 30 60 ← same input, different output
```

**An impure component, with and without StrictMode:**

```tsx
import { StrictMode } from "react";
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";

let guest = 0;
function Cup() {
  guest = guest + 1;                       // ❌ side effect during render
  return <h2>Tea cup for guest #{guest}</h2>;
}

const cups = <><Cup /><Cup /><Cup /></>;
console.log("normal:", render(cups).container.textContent);
guest = 0;
console.log("StrictMode:", render(<StrictMode>{cups}</StrictMode>).container.textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
normal: Tea cup for guest #1Tea cup for guest #2Tea cup for guest #3
StrictMode: Tea cup for guest #2Tea cup for guest #4Tea cup for guest #6
```

**The pure version:** the number comes in as a prop, so any number of renders gives the same result:

```tsx
function PureCup({ guest }: { guest: number }) {
  return <h2>Tea cup for guest #{guest}</h2>;
}
console.log(render(<StrictMode><PureCup guest={1} /><PureCup guest={2} /><PureCup guest={3} /></StrictMode>).container.textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
Tea cup for guest #1Tea cup for guest #2Tea cup for guest #3
```

**Local mutation is fine:** this component pushes into an array, but it's a **new** array created during this render, so nothing outside changes:

```tsx
function TeaSet({ count }: { count: number }) {
  const cupsList = [];                     // created fresh on every render
  for (let i = 1; i <= count; i++) cupsList.push(<PureCup key={i} guest={i} />);
  return <>{cupsList}</>;
}
console.log(render(<StrictMode><TeaSet count={3} /></StrictMode>).container.textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
Tea cup for guest #1Tea cup for guest #2Tea cup for guest #3
```

(`key` gives each item in a list an identity; Section [12](#12-rendering-lists-and-keys) explains it.)

### Practice

1. This component is impure. Why, and how do you fix it? `function Clock() { const hours = new Date().getHours(); document.title = `${hours}h`; return <p>{hours < 12 ? "Good morning" : "Good evening"}</p>; }`
2. Is `function List({ items }) { items.sort(); return <ul>{items.map((i) => <li key={i}>{i}</li>)}</ul>; }` pure?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. Two problems: setting `document.title` during render is a side effect (move it to an effect, Section [30](#30-effects-synchronising-with-systems-outside-react)), and reading the current time makes the output depend on something other than props or state. Pass the time in as a prop (`<Clock time={now} />`) where the parent updates `now` on a timer, as react.dev's "Fix a broken clock" challenge shows.
2. No: `items.sort()` **mutates** the array the parent passed in, changing the parent's data during render. Use `items.toSorted()` (a copy).

</details>

## 11. Conditional Rendering

![Four ways to choose what to show: if with early return, the ternary for either/or, && for show-or-nothing, and null to render nothing](images/react/11-conditional.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** components often show different things depending on data: "Sold out" or an "Add" button, a spinner while loading, an error message when something failed. Because JSX is JavaScript, you choose with ordinary JavaScript: `if` statements (above the `return`), the **ternary** `a ? b : c` for either/or, **`&&`** for "this or nothing", and returning **`null`** to render nothing at all.

**Words to know:**

- **Conditional rendering:** showing different UI depending on conditions.
- **Early return:** `if (!user) return <Login />;` at the top of a component; the rest of the function handles the normal case.
- **Ternary in JSX:** `{inStock ? <AddButton /> : <SoldOut />}`.
- **`&&` in JSX:** `{isNew && <Badge />}` shows the badge when `isNew` is truthy, otherwise renders the left value (`false` renders nothing).
- **Returning `null`:** a component that returns `null` renders nothing (it still exists and runs).
- **Conditional variable:** assigning JSX to a variable with `if`/`else` above the return, then using `{content}`.
- **Truthy / falsy pitfall:** `{count && <p>{count} items</p>}` renders `0` when count is 0, because `0` is falsy but is a renderable number. ✅ `{count > 0 && …}`.
- **Lookup object:** mapping a status to UI with an object (`const icons = { paid: "✅", failed: "❌" }`) instead of a chain of ternaries.

**Everyday picture.** A **shop sign** that flips between "Open" and "Closed" (ternary), a "Today's special" board that's only put out on some days (`&&`), and a shop that's simply not there on a holiday (`return null`).

**Choosing between forms, traced on one component.** An order status component:

```text
status = "loading"    → early return <Spinner />          (nothing else matters yet)
status = "error"      → early return <p>Couldn't load</p>
status = "ready", items = 0 → ternary: items > 0 ? <List/> : <p>Your cart is empty</p>
status = "ready", items = 3, coupon = null → coupon && <Coupon/> → null → nothing rendered
```

**When to use each:** early `if` returns for whole-component states (loading, error, not logged in); a ternary for two alternatives inside markup; `&&` for optional bits; a lookup object for 3+ cases. **When not:** deeply nested ternaries (`a ? b : c ? d : e`) are hard to read; use `if`/`else` with a variable or a lookup object.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ `{count && …}` with a number: shows `0`. ✅ `{count > 0 && …}`.
- ❌ `if` inside `{}` in JSX (a syntax error).
- ❌ Hiding with CSS when unmounting is intended (or vice versa): `return null` removes the component and resets its state; CSS `display: none` keeps it.
- ❌ Long ternary chains instead of a lookup object or `switch`.

**Used in real software:** loading/error/empty states on every data screen; feature flags (`{flags.newCheckout && <NewCheckout />}`); permission checks (`{user.isAdmin && <AdminMenu />}`; real security still has to happen on the server).

### Code

**From scratch: plain functions choosing a description.** Conditional rendering is just conditional code returning different values:

```tsx
function describeStock(qty: number) {
  if (qty === 0) return "Sold out";
  return qty < 5 ? `Only ${qty} left!` : "In stock";
}
console.log([0, 3, 20].map(describeStock));
```

**Output:**

```text
[ 'Sold out', 'Only 3 left!', 'In stock' ]
```

**All four forms in one component:**

```tsx
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";

type Status = "loading" | "error" | "ready";

function CartPanel({ status, items, coupon }: { status: Status; items: number; coupon: string | null }) {
  if (status === "loading") return <p>Loading…</p>;                       // early return
  if (status === "error") return <p role="alert">Couldn't load your cart</p>;
  return (
    <section>
      {/* either/or */}
      {items > 0 ? <p>{items} items</p> : <p>Your cart is empty</p>}
      {/* this or nothing */}
      {coupon && <p>Coupon {coupon} applied</p>}
    </section>
  );
}

for (const props of [
  { status: "loading", items: 0, coupon: null },
  { status: "error", items: 0, coupon: null },
  { status: "ready", items: 0, coupon: null },
  { status: "ready", items: 3, coupon: "CHAI10" },
] as const) {
  console.log(props.status.padEnd(7), "→", render(<CartPanel {...props} />).container.innerHTML);
}
```

**Output:**

```text
loading → <p>Loading…</p>
error   → <p role="alert">Couldn't load your cart</p>
ready   → <section><p>Your cart is empty</p></section>
ready   → <section><p>3 items</p><p>Coupon CHAI10 applied</p></section>
```

`as const` keeps the literal string types (`"loading"`, not just `string`) so they match the `Status` type; `padEnd(7)` lines the output up.

**The `0` pitfall, seen for real:**

```tsx
function Notifications({ count }: { count: number }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <span>wrong: [{count && <b>{count} new</b>}]</span>
      <span> right: [{count > 0 && <b>{count} new</b>}]</span>
    </div>
  );
}
console.log(render(<Notifications count={0} />).container.textContent);
console.log(render(<Notifications count={2} />).container.textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
wrong: [0] right: []
wrong: [2 new] right: [2 new]
```

**A lookup object instead of nested ternaries, and `null` to render nothing:**

```tsx
const statusUi = {
  placed: { icon: "🧾", text: "Order placed" },
  brewing: { icon: "🫖", text: "Brewing" },
  delivered: { icon: "✅", text: "Delivered" },
} as const;

function OrderStatus({ status }: { status: keyof typeof statusUi | "hidden" }) {
  if (status === "hidden") return null;
  const { icon, text } = statusUi[status];
  return <p>{icon} {text}</p>;
}
console.log(render(<><OrderStatus status="brewing" /><OrderStatus status="hidden" /><OrderStatus status="delivered" /></>).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<p>🫖 Brewing</p><p>✅ Delivered</p>
```

`keyof typeof statusUi` is TypeScript for "one of the keys of `statusUi`": `"placed" | "brewing" | "delivered"`.

### Practice

1. Write `PackingItem({ name, isPacked })` that shows `name ✅` when packed and just `name` otherwise, first with a ternary, then with `&&`.
2. Rewrite `{role === "admin" ? <Admin /> : role === "editor" ? <Editor /> : role === "viewer" ? <Viewer /> : null}` more readably.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function PackingItem({ name, isPacked }: { name: string; isPacked: boolean }) {
  return <li>{isPacked ? name + " ✅" : name}</li>;
}
function PackingItem2({ name, isPacked }: { name: string; isPacked: boolean }) {
  return <li>{name} {isPacked && "✅"}</li>;
}
console.log(render(<ul><PackingItem name="Tea leaves" isPacked /><PackingItem2 name="Kettle" isPacked={false} /></ul>).container.innerHTML);

const Admin = () => <b>admin tools</b>, Editor = () => <i>editor tools</i>, Viewer = () => <span>read only</span>;
const panels = { admin: Admin, editor: Editor, viewer: Viewer };
function RolePanel({ role }: { role: string }) {
  const Panel = panels[role as keyof typeof panels];
  return Panel ? <Panel /> : null;
}
console.log(render(<><RolePanel role="editor" /><RolePanel role="guest" /></>).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<ul><li>Tea leaves ✅</li><li>Kettle </li></ul>
<i>editor tools</i>
```

1. Both work; the `&&` version leaves a trailing space after the name when not packed, which is harmless.
2. A lookup object from role to **component**. The variable holding a component must start with a capital letter (`Panel`) so `<Panel />` is treated as a component.

</details>

## 12. Rendering Lists and Keys

![Keys tell React which item is which: with stable ids, removing the first item keeps the other rows (and their typed text); with index keys, every row shifts and state lands on the wrong item](images/react/12-keys.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** to show a list, turn an array of data into an array of JSX with **`map`**. Each item needs a **`key`**: a string or number that **uniquely and permanently identifies that item** among its siblings, usually its id from the database. Keys let React match items between renders, so when the list is sorted, filtered or an item is inserted, React moves the right DOM nodes (and the state inside them) instead of mixing them up.

**Words to know:**

- **List rendering:** producing one element per array item, usually with `items.map(item => <Row … />)`.
- **`key`:** a special attribute that identifies an element among its siblings. It is not passed to your component as a prop (read `item.id` separately if you need it).
- **Stable key:** a key that stays the same for the same item across renders (a database id, a slug, a UUID created when the item was created).
- **Index key:** using the array position (`key={index}`) as the key; fine for static lists that never reorder, wrong when items are inserted, removed or reordered.
- **Sibling uniqueness:** keys only need to be unique among siblings in the same list, not across the whole app.
- **Reconciliation by key:** when re-rendering a list, React pairs old and new children with the same key (keep and update), creates children with new keys, and removes children whose keys disappeared (Section [42](#42-the-virtual-dom-and-reconciliation-build-a-mini-react-from-scratch)).
- **`Fragment` with a key:** `<Fragment key={id}>…</Fragment>` when each item renders several siblings.
- **`filter` then `map`:** the usual way to show part of a list: `items.filter(i => i.veg).map(i => <li key={i.id}>…)`.
- **Missing-key warning:** in development React logs "Each child in a list should have a unique key prop" when keys are missing.

**Everyday picture.** A **cloakroom**. Each coat gets a numbered ticket (the key). If coats are re-hung in a different order, you still get your own coat back because the ticket follows the coat. If instead tickets were "the coat on hook 1, hook 2…" (index keys) and someone removed the first coat and shifted the rest along, everyone would walk out with their neighbour's coat.

**Why index keys break, traced by hand.** Three rows, each with an input where the user typed a note; the user then deletes "Chai" (the first row):

```text
before:  key 0 → Chai   [note: "less sugar"]     key 1 → Samosa [note: "extra chutney"]   key 2 → Vada [note: ""]
after deleting Chai, with INDEX keys:
         key 0 → Samosa  React sees key 0 still exists → keeps that DOM row (with "less sugar"!) and just changes the label
         key 1 → Vada    keeps row 1's DOM (with "extra chutney")
         key 2 → (gone)  removes the LAST row
result:  Samosa [less sugar]   Vada [extra chutney]          ← notes moved to the wrong items
with ID keys:  React sees "chai" disappeared → removes exactly that row; the other rows keep their own notes
```

**When index keys are acceptable:** a static list that never reorders and whose items hold no state (a fixed list of links). **When not:** anything users can add to, remove from, sort or filter, or whose rows contain inputs or other state. Never use `Math.random()` as a key (a new key every render means every row is destroyed and recreated).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ No key, or `key={index}` on a list that changes.
- ❌ `key={Math.random()}` or `key={crypto.randomUUID()}` generated during render.
- ❌ Putting the key on the wrong element: it goes on the outermost element **returned by `map`**, not on an element inside it.
- ❌ Expecting `props.key` inside the child (it's not passed); pass `id={item.id}` too if the child needs it.

**Used in real software:** every feed, table, chat thread and search result list; libraries such as TanStack Table and virtualised lists (Section [46](#46-long-lists-virtualisation-and-pagination)) are built around stable row keys.

### Code

**From scratch: matching items by key.** This is the idea React uses, written as a plain function that compares an old and new list of keys and reports what happens to each:

```tsx
function diffByKey(oldKeys: string[], newKeys: string[]) {
  const oldSet = new Set(oldKeys);
  const kept = newKeys.filter((k) => oldSet.has(k));
  const created = newKeys.filter((k) => !oldSet.has(k));
  const removed = oldKeys.filter((k) => !newKeys.includes(k));
  return { kept, created, removed };
}
console.log("by id:   ", diffByKey(["chai", "samosa", "vada"], ["samosa", "vada"]));
console.log("by index:", diffByKey(["0", "1", "2"], ["0", "1"]));
```

**Output:**

```text
by id:    { kept: [ 'samosa', 'vada' ], created: [], removed: [ 'chai' ] }
by index: { kept: [ '0', '1' ], created: [], removed: [ '2' ] }
```

With ids, exactly the deleted item is removed. With index keys, React believes items `0` and `1` were **kept** and item `2` was removed, so the first two rows are reused for different data.

**The React way: `map` with stable keys:**

```tsx
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";

const menu = [
  { id: "chai", name: "Masala chai", veg: true },
  { id: "roll", name: "Chicken roll", veg: false },
  { id: "samosa", name: "Samosa", veg: true },
];

function VegMenu() {
  return (
    <ul>
      {menu.filter((item) => item.veg).map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
console.log(render(<VegMenu />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<ul><li>Masala chai</li><li>Samosa</li></ul>
```

The `key` doesn't appear in the HTML; it's React's private bookkeeping.

**The bug, for real: index keys move typed text to the wrong row.** Each row has an input; the user types in the first two rows, then deletes the first item:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function NotesList({ useIndexKeys }: { useIndexKeys: boolean }) {
  const [items, setItems] = useState(["Chai", "Samosa", "Vada"]);
  return (
    <>
      {items.map((name, index) => (
        <p key={useIndexKeys ? index : name}>
          {name} <input aria-label={`note ${index}`} />
        </p>
      ))}
      <button onClick={() => setItems(items.slice(1))}>Delete first</button>
    </>
  );
}

for (const useIndexKeys of [true, false]) {
  const { container, unmount } = render(<NotesList useIndexKeys={useIndexKeys} />);
  fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("note 0"), { target: { value: "less sugar" } });
  fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("note 1"), { target: { value: "extra chutney" } });
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Delete first"));
  const rows = [...container.querySelectorAll("p")].map((p) => `${p.textContent!.trim()}: "${p.querySelector("input")!.value}"`);
  console.log(useIndexKeys ? "index keys:" : "id keys:   ", rows.join(" | "));
  unmount();
}
```

**Output:**

```text
index keys: Samosa: "less sugar" | Vada: "extra chutney"
id keys:    Samosa: "extra chutney" | Vada: ""
```

With index keys, Samosa now shows Chai's note and Vada shows Samosa's: exactly the cloakroom mix-up. With the name as key (a stable id here), every note stays with its item. `unmount()` removes the rendered component before the next loop run.

**Forgetting the key** makes React warn in development (the warning's first line is shown):

```tsx
function NoKeys() {
  return <ul>{menu.map((item) => <li>{item.name}</li>)}</ul>;   // expect-warning: no key
}
render(<NoKeys />);
```

**Output:**

```text
console.error: Each child in a list should have a unique "key" prop.
```

**Several elements per item** need a keyed `Fragment`:

```tsx
import { Fragment } from "react";

function Glossary() {
  const terms = [{ id: "jsx", term: "JSX", def: "markup in JavaScript" }, { id: "prop", term: "Prop", def: "an input to a component" }];
  return (
    <dl>
      {terms.map(({ id, term, def }) => (
        <Fragment key={id}>
          <dt>{term}</dt>
          <dd>{def}</dd>
        </Fragment>
      ))}
    </dl>
  );
}
console.log(render(<Glossary />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<dl><dt>JSX</dt><dd>markup in JavaScript</dd><dt>Prop</dt><dd>an input to a component</dd></dl>
```

### Practice

1. Given `const people = [{ id: 1, name: "Asha", job: "chemist" }, { id: 2, name: "Ravi", job: "chef" }, { id: 3, name: "Meera", job: "chemist" }]`, render two lists: chemists and everyone else, with correct keys.
2. Why is `key={Math.random()}` worse than no key at all?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
const people = [{ id: 1, name: "Asha", job: "chemist" }, { id: 2, name: "Ravi", job: "chef" }, { id: 3, name: "Meera", job: "chemist" }];
function People() {
  const chemists = people.filter((p) => p.job === "chemist");
  const others = people.filter((p) => p.job !== "chemist");
  return (
    <>
      <h2>Chemists</h2>
      <ul>{chemists.map((p) => <li key={p.id}>{p.name}</li>)}</ul>
      <h2>Everyone else</h2>
      <ul>{others.map((p) => <li key={p.id}>{p.name}</li>)}</ul>
    </>
  );
}
console.log(render(<People />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<h2>Chemists</h2><ul><li>Asha</li><li>Meera</li></ul><h2>Everyone else</h2><ul><li>Ravi</li></ul>
```

1. The same `id`s can appear in both lists' keys without conflict because keys only need to be unique among **siblings**.
2. A random key changes on every render, so React thinks every item is new: it destroys and recreates every DOM node and all their state on each render (slow, and inputs lose focus and text). No key at least falls back to position matching.

</details>

## 13. Responding to Events

![React event handlers: you pass a function to onClick; React attaches one listener at the root and calls your handler with a SyntheticEvent that bubbles through the component tree](images/react/13-events.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** to react to a click, a key press or a form submit, you pass a **function** to a prop such as `onClick`. React calls that function when the event happens, handing it an **event object**. Handlers are where **side effects** belong: changing state, sending a request, navigating. Pass the function itself (`onClick={handleClick}`), never the result of calling it (`onClick={handleClick()}`).

**Words to know:**

- **Event handler:** a function passed as an `on…` prop (`onClick`, `onChange`, `onSubmit`, `onKeyDown`) that React calls when that event fires.
- **Inline handler:** a handler written directly in JSX: `onClick={() => setOpen(true)}`.
- **SyntheticEvent:** React's wrapper around the browser's event object, with the same main properties (`target`, `currentTarget`, `preventDefault()`, `stopPropagation()`) working the same way in every browser. The original is at `event.nativeEvent`.
- **Event delegation:** attaching one listener high in the tree instead of one per element; React attaches its listeners once to the **root container** and works out which components' handlers to call.
- **Propagation in React:** React events bubble up the **component tree** (including through portals, Section [49](#49-accessibility-semantics-focus-aria-portals-and-modals)); `e.stopPropagation()` stops parents' handlers from running.
- **Capture phase (`onClickCapture`):** handlers ending in `Capture` run on the way **down**, before the target's own handler.
- **`preventDefault()`:** cancels the browser's default action, e.g. a form submit reloading the page.
- **Event handler prop (custom):** your own components can accept handler props with any name starting with `on`: `<Toolbar onPlay={...} />`; the name is your API.
- **`handle…` / `on…` naming:** props are named `onSomething`; the functions you pass are usually named `handleSomething`.

**Everyday picture.** A **doorbell**. You don't press it when you install it (that's `onClick={handleClick()}`); you wire it so it rings when a visitor presses it later. Event delegation is a building with **one receptionist** at the entrance who knows which flat each visitor wants, instead of a guard at every door.

**What happens on a click, traced by hand:**

```text
<div onClick={logDiv}>           ← parent handler
  <button onClick={buy}>Buy</button>
</div>

1. The user clicks the button; the browser fires a native "click" on the <button>.
2. It bubbles to React's single listener on the root container.
3. React finds the component path root → div → button and builds a SyntheticEvent.
4. Bubbling order in React: buy(e) runs, then logDiv(e).
5. If buy called e.stopPropagation(), logDiv is skipped.
```

**When to put logic in handlers:** anything caused by a specific user action (add to cart, submit, toggle). **When not:** work that must happen because the component is **on screen** (a chat connection) belongs in an effect (Section [30](#30-effects-synchronising-with-systems-outside-react)); calculations from props/state belong in rendering.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ `onClick={handleClick()}`: calls it during render. ✅ `onClick={handleClick}` or `onClick={() => handleClick(id)}`.
- ❌ Lowercase `onclick`: React ignores it (and TypeScript rejects it).
- ❌ Forgetting `e.preventDefault()` in `onSubmit`.
- ❌ Using `e.target` when you mean the element with the handler: in nested markup `target` may be an inner `<span>`; `e.currentTarget` is the element the handler is on.

**Used in real software:** every interactive control; design systems expose events as typed props (`onOpenChange`, `onValueChange`) so the parent decides what happens.

### Code

**From scratch: event delegation by hand.** One listener on a container handles clicks for any number of buttons by reading a `data-` attribute, which is the trick React uses at its root:

```tsx
document.body.innerHTML = `<div id="toolbar"><button data-action="play">▶ <b>Play</b></button><button data-action="stop">■ Stop</button></div>`;
const toolbar = document.querySelector("#toolbar")!;
toolbar.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = (event.target as Element).closest("button");   // the clicked <b> is inside the button
  if (button) console.log("one listener handled:", button.dataset.action);
});
(document.querySelector("b") as HTMLElement).click();
(document.querySelectorAll("button")[1] as HTMLElement).click();
```

**Output:**

```text
one listener handled: play
one listener handled: stop
```

`closest("button")` walks up from the clicked element to the nearest `button`, so clicking the bold text inside still counts. `dataset.action` reads `data-action`.

**The React way: handler props, the event object, and passing arguments:**

```tsx
import type { MouseEvent } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function Toolbar() {
  function handlePlay(e: MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) {
    console.log("play | target:", (e.target as Element).tagName, "| currentTarget:", e.currentTarget.tagName, "| native:", e.nativeEvent.type);
  }
  const handleSpeed = (speed: number) => console.log("speed set to", speed);
  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={handlePlay}>▶ <b>Play</b></button>
      {[1, 1.5, 2].map((s) => <button key={s} onClick={() => handleSpeed(s)}>{s}×</button>)}
    </div>
  );
}
render(<Toolbar />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Play"));            // click the <b> inside the button
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("1.5×"));
```

**Output:**

```text
play | target: B | currentTarget: BUTTON | native: click
speed set to 1.5
```

`e.target` is the `B` that was clicked; `e.currentTarget` is the `BUTTON` whose handler runs. Wrapping in an arrow (`() => handleSpeed(s)`) is how you pass an argument.

**Propagation: bubbling, `stopPropagation` and capture:**

```tsx
function Card() {
  return (
    <div onClick={() => console.log("card clicked (open details)")} onClickCapture={() => console.log("capture: card sees it first")}>
      <h3>Masala chai</h3>
      <button onClick={(e) => { e.stopPropagation(); console.log("added to cart"); }}>Add</button>
    </div>
  );
}
render(<Card />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Masala chai"));
console.log("---");
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Add"));
```

**Output:**

```text
capture: card sees it first
card clicked (open details)
---
capture: card sees it first
added to cart
```

Clicking the title bubbles up and opens the details; clicking **Add** stops propagation, so the card's `onClick` doesn't fire (the capture handler still runs first, on the way down).

**Custom event props: the child reports, the parent decides:**

```tsx
function PlayButton({ onPlay, children }: { onPlay: () => void; children: string }) {
  return <button onClick={onPlay}>{children}</button>;
}
function Player() {
  return <PlayButton onPlay={() => console.log("Player decided: start playback")}>Play song</PlayButton>;
}
render(<Player />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
```

**Output:**

```text
Player decided: start playback
```

**Where React listens:** React 17 and later attach listeners to the root container, not to each button and not to `document`. We can see it by watching which element's `addEventListener` React calls:

```tsx
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { act } from "react";

const container = document.createElement("div");
const original = container.addEventListener.bind(container);
const types = new Set<string>();
container.addEventListener = ((type: string, ...rest: any[]) => { types.add(type); return (original as any)(type, ...rest); }) as any;
await act(async () => createRoot(container).render(<button>hi</button>));
console.log("listeners React added on the root container:", types.size, "| includes click?", types.has("click"));
```

**Output:**

```text
listeners React added on the root container: 87 | includes click? true
```

React registers every event type it supports once on the root (both bubbling and capture versions), however many handlers your components declare.

### Practice

1. A button inside a clickable row must delete the row without opening it. Write `Row({ onOpen, onDelete })`.
2. What's wrong with `<button onClick={setCount(count + 1)}>+</button>`?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function Row({ onOpen, onDelete }: { onOpen: () => void; onDelete: () => void }) {
  return (
    <li onClick={onOpen}>
      Order #42
      <button onClick={(e) => { e.stopPropagation(); onDelete(); }}>Delete</button>
    </li>
  );
}
render(<ul><Row onOpen={() => console.log("open")} onDelete={() => console.log("delete")} /></ul>);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Delete"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/Order #42/));
```

**Output:**

```text
delete
open
```

1. `stopPropagation()` in the inner handler keeps the click from reaching the row.
2. `setCount(count + 1)` runs **during render**, which schedules another render, which runs it again: React stops this loop with a "Too many re-renders" error. Use `onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}`.

</details>

## 14. State: A Component's Memory (useState)

![useState returns the current value and a setter; calling the setter stores the new value and asks React to render the component again, which reads the new value](images/react/14-usestate.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** a normal variable inside a component is **forgotten** after every render, and changing it doesn't update the screen. **State** fixes both: `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)` gives the component a value React **remembers** between renders, and a **setter** that updates the value **and re-renders** the component. Each copy of a component on screen has its **own** state.

**Words to know:**

- **State:** data a component remembers between renders and that changes over time, causing re-renders when it does.
- **Hook:** a special function whose name starts with `use` (`useState`, `useEffect`…) that lets a component "hook into" React features. Hooks may only be called at the top level of a component or another hook (Section [39](#39-how-hooks-work-inside-build-usestate-from-scratch-and-the-rules-of-hooks)).
- **`useState(initial)`:** declares a state variable; returns a pair `[value, setValue]` (array destructuring lets you name them).
- **Setter (set function):** `setCount(5)` or `setCount(c => c + 1)`; stores the next value and queues a re-render.
- **Initial value:** used only on the **first** render; later renders ignore the argument.
- **Lazy initializer:** `useState(() => expensiveSetup())`: pass a **function** so the expensive setup runs only on the first render, not every render.
- **Local / isolated state:** each rendered instance of a component has independent state; two `<Counter />`s count separately.
- **Stateful vs stateless component:** one that has state vs one that only uses props.
- **Re-render:** React calling the component again (with the new state) to compute new JSX.

**Everyday picture.** A **sticky note on your monitor**. A normal variable is a thought you have during one meeting and forget when it ends (every render starts from scratch). State is the sticky note: React keeps it next to that particular component (each desk has its own note), and writing a new number on it (the setter) makes the component "re-read" its note and redraw.

**Why a plain variable fails, traced by hand:**

```text
function Counter() { let count = 0; return <button onClick={() => { count = count + 1; }}>{count}</button>; }

render 1: count = 0 → button shows 0
click:    the handler sets the local count to 1 … but nothing asks React to render again → screen still 0
(if something else re-rendered it) render 2: the function runs again → let count = 0 → still 0
```

With `useState`: render 1 reads 0 → click calls `setCount(1)` → React stores 1 and renders again → render 2 reads **1** from React's memory → the button shows 1.

**When to use state:** for data that changes over time **and** affects what's shown (input text, open/closed, selected tab, fetched data). **When not:** values you can **calculate** from props or other state (a total, a filtered list; Section [22](#22-choosing-the-state-structure)), values that don't affect rendering (a timer id → a ref, Section [28](#28-refs-remembering-values-without-re-rendering)), and constants.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Using a normal variable for something that changes on screen.
- ❌ Expecting `count` to change immediately after `setCount` (it's a snapshot; Section [16](#16-state-as-a-snapshot-batching-and-updater-functions)).
- ❌ `useState(expensive())`, which runs `expensive()` on every render. ✅ `useState(() => expensive())` or `useState(expensive)`.
- ❌ Calling `useState` inside an `if`, a loop or a nested function (breaks the Rules of Hooks).

**Used in real software:** UI state everywhere: whether a dropdown is open, the current step in a checkout, the text in a search box, the selected photo in a gallery.

### Code

**From scratch: why a local variable isn't enough.** The variable changes, but React has no idea, so the page doesn't:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function BrokenCounter() {
  let count = 0;
  return <button onClick={() => { count = count + 1; console.log("local count is now", count); }}>clicked {count} times</button>;
}
render(<BrokenCounter />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
console.log("screen shows:", screen.getByRole("button").textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
local count is now 1
local count is now 2
screen shows: clicked 0 times
```

**From scratch: memory that survives a "render".** Keep the value **outside** the render function and redraw when it changes; this is the idea `useState` packages up (the full hand-made `useState` is in Section [39](#39-how-hooks-work-inside-build-usestate-from-scratch-and-the-rules-of-hooks)):

```tsx
function makeCounterWidget(container: HTMLElement) {
  let memory = 0;                                    // lives outside renderOnce, like React's state storage
  function setMemory(next: number) { memory = next; renderOnce(); }
  function renderOnce() {
    container.innerHTML = `<button>clicked ${memory} times</button>`;
    container.querySelector("button")!.onclick = () => setMemory(memory + 1);
  }
  renderOnce();
}
const box = document.createElement("div");
makeCounterWidget(box);
box.querySelector("button")!.click(); box.querySelector("button")!.click();
console.log(box.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<button>clicked 2 times</button>
```

**The React way: `useState`:**

```tsx
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>clicked {count} times</button>;
}
render(<Counter />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
console.log("screen shows:", screen.getByRole("button").textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
screen shows: clicked 2 times
```

**Several state variables, and each instance is independent.** A photo gallery: one component, two copies, separate memories:

```tsx
const photos = ["Darjeeling garden", "Assam estate", "Nilgiri hills"];

function Gallery({ title }: { title: string }) {
  const [index, setIndex] = useState(0);
  const [showDetails, setShowDetails] = useState(false);
  return (
    <section aria-label={title}>
      <h3>{title}: {photos[index]} ({index + 1} of {photos.length})</h3>
      <button onClick={() => setIndex((index + 1) % photos.length)}>Next {title}</button>
      <button onClick={() => setShowDetails(!showDetails)}>{showDetails ? "Hide" : "Show"} details {title}</button>
      {showDetails && <p>Grown at high altitude.</p>}
    </section>
  );
}

const { container } = render(<><Gallery title="A" /><Gallery title="B" /></>);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Next A"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Next A"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Show details B"));
console.log([...container.querySelectorAll("section")].map((s) => s.textContent).join("\n"));
```

**Output:**

```text
A: Nilgiri hills (3 of 3)Next AShow details A
B: Darjeeling garden (1 of 3)Next BHide details BGrown at high altitude.
```

`(index + 1) % photos.length` wraps back to 0 after the last photo (`%` is the remainder). Gallery A moved twice; gallery B didn't move but shows its details.

**The initial value is used once; a lazy initializer runs once:**

```tsx
let setupCalls = 0;
function loadSavedDraft() { setupCalls++; return "Ring the bell"; }

function Draft({ lazy }: { lazy: boolean }) {
  const [draft, setDraft] = lazy ? useState(() => loadSavedDraft()) : useState(loadSavedDraft());
  return <input value={draft} onChange={(e) => setDraft(e.target.value)} />;
}
for (const lazy of [false, true]) {
  setupCalls = 0;
  const { unmount } = render(<Draft lazy={lazy} />);
  for (const text of ["R", "Ri", "Rin"]) fireEvent.change(screen.getByRole("textbox"), { target: { value: text } });
  console.log(lazy ? "lazy:  " : "eager: ", "setup ran", setupCalls, "times over 4 renders");
  unmount();
}
```

**Output:**

```text
eager:  setup ran 4 times over 4 renders
lazy:   setup ran 1 times over 4 renders
```

(Calling a hook inside a ternary normally breaks the Rules of Hooks; it's safe here only because `lazy` never changes for a given instance. Don't do this in real code.)

### Practice

1. Build a `LikeButton` that shows `🤍 0`, becomes `❤️ 1` when clicked, and goes back to `🤍 0` on a second click.
2. A `Form` has `const [firstName, setFirstName] = useState("")` and `const [lastName, setLastName] = useState("")`. Is one object `useState({ firstName: "", lastName: "" })` better? When?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function LikeButton() {
  const [liked, setLiked] = useState(false);
  return <button onClick={() => setLiked(!liked)}>{liked ? "❤️ 1" : "🤍 0"}</button>;
}
render(<LikeButton />);
const btn = screen.getByRole("button");
const seen = [btn.textContent];
fireEvent.click(btn); seen.push(btn.textContent);
fireEvent.click(btn); seen.push(btn.textContent);
console.log(seen.join(" → "));
```

**Output:**

```text
🤍 0 → ❤️ 1 → 🤍 0
```

1. One boolean is enough: the count is derived from it, so it isn't separate state.
2. Separate variables are simplest when values change independently. One object is good when fields always change together or there are many of them (a form), but then you must copy the object when updating one field (Section [17](#17-updating-objects-in-state)).

</details>

## 15. Render and Commit: What Happens When State Changes

![Trigger, render, commit: a state update triggers a render (React calls components to compute new JSX), then the commit applies only the differences to the DOM, then the browser paints](images/react/02-render-cycle.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** getting something on screen happens in three steps. **Trigger:** the first render, or a state update. **Render:** React calls your components to find out what the UI should look like now. **Commit:** React compares the result with the previous one and changes **only the DOM nodes that differ**. Then the browser paints. "Rendering" in React means *calling your components*, not touching the screen.

**Words to know:**

- **Trigger:** what starts a render: the initial `root.render(...)`, or a state setter being called (in this component or an ancestor).
- **Render (React):** calling component functions to compute JSX; pure and side-effect free (Section [10](#10-keeping-components-pure)).
- **Commit:** applying the computed changes to the DOM (insert, update, remove nodes) in one go.
- **Initial render vs re-render:** the first render creates all DOM nodes; re-renders only update what changed.
- **Recursive rendering:** when a component re-renders, React also re-renders all of its children by default (whether or not their props changed); Section [44](#44-why-components-re-render-and-measuring-with-the-profiler) and Section [45](#45-memo-usememo-usecallback-and-the-react-compiler) cover skipping that.
- **Bail out:** if a setter is called with a value equal to the current one (`Object.is`), React may skip re-rendering that component.
- **Paint:** the browser drawing the updated DOM on screen, after the commit.
- **`MutationObserver`:** a browser API that reports DOM changes; used below to count exactly what React changed.

**Everyday picture.** A **restaurant order**. The customer ordering (trigger) → the chef cooking from the recipe (render: computing what the plate should be) → the waiter bringing **only the new dish** to the table and leaving the rest (commit) → the customer seeing it (paint). The waiter doesn't clear and re-lay the whole table for one extra dish.

**One click, traced:**

```text
<Clock time={time} /> renders <h1>{time}</h1><input />
state "time" changes from 10:00 to 10:01 (trigger)
render: React calls Clock → <h1>10:01</h1><input />
compare with last result: h1 text differs; input is identical
commit: React sets the h1's text node to "10:01"; the <input> DOM node is untouched (keeps focus and typed text)
paint: the browser redraws the heading
```

**When it matters:** understanding this explains why typed text survives re-renders, why "re-render" isn't expensive by itself, and where to put side effects (never in render). **When not to worry:** re-rendering is usually cheap; only optimise after measuring (Section [44](#44-why-components-re-render-and-measuring-with-the-profiler)).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Thinking "re-render" means the DOM is rebuilt. It doesn't; only differences are committed.
- ❌ Thinking a child only re-renders when its props change. By default it re-renders whenever its parent does.
- ❌ Doing side effects during render because "it only renders once" (it may render many times).

**Used in real software:** the same three phases exist in every React renderer: React DOM (web), React Native (mobile views), and libraries that render React to PDFs, terminals (Ink) or 3D scenes (React Three Fiber).

### Code

**Counting real DOM changes.** A `MutationObserver` records every DOM change React makes during the commit; the component logs each render:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent, act } from "@testing-library/react";

function Clock({ time }: { time: string }) {
  console.log("  render Clock", time);
  return (
    <>
      <h1>{time}</h1>
      <input aria-label="note" />
      <Footer />
    </>
  );
}
function Footer() {
  console.log("  render Footer (no props, still re-rendered)");
  return <small>Chai Point</small>;
}
function App() {
  const [time, setTime] = useState("10:00");
  return <><Clock time={time} /><button onClick={() => setTime("10:01")}>tick</button></>;
}

const { container } = render(<App />);
const input = screen.getByLabelText("note") as HTMLInputElement;
fireEvent.change(input, { target: { value: "less sugar" } });   // the user types a note first
const changes: string[] = [];
const observer = new MutationObserver((records) => records.forEach((r) => changes.push(`${r.type} on ${r.target.nodeName}`)));
observer.observe(container, { subtree: true, childList: true, characterData: true, attributes: true });
console.log("click:");
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("tick"));
await act(async () => {});                           // let the observer deliver its records
console.log("DOM changes committed:", changes);
console.log("input untouched:", screen.getByLabelText("note") === input, (screen.getByLabelText("note") as HTMLInputElement).value);
```

**Output:**

```text
  render Clock 10:00
  render Footer (no props, still re-rendered)
click:
  render Clock 10:01
  render Footer (no props, still re-rendered)
DOM changes committed: [
  'characterData on #text',
  'attributes on INPUT',
  'attributes on INPUT'
]
input untouched: true less sugar
```

Both components **rendered** again, yet the commit changed exactly **one** text node: the heading's. The two attribute records are React DOM's routine housekeeping on `<input>` elements: whenever it updates one, it briefly sets and then removes the `name` attribute (a guard that keeps radio-button groups consistent). The input element itself is the same object and still holds its text, so nothing the user typed was lost.

**Compare: redraw-everything by hand** (Section [5](#5-why-react-updating-a-page-by-hand-vs-describing-it)) changes far more of the DOM for the same update:

```tsx
const box = document.createElement("div");
document.body.appendChild(box);
const draw = (time: string) => { box.innerHTML = `<h1>${time}</h1><input aria-label="note"><small>Chai Point</small>`; };
draw("10:00");
let count = 0;
const watcher = new MutationObserver((records) => { count += records.reduce((n, r) => n + r.addedNodes.length + r.removedNodes.length, 0); });
watcher.observe(box, { subtree: true, childList: true, characterData: true });
draw("10:01");
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0));
console.log("nodes removed + added by the innerHTML redraw:", count);
```

**Output:**

```text
nodes removed + added by the innerHTML redraw: 6
```

**Bail out on the same value.** Setting state to the value it already has doesn't re-render the component:

```tsx
let renders = 0;
function Toggle() {
  renders++;
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false);
  return <button onClick={() => setOn(true)}>{on ? "on" : "off"}</button>;
}
render(<Toggle />);
const counts = [renders];
for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) { fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button")); counts.push(renders); }
console.log("total renders after each click (all clicks set true):", counts.join(" → "));
```

**Output:**

```text
total renders after each click (all clicks set true): 1 → 2 → 3 → 3 → 3
```

The first click changes `false` to `true` (a render). The second click sets `true` again: React renders the component **once more** because it can't always know cheaply that nothing changed, then sees the same value and throws that result away (no commit, children skipped). From then on it bails out before rendering at all. So "same value" means "no commit and no re-render of children", not always "zero renders".

### Practice

1. A parent re-renders 10 times per second (a clock). Its child `<ProductList />` receives no props. How many times does `ProductList` render per second by default, and how many DOM changes does it cause?
2. True or false: calling `setState` makes React rebuild the whole DOM of that component.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. 10 renders per second (children re-render with their parent), but **zero** DOM changes if its output doesn't change: render is computation; commit only applies differences. If those renders are expensive, `memo` or the React Compiler can skip them (Section [45](#45-memo-usememo-usecallback-and-the-react-compiler)), or move the clock state down into a small component (Section [44](#44-why-components-re-render-and-measuring-with-the-profiler)).
2. False. React re-runs the component and commits only the nodes whose output differs.

</details>
