## 24. Preserving and Resetting State: Tree Position and Keys

![React keeps state by position in the tree: the same component type at the same position keeps its state; a different type or a different key resets it](images/react/24-preserve-reset.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** state isn't stored "inside" your component function; React keeps it next to the component's **position in the UI tree**. As long as the **same component type** renders at the **same position**, its state is **kept**, even if its props change. Render a different type there, or remove it, and the state is **destroyed**. To deliberately reset a component (a chat box when you switch contacts), give it a different **`key`**.

**Words to know:**

- **UI tree / render tree:** the tree of components React builds from your JSX; state is attached to positions in it.
- **Position:** where a component sits among its parent's children (first child, second child…), regardless of variable names in your code.
- **Preserved state:** the same type at the same position across renders keeps its state.
- **Reset (remount):** React destroys a component and its whole subtree's state and creates a fresh one: when its type changes, it's removed, or its key changes.
- **Mount / unmount:** a component appearing in the tree (created) / disappearing from it (destroyed, state lost).
- **`key` outside lists:** any component can take a key; changing it tells React "this is a different instance", so it resets.
- **Nested component definition bug:** defining a component inside another creates a **new type** every render, so React resets it every render.
- **Preserving hidden state:** to keep state of something that's hidden, keep it rendered but hidden with CSS, lift its state up, or use `<Activity>` (Section [63](#63-transitions-usetransition-usedeferredvalue-activity-and-viewtransition)).

**Everyday picture.** **Hotel rooms.** The hotel (React) remembers what's in room 2 (position), not who you are. If a guest of the same kind stays on (same type), their luggage stays. Swap in a different kind of occupant (a different type) and the room is cleared. And if reception issues a new booking number for the room (a new key), it's cleaned out even though it's still room 2.

**Same position, different variables, traced:**

```text
{isFancy ? <Counter isFancy={true} /> : <Counter isFancy={false} />}
→ both branches put a <Counter> as the FIRST child → same type, same position → state KEPT when isFancy flips

{isPaused ? <p>See you later!</p> : <Counter />}
→ position 1 changes from Counter to p → Counter unmounted → its state DESTROYED

{isPlayerA ? <Counter key="Taylor" /> : <Counter key="Sarah" />}
→ different keys → React treats them as different counters → each switch RESETS
```

**When to reset with a key:** switching which record an editor shows (chat recipient, profile being edited), resetting a form after submit, restarting an animation. **When to preserve:** tabs where users expect their scroll position or draft to survive (keep them mounted, or lift state up).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Defining components inside components (state resets every render, inputs lose focus on each keystroke).
- ❌ Expecting state to reset when only props change (it doesn't; use a key, or derive from props).
- ❌ Using an effect to reset state when a prop changes; a key is simpler and avoids a wasted render (Section [32](#32-you-might-not-need-an-effect)).

**Used in real software:** `key={userId}` on profile and chat screens is a standard pattern; routers reset page state by rendering a different component per route; editors reset the form with `key={document.id}`.

### Code

**Same type, same position: state survives a prop change:**

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function Counter({ person, fancy = false }: { person: string; fancy?: boolean }) {
  const [score, setScore] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setScore(score + 1)}>{fancy ? "✨ " : ""}{person}: {score}</button>;
}
function Scoreboard({ mode }: { mode: "position" | "key" }) {
  const [isA, setIsA] = useState(true);
  return (
    <>
      {mode === "position"
        ? (isA ? <Counter person="Taylor" /> : <Counter person="Sarah" fancy />)
        : (isA ? <Counter key="Taylor" person="Taylor" /> : <Counter key="Sarah" person="Sarah" />)}
      <button onClick={() => setIsA(!isA)}>next player</button>
    </>
  );
}
for (const mode of ["position", "key"] as const) {
  const { unmount } = render(<Scoreboard mode={mode} />);
  const scoreButton = () => screen.getAllByRole("button")[0];
  fireEvent.click(scoreButton()); fireEvent.click(scoreButton()); fireEvent.click(scoreButton());
  const before = scoreButton().textContent;
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("next player"));
  console.log(`${mode.padEnd(8)}: ${before} → after switching: ${scoreButton().textContent}`);
  unmount();
}
```

**Output:**

```text
position: Taylor: 3 → after switching: ✨ Sarah: 3
key     : Taylor: 3 → after switching: Sarah: 0
```

Without keys, Sarah **inherits** Taylor's score of 3: React only sees "a Counter at position 1" both times. With different keys, Sarah starts at 0.

**A different type at the same position destroys the state:**

```tsx
function PauseDemo() {
  const [paused, setPaused] = useState(false);
  return <>{paused ? <p>See you later!</p> : <Counter person="Ravi" />}<button onClick={() => setPaused(!paused)}>toggle</button></>;
}
render(<PauseDemo />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Ravi: 0"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Ravi: 1"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("toggle"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("toggle"));
console.log("after pausing and resuming:", screen.getAllByRole("button")[0].textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
after pausing and resuming: Ravi: 0
```

**Resetting a form with a key:** switching chat contact should clear the draft:

```tsx
const contacts = [{ id: 1, name: "Asha" }, { id: 2, name: "Ravi" }];
function Chat({ contact }: { contact: { id: number; name: string } }) {
  const [text, setText] = useState("");
  return <textarea aria-label="draft" placeholder={`Chat to ${contact.name}`} value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)} />;
}
function Messenger({ useKey }: { useKey: boolean }) {
  const [to, setTo] = useState(contacts[0]);
  return (
    <>
      {contacts.map((c) => <button key={c.id} onClick={() => setTo(c)}>{c.name}</button>)}
      {useKey ? <Chat key={to.id} contact={to} /> : <Chat contact={to} />}
    </>
  );
}
for (const useKey of [false, true]) {
  const { unmount } = render(<Messenger useKey={useKey} />);
  fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("draft"), { target: { value: "Hi Asha, chai at 5?" } });
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Ravi"));
  const draft = screen.getByLabelText("draft") as HTMLTextAreaElement;
  console.log(useKey ? "key={to.id}:" : "no key:     ", `${draft.placeholder} → "${draft.value}"`);
  unmount();
}
```

**Output:**

```text
no key:      Chat to Ravi → "Hi Asha, chai at 5?"
key={to.id}: Chat to Ravi → ""
```

Without the key, the message meant for Asha is still in the box after switching to Ravi: easy to send to the wrong person.

**The nested-definition bug:** the inner component is a **new type** on every render, so its state resets each time the parent re-renders:

```tsx
function Parent() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  function Inner() {                                   // ❌ defined inside Parent
    const [text, setText] = useState("");
    return <input aria-label="inner" value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)} />;
  }
  return <><Inner /><button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>parent re-render {count}</button></>;
}
render(<Parent />);
const before = screen.getByLabelText("inner");
fireEvent.change(before, { target: { value: "typed text" } });
fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
const after = screen.getByLabelText("inner") as HTMLInputElement;
console.log(`same input element? ${after === before} | value now: "${after.value}"`);
```

**Output:**

```text
same input element? false | value now: ""
```

### Practice

1. A profile editor shows `<ProfileForm user={user} />` and keeps old field values when you pick a different user. Fix it in one attribute.
2. Two tabs, "Write" and "Preview", render `{tab === "write" ? <Editor /> : <Preview />}`. Switching to Preview and back loses the draft. Give two fixes.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. `<ProfileForm key={user.id} user={user} />`: a new key per user remounts the form with fresh state.
2. (a) Lift the draft state into the parent and pass it to `Editor` as `value`/`onChange`; (b) keep both mounted and hide the inactive one (CSS `hidden`, or React 19.2's `<Activity mode="hidden">`, which keeps state while hidden, Section [63](#63-transitions-usetransition-usedeferredvalue-activity-and-viewtransition)).

</details>

## 25. Composition: children, Slots and Layout Components

![Composition: a Card component renders whatever it receives as children; slots are extra props that take JSX (header, footer, actions); passing elements down avoids prop drilling](images/react/25-composition.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** components can take **other JSX as input**. Whatever you nest between a component's tags arrives as the **`children`** prop, so a `Card`, `Modal` or `Layout` can wrap any content without knowing what it is. For several "holes", pass JSX through ordinary props (**slots**: `header`, `footer`, `actions`). Building UIs by putting components inside components (**composition**) is how React reuses code, instead of inheritance.

**Words to know:**

- **Composition:** building complex components by combining simpler ones, passing components and elements into each other.
- **`children`:** the prop containing the JSX between a component's opening and closing tags.
- **Slot (named slot):** a prop that receives JSX for a specific place: `<Layout sidebar={<Nav />} main={<Feed />} />`.
- **Container / layout component:** a component whose job is arrangement and styling (a card frame, a two-column page) and which renders `children` inside.
- **Wrapper component:** wraps children to add behaviour or styling (`<Tooltip text="…"><button/></Tooltip>`).
- **Specialisation:** making a specific component by configuring a generic one (`WelcomeDialog` renders `Dialog` with fixed title).
- **Prop drilling:** passing a prop through many intermediate components that don't use it, only to reach a deep child.
- **Passing elements to avoid drilling:** the parent that owns the data creates the deep element itself and passes it **down as JSX** through the layout, so the middle layers never see the data.
- **Render prop:** a prop that is a **function returning JSX** (`renderItem={(item) => <Row … />}`), letting the parent decide how each part renders (more in Section [67](#67-legacy-react-class-components-lifecycles-hocs-and-render-props)).
- **`ReactNode`:** the TypeScript type for anything renderable (elements, strings, numbers, arrays, `null`), used for `children` and slot props.
- **Inheritance:** making a class from another class; React apps essentially never use it for components; composition covers every case.

**Everyday picture.** A **picture frame**. The framer (the `Card` component) makes the frame, mount and glass without caring whether you put a family photo, a certificate or a child's drawing in it (`children`). A frame with a separate slot for a nameplate is a component with a `footer` slot.

**Passing elements to avoid drilling, traced:**

```text
drilling:  App(user) → Page(user) → Sidebar(user) → Avatar(user)      Page and Sidebar only pass it along
composed:  App(user) renders  <Page sidebar={<Sidebar><Avatar user={user} /></Sidebar>} />
           Page just places {sidebar}; Sidebar just places {children}; neither knows "user" exists
```

**When to use which:** `children` for one content area; slot props for several areas; a render prop when the parent must render per-item content with data the child provides; context (Section [36](#36-context-passing-data-deeply)) when **many** components at different depths need the same data. **When not:** don't pass JSX through props just to avoid writing a small, clear prop chain of two levels.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Reaching into `children` to change them (`React.Children`, `cloneElement` are legacy tools; prefer explicit props).
- ❌ Reaching for context or a global store at the first sign of prop drilling, before trying composition.
- ❌ Typing `children` as `JSX.Element` (rejects strings and lists). ✅ `React.ReactNode`.

**Used in real software:** every design system's `Card`, `Dialog`, `Popover`, `Layout` and `Tabs` take `children` and slots; Next.js layouts receive the page as `children` (Section [62](#62-nextjs-app-router-layouts-server-functions-and-caching)); libraries like Radix UI and shadcn/ui are built almost entirely from composition.

### Code

**`children`: a frame for any content:**

```tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function Card({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return <div className="card">{children}</div>;
}
const html = render(
  <>
    <Card><h2>Masala chai</h2><p>₹180</p></Card>
    <Card>Just some text, 42, and a list: {["a", "b"]}</Card>
  </>,
).container.innerHTML;
console.log(html);
```

**Output:**

```text
<div class="card"><h2>Masala chai</h2><p>₹180</p></div><div class="card">Just some text, 42, and a list: ab</div>
```

**Slots: several holes, filled with JSX props:**

```tsx
function Dialog({ title, children, actions }: { title: ReactNode; children: ReactNode; actions?: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <section role="dialog" aria-label={typeof title === "string" ? title : undefined}>
      <header>{title}</header>
      <div>{children}</div>
      {actions && <footer>{actions}</footer>}
    </section>
  );
}
function ConfirmDelete({ onConfirm }: { onConfirm: () => void }) {      // specialisation of Dialog
  return (
    <Dialog title="Delete order?" actions={<><button>Cancel</button><button onClick={onConfirm}>Delete</button></>}>
      This can't be undone.
    </Dialog>
  );
}
console.log(render(<ConfirmDelete onConfirm={() => {}} />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<section role="dialog" aria-label="Delete order?"><header>Delete order?</header><div>This can't be undone.</div><footer><button>Cancel</button><button>Delete</button></footer></section>
```

**Avoiding prop drilling by passing elements down.** First the drilled version, then the composed one; the middle components shrink to pure layout:

```tsx
type User = { name: string; plan: string };
function AvatarBadge({ user }: { user: User }) { return <b>{user.name} ({user.plan})</b>; }

// drilled: Page and Sidebar take `user` only to pass it on
function DrilledSidebar({ user }: { user: User }) { return <aside><AvatarBadge user={user} /></aside>; }
function DrilledPage({ user }: { user: User }) { return <main><DrilledSidebar user={user} /><article>Feed</article></main>; }

// composed: Page and Sidebar know nothing about users
function Sidebar({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { return <aside>{children}</aside>; }
function Page({ sidebar, children }: { sidebar: ReactNode; children: ReactNode }) { return <main>{sidebar}<article>{children}</article></main>; }

const user = { name: "Asha", plan: "Pro" };
const a = render(<DrilledPage user={user} />).container.innerHTML;
const b = render(<Page sidebar={<Sidebar><AvatarBadge user={user} /></Sidebar>}>Feed</Page>).container.innerHTML;
console.log(a === b, b);
```

**Output:**

```text
true <main><aside><b>Asha (Pro)</b></aside><article>Feed</article></main>
```

Same HTML, but in the composed version only the top component and `AvatarBadge` mention `user`.

**A render prop: the list decides *where*, the parent decides *how*:**

```tsx
function List<T>({ items, renderItem, empty = "Nothing here" }: { items: T[]; renderItem: (item: T, index: number) => ReactNode; empty?: ReactNode }) {
  if (items.length === 0) return <p>{empty}</p>;
  return <ul>{items.map((item, i) => <li key={i}>{renderItem(item, i)}</li>)}</ul>;
}
const orders = [{ id: 90312, total: 1499 }, { id: 90313, total: 180 }];
console.log(render(<List items={orders} renderItem={(o) => <>#{o.id}: ₹{o.total}</>} />).container.innerHTML);
console.log(render(<List items={[] as string[]} renderItem={(s) => s} empty={<em>No orders yet</em>} />).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<ul><li>#90312: ₹1499</li><li>#90313: ₹180</li></ul>
<p><em>No orders yet</em></p>
```

`List<T>` is a **generic component**: TypeScript works out `T` from `items`, so `o` in `renderItem` is known to have `id` and `total` (Section [26](#26-typescript-with-react-typing-props-state-events-and-children)). Index keys are acceptable here only because this demo list never reorders.

**Composition and state: `children` keep their own state when a wrapper re-renders:**

```tsx
function Collapsible({ title, children }: { title: string; children: ReactNode }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(true);
  return <section><button onClick={() => setOpen(!open)}>{open ? "▾" : "▸"} {title}</button>{open && children}</section>;
}
render(<Collapsible title="Notes"><textarea aria-label="notes" defaultValue="buy cardamom" /></Collapsible>);
console.log((screen.getByLabelText("notes") as HTMLTextAreaElement).value);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/Notes/));
console.log("collapsed, textarea present?", screen.queryByLabelText("notes") !== null);
```

**Output:**

```text
buy cardamom
collapsed, textarea present? false
```

### Practice

1. Write a `TwoColumn({ left, right })` layout and use it to show a `Menu` on the left and a `Cart` on the right.
2. `App` has the logged-in user and renders `<Layout><Header /><Main /></Layout>`, and only the deep `UserMenu` (inside `Header`) needs the user. Avoid drilling through `Layout` and `Header` without context.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function TwoColumn({ left, right }: { left: ReactNode; right: ReactNode }) {
  return <div className="cols"><div>{left}</div><div>{right}</div></div>;
}
console.log(render(<TwoColumn left={<nav>Menu</nav>} right={<aside>Cart (2)</aside>} />).container.innerHTML);

function Header({ userMenu }: { userMenu: ReactNode }) { return <header>Chai Point {userMenu}</header>; }
function Layout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { return <div className="layout">{children}</div>; }
function UserMenu({ user }: { user: User }) { return <span>👤 {user.name}</span>; }
console.log(render(<Layout><Header userMenu={<UserMenu user={user} />} /><main>…</main></Layout>).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<div class="cols"><div><nav>Menu</nav></div><div><aside>Cart (2)</aside></div></div>
<div class="layout"><header>Chai Point <span>👤 Asha</span></header><main>…</main></div>
```

2. `App` builds `<UserMenu user={user} />` itself and passes it into `Header` as a slot; `Layout` and `Header` never touch `user`.

</details>

## 26. TypeScript with React: Typing Props, State, Events and Children

![What to type in a React component: props as an object type, state via inference or a generic, event handlers with React's event types, children as ReactNode, and unions for variants](images/react/26-typescript.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** TypeScript adds **types** to your JavaScript so mistakes show up in the editor instead of in front of users: a missing prop, a prop of the wrong type, a typo in a field name, calling something that might be `undefined`. In React you mostly type **props** (an object type per component); state and most other values are **inferred** automatically. A handful of React types cover the rest: `ReactNode`, event types, `ComponentProps`.

**Words to know:**

- **Type annotation:** `: string` after a name tells TypeScript its type: `function f(name: string)`.
- **Type inference:** TypeScript working out types itself: `useState(0)` → `number`.
- **Object type / `type` alias / `interface`:** describing an object's shape: `type Props = { name: string; price?: number }`; `interface Props { … }` does the same for objects.
- **Optional property (`?`):** may be missing (its type includes `undefined`).
- **Union type (`A | B`):** one of several types: `"sm" | "md" | "lg"`, `string | null`.
- **Literal type:** an exact value used as a type: `"success"`.
- **Discriminated union:** a union of object types that share a tag field (`status`), so checking the tag tells TypeScript which other fields exist.
- **Generic (`<T>`):** a type parameter, a "type variable" filled in at use: `useState<string | null>(null)`, `List<T>`.
- **`ReactNode`:** anything React can render; use it for `children` and slots.
- **Event types:** `React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`, `React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>`, `React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>`, `React.KeyboardEvent`: the type of `e` in handlers (inferred automatically when the handler is written inline).
- **`ComponentProps<"button">`:** all the props a `<button>` accepts; used to make wrapper components that pass everything through.
- **`as const`:** makes TypeScript keep exact literal values (`["sm", "md"] as const` → a readonly tuple of `"sm" | "md"`).
- **Non-null assertion (`!`):** `document.getElementById("root")!` tells TypeScript "this isn't null" (you take responsibility).
- **`tsc` / type check:** the TypeScript compiler; `tsc --noEmit` checks types without producing files.

**Everyday picture.** **Labelled sockets and plugs.** Without types, any plug fits any socket and you find out by sparks (a runtime crash). Types are shaped sockets: a three-pin plug simply won't go into a two-pin socket, so the mistake is caught while you're still building (the editor underlines it).

**What to type, decided by hand:**

| Thing | Write a type? | Example |
|---|---|---|
| props | **yes**, always | `function Card({ title }: { title: string })` |
| `useState(0)`, `useState("")` | no, inferred | `const [n, setN] = useState(0)` |
| state that starts empty | **yes**, a generic | `useState<User \| null>(null)`, `useState<string[]>([])` |
| inline handlers | no, inferred | `onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)}` |
| handlers defined separately | **yes** | `function handle(e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>)` |
| `children` / slots | **yes** | `children: React.ReactNode` |
| return type of components | no | inferred as JSX |

**When TypeScript pays off:** any app beyond a toy: refactoring a prop name updates every caller, and editors autocomplete props. **When not to fight it:** don't write complex types for things inference handles; avoid `any` (it switches checking off), and use `unknown` plus checks for data from outside (Section [54](#54-form-libraries-react-hook-form-and-zod-validation) uses Zod for that).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ `useState(null)` for something that will hold an object: inferred as `null` forever. ✅ `useState<User | null>(null)`.
- ❌ `useState([])`: inferred as `never[]`. ✅ `useState<Todo[]>([])`.
- ❌ `children: JSX.Element` (too narrow). ✅ `ReactNode`.
- ❌ `any` everywhere; ❌ `!` on values that really can be null.
- ❌ `React.FC` for every component (it used to add implicit `children`; today plain functions with typed props are the norm).

**Used in real software:** most React codebases use TypeScript (it's the default in Vite's and Next.js's templates); `@types/react` provides the types used below.

### Code

**Typed props, optional props and a union for variants:**

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import type { ReactNode, ComponentProps, ChangeEvent } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

type BadgeProps = { label: string; tone?: "info" | "success" | "danger"; count?: number };
function Badge({ label, tone = "info", count }: BadgeProps) {
  return <span className={`badge badge-${tone}`}>{label}{count !== undefined && ` (${count})`}</span>;
}
console.log(render(<><Badge label="New" /><Badge label="Paid" tone="success" count={3} /></>).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<span class="badge badge-info">New</span><span class="badge badge-success">Paid (3)</span>
```

**TypeScript catches the mistakes:** a missing required prop, a wrong type, a value outside the union, and a typo:

```tsx
type BadgeProps = { label: string; tone?: "info" | "success" | "danger"; count?: number };
function Badge(props: BadgeProps) { return <span>{props.label}</span>; }

const a = <Badge tone="info" />;
const b = <Badge label="Paid" count="3" />;
const c = <Badge label="Paid" tone="warning" />;
const d = <Badge label="Paid" colour="red" />;
```

**Compiler output:**

```text
example.tsx(4,12): error TS2741: Property 'label' is missing in type '{ tone: "info"; }' but required in type 'BadgeProps'.
example.tsx(5,31): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
example.tsx(6,31): error TS2322: Type '"warning"' is not assignable to type '"danger" | "info" | "success" | undefined'.
example.tsx(7,31): error TS2322: Type '{ label: string; colour: string; }' is not assignable to type 'IntrinsicAttributes & BadgeProps'.
  Property 'colour' does not exist on type 'IntrinsicAttributes & BadgeProps'.
```

**State that starts empty needs a generic**; otherwise the type is too narrow:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
type User = { name: string };
function Profile() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [tags, setTags] = useState([]);
  setUser({ name: "Asha" });
  setTags(["tea"]);
  return null;
}
```

**Compiler output:**

```text
example.tsx(6,13): error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'name' does not exist in type '(prevState: null) => null'.
example.tsx(7,12): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'never'.
```

**The fix,** and how narrowing makes `null` safe:

```tsx
type User = { name: string; email: string };
function Profile() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);
  const [tags, setTags] = useState<string[]>([]);
  return (
    <>
      {user === null ? <button onClick={() => { setUser({ name: "Asha", email: "asha@example.com" }); setTags(["tea"]); }}>log in</button>
                     : <p>{user.name} · {user.email} · {tags.join(",")}</p>}
    </>
  );
}
render(<Profile />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("log in"));
console.log(screen.getByText(/Asha/).textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
Asha · asha@example.com · tea
```

Inside the `: …` branch TypeScript **knows** `user` isn't `null` (narrowing), so `user.name` is allowed.

**Event types: inferred inline, written out when the handler is separate:**

```tsx
function Search({ onSearch }: { onSearch: (q: string) => void }) {
  const [q, setQ] = useState("");
  function handleChange(e: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {     // separate handler: annotate
    setQ(e.target.value);
  }
  return (
    <form onSubmit={(e) => { e.preventDefault(); onSearch(q.trim()); }}>   {/* inline: e is inferred */}
      <input aria-label="q" value={q} onChange={handleChange} />
    </form>
  );
}
render(<Search onSearch={(q) => console.log("searching for", JSON.stringify(q))} />);
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("q"), { target: { value: "  ginger  " } });
fireEvent.submit(screen.getByLabelText("q").closest("form")!);
```

**Output:**

```text
searching for "ginger"
```

**Wrapping a native element: accept all its props with `ComponentProps`:**

```tsx
type ButtonProps = ComponentProps<"button"> & { variant?: "primary" | "ghost" };
function Button({ variant = "primary", className = "", ...rest }: ButtonProps) {
  return <button {...rest} className={`btn btn-${variant} ${className}`.trim()} />;
}
console.log(render(<Button type="submit" disabled aria-label="save" onClick={() => {}}>Save</Button>).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<button type="submit" disabled="" aria-label="save" class="btn btn-primary">Save</button>
```

Every standard button prop (`type`, `disabled`, `aria-label`, `onClick`, `children`…) is accepted and type-checked, and passed through with `{...rest}`.

**Discriminated union props:** a `status` tag decides which other fields exist:

```tsx
type UploadProps =
  | { status: "uploading"; percent: number }
  | { status: "done"; url: string }
  | { status: "failed"; error: string; onRetry: () => void };

function UploadStatus(props: UploadProps) {
  switch (props.status) {
    case "uploading": return <progress value={props.percent} max={100} />;
    case "done": return <a href={props.url}>View file</a>;
    case "failed": return <p>{props.error} <button onClick={props.onRetry}>Retry</button></p>;
  }
}
console.log(render(<><UploadStatus status="uploading" percent={40} /><UploadStatus status="done" url="/f/1.pdf" /></>).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<progress value="40" max="100"></progress><a href="/f/1.pdf">View file</a>
```

In the `"done"` case TypeScript knows `props.url` exists and `props.percent` doesn't; writing `<UploadStatus status="done" percent={5} />` is a compile error.

### Practice

1. Type a `Select` component that takes `options: { value: string; label: string }[]`, `value: string` and `onChange: (value: string) => void`.
2. What's wrong with `const [items, setItems] = useState([]);` in a `.tsx` file, and what's the fix?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
type Option = { value: string; label: string };
function Select({ options, value, onChange }: { options: Option[]; value: string; onChange: (value: string) => void }) {
  return (
    <select aria-label="size" value={value} onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)}>
      {options.map((o) => <option key={o.value} value={o.value}>{o.label}</option>)}
    </select>
  );
}
function SizePicker() {
  const [size, setSize] = useState("m");
  return <><Select options={[{ value: "s", label: "Small" }, { value: "m", label: "Medium" }]} value={size} onChange={setSize} /> {size}</>;
}
const sp = render(<SizePicker />);
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("size"), { target: { value: "s" } });
console.log(sp.container.textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
SmallMedium s
```

2. The type is inferred as `never[]` (an array that can hold nothing), so `setItems([...items, newItem])` fails to compile. Write `useState<Item[]>([])`.

</details>

## 27. Styling React Apps: CSS, CSS Modules, Tailwind and CSS-in-JS

![A real screenshot of the two menu cards rendered by this section's code: an in-stock card and a sold-out card styled with plain CSS, CSS variables and a conditional class](images/react/27-styled-cards.png)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** React doesn't style anything itself; you use CSS like any web page and attach it with `className`. The main options are: **plain CSS files** (simple, global), **CSS Modules** (each component's class names made unique automatically), **Tailwind CSS** (small utility classes written directly in JSX), and **CSS-in-JS** (styles written in JavaScript). Conditional styling is just conditional class names, and **CSS variables** handle themes.

**Words to know:**

- **`className`:** the JSX prop for the HTML `class` attribute; a string of space-separated class names.
- **Global CSS:** a normal stylesheet whose class names apply everywhere; two components using `.title` clash.
- **CSS Modules:** files named `*.module.css`; the build tool renames each class to something unique (`_title_x1y2z`) and gives you an object mapping your names to the real ones: `styles.title`.
- **Utility-first CSS / Tailwind CSS:** many tiny single-purpose classes (`p-4`, `rounded-xl`, `text-green-700`) combined in `className`; Tailwind scans your files and generates only the classes you use.
- **CSS-in-JS:** writing styles in JavaScript (styled-components, Emotion); runtime versions inject `<style>` tags while the app runs, which costs performance and works poorly with Server Components, so **zero-runtime** tools (vanilla-extract, Panda CSS, StyleX) extract static CSS at build time instead.
- **Inline styles (`style={{…}}`):** fine for truly dynamic values (a progress bar's width), poor for everything else (no hover states, media queries or reuse).
- **CSS custom properties (CSS variables):** `--accent: #16a34a;` defined once and used as `var(--accent)`; change one variable to re-theme everything (dark mode).
- **`clsx` / `classnames`:** tiny helpers that join class names conditionally: `clsx("card", soldOut && "card--soldout")`.
- **Specificity:** CSS's rules for which style wins when several apply; scoped approaches (Modules, Tailwind) avoid most specificity fights.
- **Design tokens:** named values for colours, spacing and fonts shared by a design system (often as CSS variables).

**Everyday picture.** Dressing for work. **Global CSS** is one shared wardrobe for the whole family (someone always takes your shirt). **CSS Modules** sew a name tag into each item. **Tailwind** is a big box of standard pieces you combine on the spot. **CSS-in-JS** is a tailor who makes clothes as you walk in (flexible, but you wait each time, unless they pre-make them: zero-runtime).

**What CSS Modules do, traced:**

```text
Card.module.css:   .title { font-weight: 700 }
Card.tsx:          import styles from "./Card.module.css";   <h2 className={styles.title}>
build output CSS:  ._title_k3j2f_1 { font-weight: 700 }
JS object:         styles = { title: "_title_k3j2f_1" }      → <h2 class="_title_k3j2f_1">
another component's .title becomes a different name → no clash
```

**Which to choose (2026):**

| Option | Good for | Watch out |
|---|---|---|
| plain CSS + BEM naming | small apps, learning | global name clashes |
| CSS Modules | component-scoped CSS with zero new syntax (built into Vite and Next.js) | sharing variables needs CSS variables |
| Tailwind CSS v4 | fast building, consistent spacing/colours, used by shadcn/ui | long class strings; learn the naming |
| zero-runtime CSS-in-JS (vanilla-extract, StyleX, Panda) | typed styles in TS, big design systems | build setup |
| runtime CSS-in-JS (styled-components, Emotion) | existing codebases | runtime cost; Server Components need extra setup |

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ `class=` instead of `className=` (TypeScript flags it, Section [8](#8-jsx-markup-inside-javascript-and-what-it-compiles-to)).
- ❌ Building class strings with `+` and stray `false`/`undefined`: `"card " + (soldOut && "soldout")` gives `"card false"`. ✅ `clsx`.
- ❌ Inline styles for everything (no `:hover`, no media queries).
- ❌ Constructing Tailwind class names dynamically (`` `text-${color}-700` ``); Tailwind only generates classes it can find written out in full.

**Used in real software:** CSS Modules ship with Vite and Next.js; Tailwind is among the most popular styling tools and underpins shadcn/ui; Meta uses StyleX on facebook.com; CSS variables power dark mode almost everywhere.

### Code

**From scratch: conditional class names.** The naive way leaks `false` into the class; `clsx` handles it:

```tsx
import clsx from "clsx";

const soldOut = false, featured = true;
console.log(JSON.stringify("card " + (soldOut && "card--soldout")));
console.log(JSON.stringify(["card", soldOut && "card--soldout", featured && "card--featured"].filter(Boolean).join(" ")));
console.log(JSON.stringify(clsx("card", { "card--soldout": soldOut, "card--featured": featured })));
```

**Output:**

```text
"card false"
"card card--featured"
"card card--featured"
```

**Plain CSS + CSS variables + a conditional class, rendered for real.** The component is rendered to an HTML string with React DOM's server renderer (Section [58](#58-rendering-strategies-csr-ssr-ssg-and-isr)) and saved with its stylesheet; the screenshot at the top of this section is Chrome's rendering of exactly this file:

```tsx
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from "react-dom/server";
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

function MenuCard({ name, pricePaise, soldOut = false }: { name: string; pricePaise: number; soldOut?: boolean }) {
  return (
    <article className={clsx("card", soldOut && "card--soldout")} style={{ "--accent": soldOut ? "#94a3b8" : "#16a34a" } as React.CSSProperties}>
      <h2 className="card__title">{name}</h2>
      <p className="card__price">₹{(pricePaise / 100).toFixed(0)}</p>
      <button className="card__button" disabled={soldOut}>{soldOut ? "Sold out" : "Add to cart"}</button>
    </article>
  );
}
const css = `
  body { font-family: ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif; margin: 0; padding: 24px; background: #f1f5f9; display: flex; gap: 20px; }
  .card { background: white; border-radius: 16px; padding: 20px 24px; width: 220px; box-shadow: 0 1px 3px #0002; border-top: 6px solid var(--accent); }
  .card__title { margin: 0 0 4px; font-size: 20px; color: #0f172a; }
  .card__price { margin: 0 0 16px; font-size: 28px; font-weight: 700; color: var(--accent); }
  .card__button { width: 100%; padding: 10px; border: 0; border-radius: 10px; background: var(--accent); color: white; font-size: 15px; font-weight: 600; }
  .card--soldout { opacity: .75 } .card--soldout .card__title { text-decoration: line-through; }`;
const body = renderToStaticMarkup(<><MenuCard name="Masala chai" pricePaise={18000} /><MenuCard name="Kashmiri kahwa" pricePaise={26000} soldOut /></>);
writeFileSync("cards.html", `<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8"><style>${css}</style>${body}`);
console.log(body);
```

**Output:**

```text
<article class="card" style="--accent:#16a34a"><h2 class="card__title">Masala chai</h2><p class="card__price">₹180</p><button class="card__button">Add to cart</button></article><article class="card card--soldout" style="--accent:#94a3b8"><h2 class="card__title">Kashmiri kahwa</h2><p class="card__price">₹260</p><button class="card__button" disabled="">Sold out</button></article>
```

The CSS variable `--accent` is set per card through `style` (TypeScript needs the `as React.CSSProperties` cast for custom properties) and every rule reads it with `var(--accent)`: one value re-colours the border, price and button.

**CSS Modules, built for real with Vite.** These files make a tiny app; the build renames the classes:

```css
.title { font-weight: 700; color: #0f172a; }
.price { color: #16a34a; }
```

```css
.title { font-style: italic; }
```

```tsx
declare module "*.module.css" { const classes: Record<string, string>; export default classes; }
```

```tsx
import styles from "./Card.module.css";
import other from "./Other.module.css";
console.log(JSON.stringify({ card: styles, other }));
```

```html
<!doctype html><html><body><script type="module" src="/main.tsx"></script></body></html>
```

```bash
npx vite build --logLevel error > /dev/null && cat dist/assets/*.css && echo && grep -oE '\{card:\{[^}]*\},other:\{[^}]*\}\}' dist/assets/*.js
```

**Output:**

```text
._title_1hezv_1{color:#0f172a;font-weight:700}._price_1hezv_2{color:#16a34a}._title_1sido_1{font-style:italic}

{card:{title:`_title_1hezv_1`,price:`_price_1hezv_2`},other:{title:`_title_1sido_1`}}
```

Both files declared `.title`, yet they became two different names (`_title_…` with different hashes), so they can never clash. The JavaScript object (`styles.title`) holds the generated name for you to use in `className`. The small `css-modules.d.ts` file tells TypeScript what importing a `.module.css` file gives you (an object of strings); Vite's `vite/client` types include an equivalent declaration. The second line is the object, as found in the minified JavaScript bundle, that the component code receives.

**Tailwind CSS v4: the CLI scans your files and generates only the classes you used:**

```tsx
export function Badge({ soldOut }: { soldOut: boolean }) {
  return <span className={soldOut ? "rounded-full bg-slate-200 px-3 py-1 text-slate-500" : "rounded-full bg-green-100 px-3 py-1 text-green-700"}>{soldOut ? "Sold out" : "In stock"}</span>;
}
```

```css
@import "tailwindcss/theme" layer(theme);
@import "tailwindcss/utilities" layer(utilities) source(none);
@source "./Badge.tsx";
```

```bash
npx @tailwindcss/cli -i tw.css -o tw-out.css 2>/dev/null; grep -oE '^  \.[a-z0-9-]+' tw-out.css | sed 's/^  //' | sort | tr '\n' ' '; echo; grep -A2 '^  \.px-3' tw-out.css
```

**Output:**

```text
.bg-green-100 .bg-slate-200 .px-3 .py-1 .rounded-full .text-green-700 .text-slate-500 
  .px-3 {
    padding-inline: calc(var(--spacing) * 3);
  }
```

Exactly the seven utilities written in `Badge.tsx` were generated (`source(none)` switches off Tailwind's automatic scanning of the whole folder, and `@source` names the one file to scan), and each is a single small rule built from theme variables (`--spacing`), which is how Tailwind keeps spacing consistent. Writing `` `text-${tone}-700` `` would generate nothing, because Tailwind looks for complete class names in the source text.

### Practice

1. Using `clsx`, write `Tab({ active, disabled })` that always has class `tab`, adds `tab--active` when active and `tab--disabled` when disabled.
2. Why does Tailwind not style `<p className={"text-" + color + "-700"}>`, and what's the fix?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";
function Tab({ active, disabled, children }: { active?: boolean; disabled?: boolean; children: string }) {
  return <button className={clsx("tab", { "tab--active": active, "tab--disabled": disabled })} disabled={disabled}>{children}</button>;
}
console.log(render(<><Tab active>Menu</Tab><Tab>Cart</Tab><Tab disabled>Orders</Tab></>).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<button class="tab tab--active">Menu</button><button class="tab">Cart</button><button class="tab tab--disabled" disabled="">Orders</button>
```

2. Tailwind finds classes by scanning source text for complete names; `"text-" + color + "-700"` never appears in full, so no CSS is generated. Map values to full class names: `const tone = { green: "text-green-700", red: "text-red-700" }[color]`.

</details>

# Part 5 — Moderate: Escape Hatches (Refs and Effects)

> **Goal:** Step outside React's pure render-and-commit world safely: remember values without re-rendering, work with real DOM nodes, synchronise with outside systems (timers, connections, subscriptions, the document), know when an effect is the wrong tool, keep effects free of unnecessary dependencies, and fetch data without race conditions.  
> **You need:** Parts 3–4 (state, snapshots, render and commit, keys and resetting state).

---

## 28. Refs: Remembering Values Without Re-rendering

![A ref is a box React keeps between renders: you can read and write ref.current at any time and React does not re-render when it changes, unlike state](images/react/28-refs.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** a **ref** is a little box, `{ current: value }`, that React keeps for your component between renders, like state. The difference: **changing `ref.current` does not cause a re-render**. Use refs for values your component needs to **remember** but that don't affect what's **shown**: a timer id, the latest value for a callback, a DOM node (Section [29](#29-refs-to-dom-elements-focus-scroll-measure-and-media)), a counter for analytics.

**Words to know:**

- **Ref:** a plain object `{ current: … }` that persists for the component's lifetime and can be changed freely.
- **`useRef(initial)`:** returns the same ref object on every render; `initial` is used only on the first.
- **`ref.current`:** the stored value; read and write it directly (`ref.current = 5`).
- **Mutable:** a ref is meant to be mutated (unlike state, which you replace).
- **Escape hatch:** a feature for stepping outside React's normal data flow (refs, effects); useful, but use sparingly.
- **Interval / timeout id:** the number `setInterval`/`setTimeout` return; needed later to cancel with `clearInterval`/`clearTimeout`.
- **Reading refs during render:** not allowed (except for one-time lazy initialisation), because the result wouldn't update the UI and breaks purity; read and write refs in event handlers and effects.
- **Ref vs state vs variable:** a local variable resets every render; state persists **and** re-renders; a ref persists **without** re-rendering.

**Everyday picture.** A **sticky note inside a drawer**. State is a note stuck on the screen: change it and everyone sees the change (a re-render). A ref is a note in your desk drawer: you can jot things on it any time (the id of the kettle timer you started) and it stays there between meetings, but writing on it doesn't redraw the screen.

**State vs ref, traced on a click counter:**

```text
state:  click → setCount(1) → React re-renders → button shows 1
ref:    click → ref.current = 1 → no re-render → button still shows 0 (although the ref holds 1)
        any later re-render (from some other state) would read 1 … but reading it during render is the mistake
```

**When to use a ref:** timer and interval ids, the previous value of something, "latest value" storage for callbacks, DOM nodes, instances of non-React libraries (a map, a chart, a video player), flags such as "has this already run". **When not:** anything shown on screen (use state), and as a way to dodge re-renders that the UI actually needs.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Showing `ref.current` in JSX and expecting it to update.
- ❌ Writing `ref.current = …` during rendering (impure; the React Compiler's lint rules flag it).
- ❌ Using state for a timer id (an unnecessary re-render every time you store it).
- ❌ Forgetting to clear an interval whose id you stored.

**Used in real software:** debounced search inputs keep their timeout id in a ref; video players, maps (Leaflet, Mapbox) and charts (Chart.js, D3) keep their instance in a ref; form libraries keep field registrations in refs to avoid re-rendering on every keystroke (Section [54](#54-form-libraries-react-hook-form-and-zod-validation)).

### Code

**From scratch: a ref is just a state box you never replace.** `useRef` behaves like this one-liner (React's real implementation is equivalent):

```tsx
import { useRef, useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent, act } from "@testing-library/react";

function useMyRef<T>(initial: T) {
  const [box] = useState(() => ({ current: initial }));   // the same object every render; we never call a setter
  return box;
}
function Probe() {
  const mine = useMyRef(0);
  const real = useRef(0);
  const [, force] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => { mine.current++; real.current++; if (mine.current === 3) force(1); }}>{`${mine.current}/${real.current}`}</button>;
}
render(<Probe />);
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
console.log(screen.getByRole("button").textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
3/3
```

Both boxes counted every click, but the screen only caught up when the third click triggered a re-render through state. (It reads `.current` during render here only to make the hidden value visible; real code shouldn't.)

**State vs ref, side by side:**

```tsx
function Counters() {
  const [stateCount, setStateCount] = useState(0);
  const refCount = useRef(0);
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setStateCount(stateCount + 1)}>state: {stateCount}</button>
      <button onClick={() => { refCount.current++; console.log("ref is now", refCount.current, "(no re-render)"); }}>ref click</button>
    </>
  );
}
render(<Counters />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("ref click"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("ref click"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/state:/));
console.log(screen.getByText(/state:/).textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
ref is now 1 (no re-render)
ref is now 2 (no re-render)
state: 1
```

**A stopwatch: the interval id belongs in a ref, the elapsed time in state.** The timer runs for real (10 ms ticks):

```tsx
function Stopwatch() {
  const [startTime, setStartTime] = useState<number | null>(null);
  const [now, setNow] = useState<number | null>(null);
  const intervalRef = useRef<ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | null>(null);
  function handleStart() {
    setStartTime(Date.now()); setNow(Date.now());
    if (intervalRef.current) clearInterval(intervalRef.current);       // don't start two intervals
    intervalRef.current = setInterval(() => setNow(Date.now()), 10);
  }
  function handleStop() {
    if (intervalRef.current) clearInterval(intervalRef.current);       // needs the id from the ref
  }
  const seconds = startTime !== null && now !== null ? (now - startTime) / 1000 : 0;
  return <><p>{seconds >= 0.05 ? "≥ 0.05" : "< 0.05"} s elapsed</p><button onClick={handleStart}>Start</button><button onClick={handleStop}>Stop</button></>;
}
render(<Stopwatch />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Start"));
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 120)));       // let ~12 ticks happen
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Stop"));
const stopped = screen.getByText(/elapsed/).textContent;
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50)));
console.log(stopped, "| still the same after stopping?", screen.getByText(/elapsed/).textContent === stopped);
```

**Output:**

```text
≥ 0.05 s elapsed | still the same after stopping? true
```

(Exact milliseconds vary between runs, so the example prints a threshold instead of a number.) `ReturnType<typeof setInterval>` is "whatever `setInterval` returns", which differs between browsers and Node.

**Debouncing with a ref:** wait until the user stops typing for 50 ms, then search once. The pending timeout id lives in a ref so each keystroke can cancel the previous one:

```tsx
function DebouncedSearch({ onSearch }: { onSearch: (q: string) => void }) {
  const timeoutRef = useRef<ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined>(undefined);
  return (
    <input aria-label="search" onChange={(e) => {
      const q = e.target.value;
      clearTimeout(timeoutRef.current);
      timeoutRef.current = setTimeout(() => onSearch(q), 50);
    }} />
  );
}
render(<DebouncedSearch onSearch={(q) => console.log("search sent for:", q)} />);
for (const q of ["c", "ch", "cha", "chai"]) fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("search"), { target: { value: q } });
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100)));
```

**Output:**

```text
search sent for: chai
```

Four keystrokes, one request. A plain variable instead of the ref wouldn't work: each re-render would create a fresh variable and lose the previous timeout id.

### Practice

1. Build a "send in 3 seconds… Undo" button: clicking Send schedules the send; clicking Undo before it fires cancels it. Where does the timeout id go?
2. Why is `return <p>Rendered {renders.current} times</p>` with `renders.current++` in the component body wrong?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function UndoSend() {
  const [status, setStatus] = useState("idle");
  const pending = useRef<ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined>(undefined);
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => { setStatus("sending"); pending.current = setTimeout(() => setStatus("sent"), 30); }}>Send</button>
      <button onClick={() => { clearTimeout(pending.current); setStatus("cancelled"); }}>Undo</button>
      <p>{status}</p>
    </>
  );
}
render(<UndoSend />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Send"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Undo"));
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 60)));
console.log(screen.getByText(/sent|cancelled|sending/).textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
cancelled
```

1. In a ref: Undo needs the id that Send created, without causing a render when it's stored.
2. It mutates a ref during render (impure: StrictMode's double render and concurrent rendering make the count wrong) and the display won't update when only the ref changes. Count renders with the React Profiler or DevTools instead (Section [44](#44-why-components-re-render-and-measuring-with-the-profiler)).

</details>

## 29. Refs to DOM Elements: Focus, Scroll, Measure and Media

![Passing a ref to a JSX element makes React put the real DOM node in ref.current after commit, so event handlers and effects can call focus(), scrollIntoView(), getBoundingClientRect() or play()](images/react/29-dom-refs.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** sometimes you need the **real DOM node**: to focus an input, scroll to an item, measure an element's size, or play a video. Create a ref with `useRef(null)`, pass it as `ref={myRef}` to a JSX element, and after React commits, `myRef.current` is the actual DOM element. In React 19 you can pass `ref` to your **own** components as a normal prop, and a **ref callback** (a function) can run code when the node appears and clean up when it goes.

**Words to know:**

- **DOM ref:** a ref whose `current` React sets to a DOM node: `<input ref={inputRef} />`. It's `null` before the commit and after the node is removed.
- **`focus()` / `select()` / `blur()`:** DOM methods that move keyboard focus to an element / select its text / remove focus.
- **`scrollIntoView()`:** scrolls the page or container so an element is visible.
- **`getBoundingClientRect()`:** returns an element's size and position on screen (needs a real layout engine).
- **`play()` / `pause()`:** start and stop a `<video>` or `<audio>`.
- **Ref callback:** passing a **function** as `ref`: React calls it with the node when it attaches; since React 19 the function may **return a cleanup** function, called when the node detaches.
- **`ref` as a prop (React 19):** function components can accept `ref` like any prop and pass it to an inner element. Older code needed `forwardRef` for this (still supported, being phased out).
- **`useImperativeHandle`:** limits what a parent can do through a ref to a few methods you choose (Section [40](#40-more-hooks-uselayouteffect-useid-usesyncexternalstore-useimperativehandle-and-ref-as-a-prop)).
- **Layout engine:** the part of a browser that computes sizes and positions; **jsdom doesn't have one**, so measuring and scrolling can't be shown for real in these Node examples.
- **`flushSync` + scroll:** to scroll to an item added by a state update, apply the update synchronously first (Section [16](#16-state-as-a-snapshot-batching-and-updater-functions)), then scroll.

**Everyday picture.** A **name badge clipped onto a specific chair**. Normally you just say "seat the guests" (declarative JSX). Occasionally you need one particular chair (to pull it out for someone): the ref is the badge that lets you find that exact chair instantly, but only after the chairs have actually been set out (the commit).

**When `ref.current` is set, traced:**

```text
render 1:   <input ref={inputRef} />   → inputRef.current is still null (no DOM yet)
commit:     React creates <input> → sets inputRef.current = the <input> node
            (ref callbacks run here; effects run after this)
click:      handler calls inputRef.current.focus() → works
unmount:    React sets inputRef.current = null (or calls the ref callback's cleanup)
```

**When to use DOM refs:** focus management (search fields, modals, form errors), scrolling to items, measuring for tooltips and popovers, media playback, and integrating non-React widgets. **When not:** anything you can do declaratively: showing/hiding (state), changing text or classes (JSX), and **never** add/remove DOM nodes React manages (React would fight you).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Reading `ref.current` during render (it's `null` on the first render, and impure anyway).
- ❌ Changing React-managed DOM by hand (`ref.current.remove()`, `innerHTML = …`).
- ❌ Using a ref to set `value` on an input instead of state.
- ❌ Expecting `ref` on a custom component to reach a DOM node when the component doesn't pass it through.

**Used in real software:** auto-focusing a search box, returning focus to the trigger when a modal closes (Section [49](#49-accessibility-semantics-focus-aria-portals-and-modals)), "scroll to the newest message" in chat apps, virtualised lists measuring rows (Section [46](#46-long-lists-virtualisation-and-pagination)), and every wrapper around a chart, map or video player.

### Code

**From scratch: the DOM way.** Without React you find a node and call methods on it:

```tsx
document.body.innerHTML = `<input id="q"><button id="go">Search</button>`;
document.getElementById("go")!.addEventListener("click", () => (document.getElementById("q") as HTMLInputElement).focus());
(document.getElementById("go") as HTMLButtonElement).click();
console.log("focused element id:", document.activeElement?.id);
```

**Output:**

```text
focused element id: q
```

**The React way: `useRef` + `ref={…}`:**

```tsx
import { useRef, useState } from "react";
import type { Ref } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function SearchForm() {
  const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
  console.log("during render, inputRef.current is", inputRef.current === null ? "null" : "an " + inputRef.current.tagName);
  return (
    <>
      <input ref={inputRef} aria-label="query" defaultValue="masala chai" />
      <button onClick={() => { inputRef.current!.focus(); inputRef.current!.select(); }}>Focus search</button>
    </>
  );
}
render(<SearchForm />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Focus search"));
const input = screen.getByLabelText("query") as HTMLInputElement;
console.log("focused:", document.activeElement === input, "| selected text:", input.value.slice(input.selectionStart!, input.selectionEnd!));
```

**Output:**

```text
during render, inputRef.current is null
focused: true | selected text: masala chai
```

The ref is `null` during the first render and filled in by the commit, so handlers (which run later) can use it.

**`ref` as a prop on your own component (React 19):** the child simply passes it on to its `<input>`:

```tsx
function TextField({ label, ref }: { label: string; ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement> }) {
  return <label>{label} <input ref={ref} /></label>;
}
function Signup() {
  const emailRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
  return <><TextField label="Email" ref={emailRef} /><button onClick={() => emailRef.current?.focus()}>Fix email</button></>;
}
render(<Signup />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Fix email"));
console.log("focused the inner input:", document.activeElement === screen.getByLabelText("Email"));
```

**Output:**

```text
focused the inner input: true
```

`Ref<HTMLInputElement>` is the TypeScript type for "a ref (object or callback) to an input".

**Ref callbacks with cleanup, and refs to a list of items.** A `Map` from id to node lets one ref hold many elements. jsdom has no layout engine, so `scrollIntoView` doesn't exist here; the example installs a stand-in that logs which element a browser would scroll to:

```tsx
(HTMLElement.prototype as any).scrollIntoView = function () { console.log("browser would scroll to:", this.textContent); };

const cats = ["Tabby", "Siamese", "Maine Coon"];
function CatList() {
  const nodes = useRef(new Map<string, HTMLLIElement>());
  const [shown, setShown] = useState(cats);
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => nodes.current.get("Maine Coon")?.scrollIntoView()}>Jump to Maine Coon</button>
      <button onClick={() => setShown(shown.slice(1))}>Remove first</button>
      <ul>
        {shown.map((cat) => (
          <li key={cat} ref={(node) => {
            nodes.current.set(cat, node!);
            console.log("attached", cat);
            return () => { nodes.current.delete(cat); console.log("detached", cat); };   // cleanup (React 19)
          }}>{cat}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
}
const cats1 = render(<CatList />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Jump to Maine Coon"));
console.log("-- click Remove first");
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Remove first"));
console.log("-- unmount");
cats1.unmount();
```

**Output:**

```text
attached Tabby
attached Siamese
attached Maine Coon
browser would scroll to: Maine Coon
-- click Remove first
detached Tabby
detached Siamese
detached Maine Coon
attached Siamese
attached Maine Coon
-- unmount
detached Siamese
detached Maine Coon
```

"Remove first" logs more than one might expect. An inline ref callback is a **new function** on every render, so on each re-render React runs every row's old cleanup and then attaches the new callbacks: Tabby is detached for good, while Siamese and Maine Coon are detached and attached again. On unmount every remaining row is detached. That's harmless for cheap callbacks like this; for expensive setup, define the callback once (outside the component or with `useCallback`).

### Practice

1. Write `Gallery` with three images and "Next" / "Previous" buttons that scroll the selected image into view (use a `Map` of refs).
2. A component reads `inputRef.current.value` during render to show a character count. What's wrong, and what should it do instead?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. Keep `index` in state; on click, compute the next index, then `nodes.current.get(index)?.scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth", inline: "center" })`. If the item must render first, wrap the state update in `flushSync` before scrolling. (react.dev's "Scrolling an image carousel" challenge.)
2. On the first render `current` is `null` (crash), and later the count won't update as the user types because refs don't cause renders. Make the input controlled (`value` + `onChange` + state) and compute the count from state.

</details>

## 30. Effects: Synchronising with Systems Outside React

![useEffect runs after React commits and the browser paints: render, commit, paint, then the effect; cleanup runs before the next effect and on unmount](images/react/03-effect-lifecycle.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** an **effect** is code that runs **after** React has updated the screen, to keep something **outside React** in step with your component: connect to a chat server while a chat room is shown, set the page title, start a timer, subscribe to window events, or control a non-React widget. You write `useEffect(() => { start(); return () => stop(); }, [deps])`. React runs the setup after rendering, runs the **cleanup** before re-running it and when the component disappears, and re-runs it only when a **dependency** changed.

**Words to know:**

- **Effect:** a function React runs after the commit (and normally after the browser paints) to synchronise with an external system.
- **External system:** anything React doesn't control: the network, browser APIs (`document.title`, `localStorage`, timers, `window` events), third-party widgets, WebSockets.
- **`useEffect(setup, dependencies?)`:** registers an effect. `setup` may return a **cleanup** function.
- **Cleanup function:** undoes the setup (disconnect, unsubscribe, clear a timer); runs before the next setup and on unmount.
- **Dependency array:** the list of reactive values the effect uses. `[a, b]`: re-run when `a` or `b` changes (compared with `Object.is`); `[]`: run only after the first render (and clean up on unmount); **no array**: re-run after every render.
- **Reactive value:** props, state, and anything computed from them in the component body; they can change between renders, so effects that read them must list them.
- **Mount / unmount (for effects):** the component appearing (effects set up) and disappearing (cleanups run).
- **StrictMode effect double-run:** in development React runs setup → cleanup → setup once on mount, to prove your cleanup works (Section [31](#31-the-lifecycle-of-an-effect-dependencies-cleanup-and-strict-mode)).
- **Side effect vs effect:** "side effect" is any change outside a function; an **Effect** (capital E in React docs) is specifically a side effect caused by rendering, not by a particular user action.

**Everyday picture.** A **radio tuned to the TV channel you're watching**. Whenever the channel (dependency) changes, you retune the radio (cleanup the old station, set up the new one). When you leave the room (unmount), you switch it off (cleanup). If you don't change channel, you don't touch the radio (no re-run).

**One component's effect, traced by hand:**

```text
<ChatRoom roomId="general" />
render → commit → paint → effect: connect("general")
user switches to roomId="travel":
render → commit → paint → cleanup: disconnect("general") → effect: connect("travel")
parent re-renders with the same roomId: render → commit → (deps unchanged → nothing)
user leaves the chat page: unmount → cleanup: disconnect("travel")
```

**When to use an effect:** synchronising with something **outside React** that must match what's on screen. **When not:** transforming data for rendering, reacting to a user action (use the event handler), or resetting state when props change (Section [32](#32-you-might-not-need-an-effect) lists them all). Effects are an escape hatch; well-written apps have fewer than you'd expect.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ No cleanup for a connection, subscription or timer (leaks, duplicate connections).
- ❌ Leaving out dependencies to "make it run once" (stale values; Section [31](#31-the-lifecycle-of-an-effect-dependencies-cleanup-and-strict-mode)).
- ❌ Setting state in an effect from data you could compute during render (an extra render every time).
- ❌ An `async` function passed directly to `useEffect` (it returns a promise, not a cleanup); define the async function inside and call it.

**Used in real software:** chat and live-data subscriptions, analytics on page view, syncing with `localStorage`, controlling map/chart/video widgets, `document.title`; data-fetching libraries also use effects internally (Section [52](#52-server-state-with-tanstack-query)).

### Code

**From scratch: the order of render, commit and effects.** Logging from each phase shows that effects run **after** the DOM is updated, children's before parents':

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState, StrictMode } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent, act } from "@testing-library/react";

function Child() {
  console.log("render Child");
  useEffect(() => { console.log("effect Child | DOM has the text?", document.body.textContent!.includes("child")); });
  return <p>child</p>;
}
function Parent() {
  console.log("render Parent");
  useEffect(() => { console.log("effect Parent"); });
  return <Child />;
}
render(<Parent />);
```

**Output:**

```text
render Parent
render Child
effect Child | DOM has the text? true
effect Parent
```

Rendering goes top-down (Parent, then Child); effects run after the commit, bottom-up (Child's first), when the DOM already contains the text.

**Synchronising with an external system: a chat connection,** with cleanup and a dependency:

```tsx
function createConnection(serverUrl: string, roomId: string) {                // a stand-in for a real chat API
  return {
    connect() { console.log(`✅ connecting to "${roomId}" at ${serverUrl}`); },
    disconnect() { console.log(`❌ disconnected from "${roomId}"`); },
  };
}
const serverUrl = "https://chat.example.com";

function ChatRoom({ roomId }: { roomId: string }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(serverUrl, roomId);
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]);
  return <h2>Welcome to {roomId}</h2>;
}
function App() {
  const [roomId, setRoomId] = useState("general");
  const [show, setShow] = useState(true);
  const [, setTick] = useState(0);
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setRoomId("travel")}>travel</button>
      <button onClick={() => setTick((t) => t + 1)}>re-render</button>
      <button onClick={() => setShow(false)}>close chat</button>
      {show && <ChatRoom roomId={roomId} />}
    </>
  );
}
render(<App />);
console.log("-- switch room"); fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("travel"));
console.log("-- re-render, same room (nothing should happen)"); fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("re-render"));
console.log("-- close"); fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("close chat"));
```

**Output:**

```text
✅ connecting to "general" at https://chat.example.com
-- switch room
❌ disconnected from "general"
✅ connecting to "travel" at https://chat.example.com
-- re-render, same room (nothing should happen)
-- close
❌ disconnected from "travel"
```

**The three dependency forms,** counted over three re-renders where only `b` changes:

```tsx
function Deps({ a, b }: { a: number; b: number }) {
  useEffect(() => { console.log("  no array: runs after every render"); });
  useEffect(() => { console.log("  []: runs after the first render only"); }, []);
  useEffect(() => { console.log("  [a]: runs when a changes"); }, [a]);
  return null;
}
const view = render(<Deps a={1} b={1} />);
for (const b of [2, 3]) { console.log(`re-render with b=${b}:`); view.rerender(<Deps a={1} b={b} />); }
```

**Output:**

```text
  no array: runs after every render
  []: runs after the first render only
  [a]: runs when a changes
re-render with b=2:
  no array: runs after every render
re-render with b=3:
  no array: runs after every render
```

`rerender` (from Testing Library) renders the same root again with new props, like a parent re-rendering.

**Strict Mode runs setup → cleanup → setup on mount in development,** to check the cleanup is correct:

```tsx
render(<StrictMode><ChatRoom roomId="general" /></StrictMode>);
```

**Output:**

```text
✅ connecting to "general" at https://chat.example.com
❌ disconnected from "general"
✅ connecting to "general" at https://chat.example.com
```

A correct cleanup makes the extra cycle invisible to users: one connection stays open. Without the `return () => connection.disconnect()`, you'd see two connections, which is exactly the bug StrictMode exists to expose.

**Effects for browser APIs: the page title and a window listener,** with a cleanup that removes the listener:

```tsx
function OnlineBadge({ cartCount }: { cartCount: number }) {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine);
  useEffect(() => { document.title = cartCount > 0 ? `(${cartCount}) Chai Point` : "Chai Point"; }, [cartCount]);
  useEffect(() => {
    const goOnline = () => setOnline(true), goOffline = () => setOnline(false);
    window.addEventListener("online", goOnline);
    window.addEventListener("offline", goOffline);
    return () => { window.removeEventListener("online", goOnline); window.removeEventListener("offline", goOffline); };
  }, []);
  return <p>{online ? "🟢 online" : "🔴 offline"}</p>;
}
const badge = render(<OnlineBadge cartCount={2} />);
console.log(document.title, "|", screen.getByText(/line/).textContent);
await act(async () => { window.dispatchEvent(new Event("offline")); });
console.log(screen.getByText(/line/).textContent);
badge.unmount();
```

**Output:**

```text
(2) Chai Point | 🟢 online
🔴 offline
```

Section [40](#40-more-hooks-uselayouteffect-useid-usesyncexternalstore-useimperativehandle-and-ref-as-a-prop) shows `useSyncExternalStore`, the dedicated hook for subscribing to outside data like the online status.

### Practice

1. Write `useDocumentTitle(title)`-style logic inline: a `Notifications` component that sets `document.title` to `"(3) Inbox"` and restores the old title when it unmounts.
2. Why doesn't `useEffect(async () => { const data = await load(); setData(data); }, [])` work as intended?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function Notifications({ count }: { count: number }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const previous = document.title;
    document.title = `(${count}) Inbox`;
    return () => { document.title = previous; };
  }, [count]);
  return <p>{count} new</p>;
}
document.title = "Chai Point";
const n = render(<Notifications count={3} />);
console.log("mounted:", document.title);
n.unmount();
console.log("after unmount:", document.title);
```

**Output:**

```text
mounted: (3) Inbox
after unmount: Chai Point
```

1. Save the previous title in the setup and restore it in the cleanup.
2. An `async` function always returns a promise, and React expects the setup to return nothing or a cleanup function; it also leaves no way to ignore a stale response. Define `async function load…` inside the effect and call it, with an `ignore` flag in the cleanup (Section [34](#34-fetching-data-in-effects-loading-errors-race-conditions-and-abortcontroller)).

</details>
