## 31. The Lifecycle of an Effect: Dependencies, Cleanup and Strict Mode

![An effect only starts and stops synchronising; when a dependency changes it stops the old synchronisation and starts a new one; the dependency list must contain every reactive value the effect reads, and the linter checks it](images/react/31-effect-deps.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** don't think of an effect as "run on mount, run on update". Think of it as **"start synchronising" + "stop synchronising"**, and React may do that pair many times. Your dependency list isn't a choice: it must include **every reactive value the effect reads** (props, state, values computed from them). If you lie to React about dependencies, your effect uses **stale values**. The `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` lint rule checks this for you.

**Words to know:**

- **Effect lifecycle:** an effect's own cycle: start syncing → (deps change) stop → start with new values → … → stop on unmount.
- **Re-synchronisation:** stopping and restarting an effect because a dependency changed.
- **Stale closure:** an effect (or callback) that captured old values from an earlier render because it wasn't re-run when they changed.
- **`exhaustive-deps` lint rule:** part of `eslint-plugin-react-hooks`; warns when an effect reads a reactive value that isn't in its dependency array.
- **Rules of Hooks lint rule (`rules-of-hooks`):** errors when hooks are called conditionally or in loops (Section [39](#39-how-hooks-work-inside-build-usestate-from-scratch-and-the-rules-of-hooks)).
- **Non-reactive value:** something that can't change between renders: module-level constants, imported functions, `useRef` objects and state setter functions; they don't need to be listed.
- **Unstable dependency:** an object or function created during render (`const options = {…}`); it's a **new** value each render, so an effect depending on it re-runs every time.
- **Development double-run:** StrictMode's mount → unmount → mount check; it only happens in development and only on mount.

**Everyday picture.** A **babysitter's shift**. The babysitter (effect) starts the shift when the parents leave and ends it when they return (start/stop). If the parents swap which child needs watching (a dependency changes), the shift ends and a new one starts for the new child. Giving the babysitter yesterday's list of allergies (a stale value) because "the list never changes" is how accidents happen.

**Deciding dependencies, traced by hand:**

```text
function ChatRoom({ roomId }) {               ← roomId: a prop → reactive
  const [serverUrl, setServerUrl] = useState("https://localhost:1234");   ← state → reactive
  const options = { serverUrl, roomId };      ← computed during render → reactive AND new every render
  useEffect(() => {
    const c = createConnection(serverUrl, roomId); c.connect(); return () => c.disconnect();
  }, [roomId, serverUrl]);                    ← reads roomId and serverUrl → both listed ✅
  // depending on `options` instead would reconnect on EVERY render (a new object each time) ❌
}
setServerUrl is stable (React guarantees it) → not needed in the list
```

**When to trust the linter:** essentially always. If the "right" dependencies cause too many re-runs, change the **code** (move objects inside the effect, use updater functions, `useEffectEvent`; Section [33](#33-separating-events-from-effects-useeffectevent-and-removing-dependencies)), never the list. **When an empty array is honest:** when the effect truly reads no reactive values.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` to silence the warning (it hides stale-value bugs).
- ❌ Objects or functions created during render as dependencies.
- ❌ Expecting an effect with `[]` to see the latest props later (it sees the first render's values forever).
- ❌ Thinking StrictMode's double-run happens in production (it doesn't).

**Used in real software:** `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` is in every major React template's lint config; since version 6/7 its recommended set also includes the React Compiler's purity and ref rules.

### Code

**Re-synchronising: switching rooms stops the old connection and starts the new one,** and the effect's cleanup always sees the values from **its own** render:

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function createConnection(serverUrl: string, roomId: string) {
  return { connect: () => console.log(`connect ${roomId} @ ${serverUrl}`), disconnect: () => console.log(`disconnect ${roomId} @ ${serverUrl}`) };
}

function ChatRoom({ roomId }: { roomId: string }) {
  const [serverUrl, setServerUrl] = useState("https://a.example");
  useEffect(() => {
    const c = createConnection(serverUrl, roomId);
    c.connect();
    return () => c.disconnect();
  }, [roomId, serverUrl]);
  return <button onClick={() => setServerUrl("https://b.example")}>change server</button>;
}
const chat = render(<ChatRoom roomId="general" />);
console.log("-- room → travel"); chat.rerender(<ChatRoom roomId="travel" />);
console.log("-- server → b");   fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("change server"));
console.log("-- unmount");      chat.unmount();
```

**Output:**

```text
connect general @ https://a.example
-- room → travel
disconnect general @ https://a.example
connect travel @ https://a.example
-- server → b
disconnect travel @ https://a.example
connect travel @ https://b.example
-- unmount
disconnect travel @ https://b.example
```

**Lying about dependencies → stale values.** This effect reads `roomId` but lists `[]`, so it never reconnects:

```tsx
function StaleChatRoom({ roomId }: { roomId: string }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const c = createConnection("https://a.example", roomId);
    c.connect();
    return () => c.disconnect();
  }, []);                                         // ❌ roomId is missing
  return <h2>Room: {roomId}</h2>;
}
const stale = render(<StaleChatRoom roomId="general" />);
stale.rerender(<StaleChatRoom roomId="travel" />);
console.log("screen says:", screen.getByRole("heading").textContent, "← but we're still connected to general");
stale.unmount();
```

**Output:**

```text
connect general @ https://a.example
screen says: Room: travel ← but we're still connected to general
disconnect general @ https://a.example
```

**An unstable object dependency re-runs on every render:**

```tsx
function NoisyRoom({ roomId }: { roomId: string }) {
  const [text, setText] = useState("");
  const options = { serverUrl: "https://a.example", roomId };          // a NEW object every render
  useEffect(() => {
    const c = createConnection(options.serverUrl, options.roomId);
    c.connect();
    return () => c.disconnect();
  }, [options]);                                                         // ❌ changes every render
  return <input aria-label="msg" value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)} />;
}
render(<NoisyRoom roomId="general" />);
console.log("-- typing two characters:");
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("msg"), { target: { value: "h" } });
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("msg"), { target: { value: "hi" } });
```

**Output:**

```text
connect general @ https://a.example
-- typing two characters:
disconnect general @ https://a.example
connect general @ https://a.example
disconnect general @ https://a.example
connect general @ https://a.example
```

Every keystroke reconnected. The fix: create the object **inside** the effect and depend on the primitive values `[roomId]`.

**The linter catches these.** Running ESLint with `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` on a file with two classic mistakes:

```js
import reactHooks from "eslint-plugin-react-hooks";
export default [
  { files: ["**/*.jsx"], languageOptions: { parserOptions: { ecmaFeatures: { jsx: true } } } },
  reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended,
];
```

```jsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

export function ChatRoom({ roomId, serverUrl }) {
  const [unread, setUnread] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(serverUrl, roomId);
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]);
  if (unread > 99) {
    const [capped] = useState(true);
  }
  return <p>{unread}</p>;
}
```

```bash
npx eslint ChatRoom.jsx | sed -E "s#^/.*/##"   # expect-fail (ESLint exits 1 when it finds errors)
```

**Output:**

```text

ChatRoom.jsx
   9:6   warning  React Hook useEffect has a missing dependency: 'serverUrl'. Either include it or remove the dependency array                 react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
  11:22  error    React Hook "useState" is called conditionally. React Hooks must be called in the exact same order in every component render  react-hooks/rules-of-hooks

✖ 2 problems (1 error, 1 warning)
```

The warning names the missing dependency (`serverUrl`); the error is the Rules of Hooks (a hook inside an `if`). (ESLint's default parser understands `.jsx`; TypeScript files need the `typescript-eslint` parser added to the config.)

### Practice

1. An effect logs `"visit " + url + " with " + cartCount + " items"` whenever the page `url` changes. `cartCount` changes often. Which dependencies does the linter require, and why is that a problem here?
2. Rewrite `NoisyRoom` so typing doesn't reconnect.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function QuietRoom({ roomId }: { roomId: string }) {
  const [text, setText] = useState("");
  useEffect(() => {
    const options = { serverUrl: "https://a.example", roomId };     // created inside the effect
    const c = createConnection(options.serverUrl, options.roomId);
    c.connect();
    return () => c.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]);
  return <input aria-label="msg2" value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)} />;
}
render(<QuietRoom roomId="general" />);
console.log("-- typing two characters:");
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("msg2"), { target: { value: "h" } });
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("msg2"), { target: { value: "hi" } });
console.log("(no reconnects)");
```

**Output:**

```text
connect general @ https://a.example
-- typing two characters:
(no reconnects)
```

1. `[url, cartCount]`, because the effect reads both; so it would also log a "visit" whenever the cart changes, which is wrong. Reading `cartCount` isn't really part of synchronising with the URL: move it into an **effect event** (Section [33](#33-separating-events-from-effects-useeffectevent-and-removing-dependencies)).
2. Above: the object is built inside the effect and only `roomId` (a string) is a dependency.

</details>

## 32. You Might Not Need an Effect

![A decision chart: computed from props or state? calculate during render. Caused by a user action? do it in the event handler. Reset when a prop changes? use a key. Synchronising with an outside system? only then use an effect](images/react/32-no-effect.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** effects are for talking to the **outside world**. Many effects in real codebases are unnecessary and make apps slower and buggier: they calculate data that could be computed during render, react to user actions that belong in event handlers, or chain state updates. Before writing `useEffect`, ask: **is this caused by rendering and does it touch something outside React?** If not, there's a simpler way.

**Words to know:**

- **Derived state anti-pattern:** storing a value computed from other state (`fullName`, `visibleTodos`) and updating it in an effect; it costs an extra render and can show stale data for one frame.
- **Memoisation (`useMemo`):** caching an expensive calculation between renders, recomputing only when its inputs change (Section [45](#45-memo-usememo-usecallback-and-the-react-compiler)).
- **Event-specific logic:** code that should run because the user **did something** (bought a product, submitted a form); it belongs in that event's handler.
- **Chain of effects:** effects that set state that triggers other effects; hard to follow, many extra renders.
- **Adjusting state during render:** for the rare case where some state must change when a prop changes, compare with the previous prop **during render** and set state there (React re-renders immediately, before the commit); a `key` is usually simpler.
- **Notify parent anti-pattern:** calling `onChange` from an effect after updating local state; call it in the event handler instead, or lift the state up.
- **`react-hooks/set-state-in-effect`:** a lint rule (React Compiler rules in `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` 7) that flags synchronous `setState` calls inside effects.

**Everyday picture.** A **sticky note telling you to update another sticky note**. If your fridge note says "milk: 2" and a second note says "total items: 5 (update this whenever the first note changes)", you'll eventually forget. Just count when you need the total. Effects that copy data around are those second notes.

**The decision, traced by hand:**

| Situation | ❌ With an effect | ✅ Instead |
|---|---|---|
| value computed from props/state | `useEffect(() => setFull(first + last), [first, last])` | `const full = first + " " + last` during render |
| expensive computation | effect + state | `useMemo(() => filter(todos), [todos, tab])` (or let the React Compiler do it) |
| reset everything when a prop changes | effect calling `setComment("")` when `userId` changes | `<Profile key={userId} />` |
| user clicked "Buy" → POST + notification | effect watching a `bought` flag | do it in `handleBuy` |
| tell the parent about a change | effect calling `onChange(isOn)` | call `onChange` in the handler, or lift state |
| synchronise with an outside system | ✅ that's what effects are for | — |
| fetch data for what's on screen | ✅ an effect with cleanup (Section [34](#34-fetching-data-in-effects-loading-errors-race-conditions-and-abortcontroller)), or better a data library | TanStack Query, router loaders, Server Components |

**When effects remain right:** subscriptions, connections, timers tied to what's displayed, analytics on display, imperative widgets, and fetching tied to what's shown. **When not:** everything else in the table.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ "Effect to sync state A with state B" (store one, derive the other).
- ❌ Running a POST request in an effect because a flag changed (it re-sends in StrictMode and on remounts).
- ❌ Initialising app-wide things (auth check, analytics init) in an effect that runs per mount; do it once at module level or guard it.

**Used in real software:** React's own docs devote a full page to removing unnecessary effects; the `set-state-in-effect` lint rule and the React Compiler push codebases in the same direction.

### Code

**Derived data in an effect costs an extra render** (and one frame of stale output); computing it during render doesn't:

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

let renders = { effect: 0, derived: 0 };
function FullNameEffect() {
  renders.effect++;
  const [first, setFirst] = useState("Asha");
  const [full, setFull] = useState("");
  useEffect(() => { setFull(first + " Rao"); }, [first]);          // ❌ derived state via an effect
  return <input aria-label="first-e" value={first} onChange={(e) => setFirst(e.target.value)} title={full} />;
}
function FullNameDerived() {
  renders.derived++;
  const [first, setFirst] = useState("Asha");
  const full = first + " Rao";                                          // ✅ computed during render
  return <input aria-label="first-d" value={first} onChange={(e) => setFirst(e.target.value)} title={full} />;
}
render(<><FullNameEffect /><FullNameDerived /></>);
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("first-e"), { target: { value: "Ravi" } });
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("first-d"), { target: { value: "Ravi" } });
console.log(renders, "| titles:", screen.getByLabelText("first-e").title, "/", screen.getByLabelText("first-d").title);
```

**Output:**

```text
{ effect: 4, derived: 2 } | titles: Ravi Rao / Ravi Rao
```

Same result, but the effect version rendered twice as often: once with the stale full name, and again after the effect set it.

**Event-specific logic belongs in the handler.** Here a purchase is sent from an effect that watches a `bought` flag kept by the parent. Navigating away from the product page and back (unmount, mount) re-runs the effect, and the purchase is sent **again**; the handler version sends exactly once per click:

```tsx
const sent: string[] = [];
function ProductPage({ bought, onBuy, inHandler }: { bought: boolean; onBuy: () => void; inHandler: boolean }) {
  useEffect(() => { if (!inHandler && bought) sent.push("effect POST /buy"); }, [bought, inHandler]);   // ❌
  return <button onClick={() => { if (inHandler) sent.push("handler POST /buy"); onBuy(); }}>buy</button>;   // ✅ when inHandler
}
function Shop({ inHandler }: { inHandler: boolean }) {
  const [bought, setBought] = useState(false);
  const [page, setPage] = useState<"product" | "home">("product");
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setPage(page === "product" ? "home" : "product")}>navigate</button>
      {page === "product" && <ProductPage bought={bought} onBuy={() => setBought(true)} inHandler={inHandler} />}
    </>
  );
}
for (const inHandler of [false, true]) {
  sent.length = 0;
  const shop = render(<Shop inHandler={inHandler} />);
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("buy"));
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("navigate"));      // away…
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("navigate"));      // …and back
  console.log(inHandler ? "handler:" : "effect: ", sent);
  shop.unmount();
}
```

**Output:**

```text
effect:  [ 'effect POST /buy', 'effect POST /buy' ]
handler: [ 'handler POST /buy' ]
```

One click, two purchases in the effect version: the effect can't tell "the user just bought this" from "this page appeared while `bought` was true". (In development, StrictMode's mount check would trigger the same duplicate the moment a page mounts with `bought` already true.) The click is the event, so the request belongs in the click handler.

**Resetting state when a prop changes: a key instead of an effect** (both versions shown; the key version never renders the stale comment):

```tsx
const seen: string[] = [];
function CommentBox({ userId }: { userId: string }) {
  const [comment, setComment] = useState("");
  seen.push(`render ${userId} comment="${comment}"`);
  return <textarea aria-label="comment" value={comment} onChange={(e) => setComment(e.target.value)} />;
}
function CommentBoxEffect({ userId }: { userId: string }) {
  const [comment, setComment] = useState("");
  useEffect(() => { setComment(""); }, [userId]);                    // ❌ resets one render too late
  seen.push(`render ${userId} comment="${comment}"`);
  return <textarea aria-label="comment" value={comment} onChange={(e) => setComment(e.target.value)} />;
}
for (const [label, make] of [["effect", (id: string) => <CommentBoxEffect userId={id} />], ["key", (id: string) => <CommentBox key={id} userId={id} />]] as const) {
  seen.length = 0;
  const v = render(make("asha"));
  fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("comment"), { target: { value: "great chai!" } });
  seen.length = 0;
  v.rerender(make("ravi"));
  console.log(label.padEnd(6), seen.join(" | "));
  v.unmount();
}
```

**Output:**

```text
effect render ravi comment="great chai!" | render ravi comment=""
key    render ravi comment=""
```

With the effect, Ravi's profile is first rendered (and committed) with **Asha's** comment, then fixed. With `key`, React creates a fresh `CommentBox` for Ravi straight away.

**The linter's newer rule spots setState in effects** (part of the React Compiler rules in `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` 7):

```js
import reactHooks from "eslint-plugin-react-hooks";
export default [
  { files: ["**/*.jsx"], languageOptions: { parserOptions: { ecmaFeatures: { jsx: true } } } },
  reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended,
];
```

```jsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

export function FullName({ first, last }) {
  const [full, setFull] = useState("");
  useEffect(() => {
    setFull(first + " " + last);
  }, [first, last]);
  return <p>{full}</p>;
}
```

```bash
npx eslint FullName.jsx | sed -E "s#^/.*/##" | cut -c1-160   # expect-fail
```

**Output:**

```text

FullName.jsx
  6:5  error  Error: Calling setState synchronously within an effect can trigger cascading renders

Effects are intended to synchronize state between React and external systems such as manually updating the DOM, state management libraries, or other platform AP
* Update external systems with the latest state from React.
* Subscribe for updates from some external system, calling setState in a callback function when external state changes.

Calling setState synchronously within an effect body causes cascading renders that can hurt performance, and is not recommended. (https://react.dev/learn/you-mi

  4 |   const [full, setFull] = useState("");
  5 |   useEffect(() => {
> 6 |     setFull(first + " " + last);
    |     ^^^^^^^ Avoid calling setState() directly within an effect
  7 |   }, [first, last]);
  8 |   return <p>{full}</p>;
  9 | }  react-hooks/set-state-in-effect

✖ 1 problem (1 error, 0 warnings)
```

### Practice

1. A `TodoList` keeps `todos` and `showActive` in state, plus `visibleTodos` updated by an effect. Rewrite it without the effect.
2. `function Toggle({ onChange }) { const [isOn, setIsOn] = useState(false); useEffect(() => { onChange(isOn); }, [isOn, onChange]); … }`: what's wrong, and what's better?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
type Todo = { id: number; text: string; done: boolean };
function TodoList({ todos }: { todos: Todo[] }) {
  const [showActive, setShowActive] = useState(false);
  const visibleTodos = showActive ? todos.filter((t) => !t.done) : todos;     // derived
  return (
    <>
      <label><input type="checkbox" checked={showActive} onChange={(e) => setShowActive(e.target.checked)} /> Active only</label>
      <ul>{visibleTodos.map((t) => <li key={t.id}>{t.text}</li>)}</ul>
    </>
  );
}
render(<TodoList todos={[{ id: 1, text: "steep", done: true }, { id: 2, text: "pour", done: false }]} />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByLabelText("Active only"));
console.log(screen.getAllByRole("listitem").map((li) => li.textContent));
```

**Output:**

```text
[ 'pour' ]
```

1. `visibleTodos` is computed during render; if filtering were expensive, wrap it in `useMemo` (or rely on the React Compiler).
2. The parent hears about the change one render late (after an extra commit), and if `onChange` isn't stable the effect fires on every render. Call `onChange(next)` in the same click handler that calls `setIsOn(next)`, or make the toggle fully controlled by the parent (lift state up).

</details>

## 33. Separating Events from Effects: useEffectEvent and Removing Dependencies

![Reactive logic re-runs when its inputs change; non-reactive logic inside an effect is moved into an effect event, which always reads the latest values but is not a dependency](images/react/33-effect-event.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** event handlers run **because of an interaction**; effects run **because something must be in sync**. Sometimes an effect contains a bit of logic that should use the **latest** props without being a reason to re-run: "connect to the room (re-run when the room changes), and when connected, show a notification in the **current theme** (don't reconnect when the theme changes)". React 19.2's **`useEffectEvent`** extracts that bit into an **effect event**. Other dependency problems are fixed by restructuring: updater functions, moving objects inside the effect, and reading primitives.

**Words to know:**

- **Reactive logic:** code whose result should update when its inputs change (effects, rendering).
- **Non-reactive logic:** code that should run only when something else triggers it, but read the latest values when it does (event handlers, effect events).
- **`useEffectEvent(fn)`:** returns a function you call **from inside effects**; it always sees the latest props and state, and it must **not** be listed as a dependency. Stable since React 19.2 (October 2025).
- **Effect event:** the function returned by `useEffectEvent`; don't pass it to other components or call it during render.
- **Removing a dependency:** changing the code so the effect no longer reads the value (not deleting it from the list).
- **Updater function trick:** `setCount(c => c + 1)` inside an interval needs no `count` dependency.
- **Moving creation inside:** create objects and functions inside the effect so they aren't unstable dependencies.
- **Reading primitives:** destructure the strings/numbers you need from an object prop **outside** the effect and depend on those.

**Everyday picture.** A **delivery driver** (the effect) follows the route to the address on the order (reactive: a new address means a new trip). They also phone the customer on arrival, using whatever phone number is **currently** on the account (latest value), but a changed phone number doesn't send them on a new trip. The phone call is an effect event.

**The theme problem, traced:**

```text
useEffect(() => {
  const c = connect(roomId);
  c.on("connected", () => showNotification("Connected!", theme));   ← reads theme
  return () => c.disconnect();
}, [roomId, theme]);                                                ← the linter demands theme
user toggles dark mode → theme changes → effect re-runs → DISCONNECT + RECONNECT  ❌

const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => showNotification("Connected!", theme));
useEffect(() => { … c.on("connected", () => onConnected()); … }, [roomId]);   ← theme no longer read by the effect
toggle theme → nothing reconnects; the next "connected" notification uses the new theme ✅
```

**When to use `useEffectEvent`:** non-reactive bits inside effects: logging analytics with the current cart, notifications with the current theme, reading the latest value inside an interval. **When not:** to hide dependencies that **should** cause re-synchronisation (a room id), or in event handlers (they already see the latest values).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Calling an effect event from an event handler or during render (it's only for effects).
- ❌ Passing the effect event to child components or listing it in dependencies.
- ❌ Using `useEffectEvent` to wrap the whole effect body to silence the linter.

**Used in real software:** analytics page-view logging, notifications and "latest value" intervals; before React 19.2 libraries used a "latest ref" pattern (`useLatest`, `useEvent` polyfills) for the same job.

### Code

**The problem: a non-reactive value forces a reconnect:**

```tsx
import { useEffect, useEffectEvent, useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent, act } from "@testing-library/react";

function createConnection(roomId: string) {
  let handler = () => {};
  return {
    connect() { console.log(`connect ${roomId}`); setTimeout(() => handler(), 5); },
    on(_event: "connected", fn: () => void) { handler = fn; },
    disconnect() { console.log(`disconnect ${roomId}`); },
  };
}
const notify = (msg: string, theme: string) => console.log(`🔔 ${msg} (${theme} theme)`);

function ChatRoomBad({ roomId, theme }: { roomId: string; theme: string }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const c = createConnection(roomId);
    c.on("connected", () => notify("Connected!", theme));
    c.connect();
    return () => c.disconnect();
  }, [roomId, theme]);
  return null;
}
const bad = render(<ChatRoomBad roomId="general" theme="light" />);
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 20)));
console.log("-- toggle theme:");
bad.rerender(<ChatRoomBad roomId="general" theme="dark" />);
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 20)));
bad.unmount();
```

**Output:**

```text
connect general
🔔 Connected! (light theme)
-- toggle theme:
disconnect general
connect general
🔔 Connected! (dark theme)
disconnect general
```

**The fix: move the non-reactive part into an effect event:**

```tsx
function ChatRoomGood({ roomId, theme }: { roomId: string; theme: string }) {
  const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => notify("Connected!", theme));   // always sees the latest theme
  useEffect(() => {
    const c = createConnection(roomId);
    c.on("connected", () => onConnected());
    c.connect();
    return () => c.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]);                                                              // theme is not a dependency
  return null;
}
const good = render(<ChatRoomGood roomId="general" theme="light" />);
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 20)));
console.log("-- toggle theme (no reconnect):");
good.rerender(<ChatRoomGood roomId="general" theme="dark" />);
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 20)));
console.log("-- switch room (reconnect, notification uses the CURRENT theme):");
good.rerender(<ChatRoomGood roomId="travel" theme="dark" />);
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 20)));
good.unmount();
```

**Output:**

```text
connect general
🔔 Connected! (light theme)
-- toggle theme (no reconnect):
-- switch room (reconnect, notification uses the CURRENT theme):
disconnect general
connect travel
🔔 Connected! (dark theme)
disconnect travel
```

**Removing a dependency with an updater function:** an interval that counts up needs no `count` dependency, so it isn't torn down and restarted every tick:

```tsx
let starts = 0;
function Timer({ useUpdater }: { useUpdater: boolean }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    starts++;
    const id = setInterval(() => (useUpdater ? setCount((c) => c + 1) : setCount(count + 1)), 5);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, useUpdater ? [] : [count]);
  return <p>{count}</p>;
}
for (const useUpdater of [false, true]) {
  starts = 0;
  const t = render(<Timer useUpdater={useUpdater} />);
  await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 60)));
  const ticks = Number(screen.getByRole("paragraph").textContent);
  console.log(useUpdater ? "updater:   " : "count dep: ", `counting? ${ticks > 0} | interval (re)started ${starts === 1 ? "once" : starts === ticks + 1 ? "once per tick (+1)" : starts + " times"}`);
  t.unmount();
}
```

**Output:**

```text
count dep:  counting? true | interval (re)started once per tick (+1)
updater:    counting? true | interval (re)started once
```

(Tick counts depend on timing, so the example prints relationships instead of exact numbers.) Both counters count, but the `[count]` version tears down and recreates the interval on every tick, so it also drifts: each restart waits a full interval again. The dependency array is computed per render here only to compare the two in one component; real code would pick one.

**A latest-value interval with an effect event:** the interval is created once, yet it logs the **current** step size:

```tsx
function Stepper() {
  const [step, setStep] = useState(1);
  const [total, setTotal] = useState(0);
  const onTick = useEffectEvent(() => setTotal((t) => t + step));
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => onTick(), 5);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, []);
  return <><button onClick={() => setStep(100)}>step 100</button><output>{total}</output></>;
}
render(<Stepper />);
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 30)));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("step 100"));
const before = Number(document.querySelector("output")!.textContent);
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 30)));
const after = Number(document.querySelector("output")!.textContent);
console.log("small steps before the click:", before < 100, "| jumps of 100 after:", (after - before) % 100 === 0 && after > before);
```

**Output:**

```text
small steps before the click: true | jumps of 100 after: true
```

### Practice

1. A page logs analytics `logVisit(url, cartItemCount)` when `url` changes. Write it so that cart changes don't log a new visit.
2. Why can't you just leave `theme` out of the dependency list instead of using `useEffectEvent`?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function Page({ url, cartCount }: { url: string; cartCount: number }) {
  const onVisit = useEffectEvent((visitedUrl: string) => console.log(`visit ${visitedUrl} with ${cartCount} items`));
  useEffect(() => { onVisit(url); }, [url]);
  return null;
}
const p = render(<Page url="/menu" cartCount={0} />);
p.rerender(<Page url="/menu" cartCount={2} />);       // cart changes: no new visit
p.rerender(<Page url="/cart" cartCount={2} />);       // url changes: visit, with the latest count
```

**Output:**

```text
visit /menu with 0 items
visit /cart with 2 items
```

1. The reactive value (`url`) is passed **into** the effect event as an argument, so each visit logs the URL it was for; `cartCount` is read inside the event, always fresh.
2. Then the effect would read a **stale** `theme` (whatever it was when the effect last ran), and the linter would warn. `useEffectEvent` reads the latest value *and* tells React it isn't a reason to re-synchronise.

</details>

## 34. Fetching Data in Effects: Loading, Errors, Race Conditions and AbortController

![Two requests race: the user searches 'ch' (slow) then 'chai' (fast); without a guard the slow stale response overwrites the newer one; an ignore flag or AbortController in the cleanup drops it](images/react/34-fetch-race.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** to load data for what's on screen, start a request in an effect, keep **loading / data / error** in state, and in the **cleanup** mark the request as stale (an `ignore` flag) or cancel it (`AbortController`). Without that, a slow response for an **old** query can arrive **after** a newer one and overwrite it: a race condition. Hand-written fetching is worth understanding, but production apps usually use a library or framework that handles caching, deduplication and races (Sections [51](#51-router-data-loaders-actions-and-pending-ui), [52](#52-server-state-with-tanstack-query), [61](#61-react-server-components-how-they-work)).

**Words to know:**

- **Loading state:** what the UI shows while waiting (`status: "loading"`).
- **Error state:** what the UI shows when the request failed, often with a retry.
- **Race condition (in fetching):** responses arriving out of order, so a stale response replaces a newer one.
- **`ignore` flag:** a local variable set to `true` in the cleanup; the response handler checks it and drops results from an effect that has since been cleaned up.
- **`AbortController`:** cancels the in-flight `fetch` in the cleanup (saves bandwidth too); the aborted `fetch` rejects with an `AbortError` that you ignore.
- **Waterfall:** requests that run one after another because each component only starts fetching after its parent rendered; slow on real networks.
- **Cache:** storing previous responses so going back to a screen is instant; hand-written effects have none.
- **Server state:** data owned by a server that your UI shows a copy of; it can go stale and needs refetching (Section [52](#52-server-state-with-tanstack-query)).

**Everyday picture.** Ordering at two counters. You order "ch…" at a slow counter, change your mind, and order "chai" at a fast one. The fast one serves you first; then the slow counter hands you the old order, and if you eat whatever arrives last, you end up with the wrong drink. The `ignore` flag is telling the slow counter "cancel that"; the `AbortController` is them actually binning it.

**The race, traced by hand:**

```text
t=0    query "ch"   → effect #1 starts fetch("ch")   (server takes 80 ms)
t=10   query "chai" → cleanup #1 runs (ignore₁ = true) → effect #2 starts fetch("chai") (20 ms)
t=30   response "chai" arrives → ignore₂ is false → setResults(chai results) ✅
t=80   response "ch" arrives   → ignore₁ is true  → dropped ✅
without the flag: at t=80 setResults(ch results) would overwrite the newer data ❌
```

**When hand-written effect fetching is OK:** small apps, learning, one-off widgets. **When not:** most production apps; you'd be re-implementing caching, retries, deduplication, refetch on focus and pagination. Use TanStack Query or SWR on the client, or your framework's loaders and Server Components.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ No cleanup → race conditions and "state update on an unmounted component" situations.
- ❌ Treating a 404 or 500 as success (check `response.ok`).
- ❌ Forgetting the error state (infinite spinner on failure).
- ❌ Fetching in a child only after the parent's fetch finished (a waterfall) when both could start together.

**Used in real software:** this is exactly the pattern libraries like SWR and TanStack Query wrap; React's docs recommend using them (or a framework) instead of raw effects for data fetching.

### Code

A local test server with a **variable delay** per query, so the race is reproducible:

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { render, screen, fireEvent, act } from "@testing-library/react";

const MENU = ["Masala chai", "Chai latte", "Cold coffee", "Chocolate shake", "Samosa"];
const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  const url = new URL(req.url!, "http://x");
  const q = url.searchParams.get("q") ?? "";
  const delay = Number(url.searchParams.get("delay") ?? 0);
  setTimeout(() => {
    if (q === "boom") { res.writeHead(500).end(); return; }
    res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    res.end(JSON.stringify(MENU.filter((m) => m.toLowerCase().includes(q.toLowerCase()))));
  }, delay);
});
await new Promise<void>((r) => server.listen(4402, r));
const delays: Record<string, number> = { c: 80, ch: 80, chai: 10, co: 10 };
const urlFor = (q: string) => `http://localhost:4402/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}&delay=${delays[q] ?? 10}`;
console.log("server ready");
```

**Output:**

```text
server ready
```

**The naive version (no cleanup) shows stale results:**

```tsx
function NaiveSearch({ query }: { query: string }) {
  const [results, setResults] = useState<string[]>([]);
  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(urlFor(query)).then((r) => r.json()).then(setResults);       // ❌ no guard
  }, [query]);
  return <p>{query}: {results.join(", ")}</p>;
}
const naive = render(<NaiveSearch query="ch" />);
naive.rerender(<NaiveSearch query="chai" />);                          // the user kept typing
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 150)));
console.log(screen.getByRole("paragraph").textContent, "  ← results for 'ch' shown under 'chai'");
naive.unmount();
```

**Output:**

```text
chai: Masala chai, Chai latte, Chocolate shake   ← results for 'ch' shown under 'chai'
```

**The correct version: loading/error states, `ignore` flag and `AbortController`:**

```tsx
type State = { status: "loading" } | { status: "error"; message: string } | { status: "success"; results: string[] };

function Search({ query }: { query: string }) {
  const [state, setState] = useState<State>({ status: "loading" });
  useEffect(() => {
    let ignore = false;
    const controller = new AbortController();
    setState({ status: "loading" });
    fetch(urlFor(query), { signal: controller.signal })
      .then((r) => { if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${r.status}`); return r.json(); })
      .then((results: string[]) => { if (!ignore) setState({ status: "success", results }); })
      .catch((e: Error) => { if (!ignore && e.name !== "AbortError") setState({ status: "error", message: e.message }); });
    return () => { ignore = true; controller.abort(); };
  }, [query]);
  if (state.status === "loading") return <p>Loading {query}…</p>;
  if (state.status === "error") return <p role="alert">Couldn't search: {state.message}</p>;
  return <p>{query}: {state.results.join(", ") || "no matches"}</p>;
}
const s = render(<Search query="ch" />);
console.log(screen.getByRole("paragraph").textContent);
s.rerender(<Search query="chai" />);
await screen.findByText(/chai:/);
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 150)));               // give the slow, aborted request time to come back
console.log(screen.getByRole("paragraph").textContent, "  ← correct");
s.rerender(<Search query="boom" />);
console.log((await screen.findByRole("alert")).textContent);
s.unmount();
server.close();
```

**Output:**

```text
Loading ch…
chai: Masala chai, Chai latte   ← correct
Couldn't search: HTTP 500
```

`setState({ status: "loading" })` at the start of the effect is one of the few acceptable `setState` calls in an effect (it marks the start of synchronising with the server). The `State` type is a discriminated union (Section [26](#26-typescript-with-react-typing-props-state-events-and-children)), so `state.results` is only available in the success branch.

### Practice

1. Turn the fetching logic into a reusable `useFetch(url)` that returns `{ status, data, error }`.
2. A `Profile` fetches the user, then renders `<Posts userId>` which fetches posts only after the profile renders. What's this called and how can you avoid it?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. Move the effect and state into a function named `useFetch` (a **custom hook**, Section [38](#38-custom-hooks-reusing-stateful-logic)) with `[url]` as the dependency; components call `const { status, data } = useFetch(url)`. Section [38](#38-custom-hooks-reusing-stateful-logic) builds exactly this, with a test.
2. A **waterfall**. Start both requests together: lift both fetches into the parent (or a route loader, Section [51](#51-router-data-loaders-actions-and-pending-ui)) and run them with `Promise.all`, or let a data library prefetch.

</details>

## 35. useReducer: State Logic in One Place

![useReducer: event handlers dispatch actions describing what happened; a pure reducer function takes the current state and the action and returns the next state](images/react/35-reducer.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** when a component's state updates get complicated (many handlers each doing slightly different spread-and-filter gymnastics), move all that logic into one function called a **reducer**. Event handlers stop saying *how* to change state and instead **dispatch an action** describing *what happened* (`{ type: "added", text }`). The reducer receives the current state and the action and **returns the next state**. `useReducer(reducer, initialState)` wires it up.

**Words to know:**

- **Reducer:** a pure function `(state, action) => nextState`. The name comes from `array.reduce`, which folds a list of values into one result the same way.
- **Action:** a plain object describing what happened, by convention with a `type` field: `{ type: "deleted", id: 3 }`.
- **Dispatch:** sending an action to the reducer: `dispatch({ type: "deleted", id: 3 })`.
- **`useReducer(reducer, initialArg, init?)`:** returns `[state, dispatch]`; the optional `init` function computes the initial state lazily.
- **Action type:** a string naming the event, past tense by convention (`"added"`, `"changed"`), describing what the user did rather than the state change.
- **Discriminated union of actions (TypeScript):** `type Action = { type: "added"; text: string } | { type: "deleted"; id: number }`, so each case knows its fields.
- **Exhaustive check:** a `default` branch that TypeScript proves unreachable (`const never: never = action`), so adding a new action type without handling it is a compile error.
- **`useImmerReducer`:** a version from `use-immer` that lets the reducer "mutate" a draft (Section [17](#17-updating-objects-in-state)).

**Everyday picture.** A **bank teller**. Customers don't walk into the vault and move money themselves (handlers mutating state); they fill in a slip saying what they want: "deposit ₹500" (an action). The teller (reducer) follows fixed rules to produce the new balance. Every change goes through one window, so it's easy to audit and test.

**Folding actions into state, traced by hand:**

```text
initial:  [ {id:0, text:"Boil water", done:true} ]
action 1: { type: "added", id: 1, text: "Add tea" }      → [ …, {id:1, text:"Add tea", done:false} ]
action 2: { type: "changed", task: {id:1, …, done:true}} → task 1 replaced with the new object
action 3: { type: "deleted", id: 0 }                     → [ {id:1, text:"Add tea", done:true} ]
the same three actions replayed from the same initial state ALWAYS give the same result (the reducer is pure)
```

**useState vs useReducer:**

| | `useState` | `useReducer` |
|---|---|---|
| code size | small for simple state | more boilerplate up front, less as logic grows |
| readability | fine for a few updates | update logic in one place, handlers read like a log of events |
| debugging | hard to see why state changed | log every action in the reducer |
| testing | needs the component | the reducer is a plain function: test it without React |

**When to use it:** several state values updated together, many event types touching the same state, logic you want to test in isolation, or as the basis of a context-based store (Section [37](#37-scaling-up-with-reducer-and-context)). **When not:** a toggle or a single input; `useState` is clearer.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Mutating `state` inside the reducer (it must return a new object).
- ❌ Side effects in the reducer (fetching, timers, `Math.random()`); reducers must be pure, and StrictMode calls them twice to check.
- ❌ Actions that are setters in disguise (`{ type: "setTasks", tasks }`); describe the event instead.
- ❌ Forgetting a `default` case (unknown actions silently return `undefined`).

**Used in real software:** Redux (and Redux Toolkit's `createSlice`) is built entirely on reducers (Section [55](#55-global-state-build-a-store-then-zustand-redux-toolkit-and-jotai)); form libraries, wizards and editors with undo use reducers internally.

### Code

**From scratch: a reducer is just what `Array.reduce` uses.** Replaying a list of actions over an initial state gives the final state:

```tsx
type Task = { id: number; text: string; done: boolean };
type Action =
  | { type: "added"; id: number; text: string }
  | { type: "changed"; task: Task }
  | { type: "deleted"; id: number };

function tasksReducer(tasks: Task[], action: Action): Task[] {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "added": return [...tasks, { id: action.id, text: action.text, done: false }];
    case "changed": return tasks.map((t) => (t.id === action.task.id ? action.task : t));
    case "deleted": return tasks.filter((t) => t.id !== action.id);
    default: { const unknown: never = action; throw new Error("Unknown action " + JSON.stringify(unknown)); }
  }
}

const initialTasks: Task[] = [{ id: 0, text: "Boil water", done: true }];
const actions: Action[] = [
  { type: "added", id: 1, text: "Add tea" },
  { type: "changed", task: { id: 1, text: "Add tea", done: true } },
  { type: "deleted", id: 0 },
];
console.log(actions.reduce(tasksReducer, initialTasks));
console.log("original untouched:", initialTasks);
```

**Output:**

```text
[ { id: 1, text: 'Add tea', done: true } ]
original untouched: [ { id: 0, text: 'Boil water', done: true } ]
```

The `default` branch assigns `action` to a variable of type `never`: if a new action type is added to `Action` but not handled, TypeScript reports an error there.

**Testing a reducer needs no React at all:**

```tsx
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
assert.deepEqual(tasksReducer([], { type: "added", id: 7, text: "Pour" }), [{ id: 7, text: "Pour", done: false }]);
assert.deepEqual(tasksReducer(initialTasks, { type: "deleted", id: 0 }), []);
console.log("reducer tests passed");
```

**Output:**

```text
reducer tests passed
```

`node:assert/strict` is Node's built-in assertion module; `deepEqual` compares structures. Section [56](#56-testing-components-vitest-testing-library-and-user-event) uses a full test runner.

**The React way: `useReducer`** with handlers that only dispatch:

```tsx
import { useReducer, useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

let nextId = 2;
function TaskApp() {
  const [tasks, dispatch] = useReducer(tasksReducer, initialTasks);
  const [text, setText] = useState("");
  return (
    <>
      <input aria-label="new task" value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)} />
      <button onClick={() => { dispatch({ type: "added", id: nextId++, text }); setText(""); }}>Add</button>
      <ul>
        {tasks.map((t) => (
          <li key={t.id}>
            <label><input type="checkbox" checked={t.done} onChange={(e) => dispatch({ type: "changed", task: { ...t, done: e.target.checked } })} />{t.text}</label>
            <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "deleted", id: t.id })}>delete {t.text}</button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
}
render(<TaskApp />);
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("new task"), { target: { value: "Add cardamom" } });
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Add"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByLabelText("Add cardamom"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("delete Boil water"));
console.log(screen.getAllByRole("listitem").map((li) => `${(li.querySelector("input") as HTMLInputElement).checked ? "☑" : "☐"} ${li.querySelector("label")!.textContent}`));
```

**Output:**

```text
[ '☑ Add cardamom' ]
```

**Logging every action** is the debugging superpower reducers give you; wrap the reducer:

```tsx
function withLogging<S, A>(reducer: (s: S, a: A) => S) {
  return (state: S, action: A) => {
    const next = reducer(state, action);
    console.log("action:", JSON.stringify(action), "→", (next as unknown as Task[]).length, "tasks");
    return next;
  };
}
function LoggedApp() {
  const [tasks, dispatch] = useReducer(withLogging(tasksReducer), initialTasks);
  return <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "added", id: 99, text: "Strain" })}>{tasks.length} tasks</button>;
}
render(<LoggedApp />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
```

**Output:**

```text
action: {"type":"added","id":99,"text":"Strain"} → 2 tasks
```

React may call a reducer twice in development (StrictMode) to check it's pure; because this example isn't wrapped in `StrictMode`, it logs once.

### Practice

1. Write a `counterReducer` handling `{ type: "incremented" }`, `{ type: "decremented" }` and `{ type: "reset"; to: number }`, with an exhaustive `default`.
2. A reducer does `state.items.push(action.item); return state;`. What goes wrong in the UI?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
type CounterAction = { type: "incremented" } | { type: "decremented" } | { type: "reset"; to: number };
function counterReducer(count: number, action: CounterAction): number {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "incremented": return count + 1;
    case "decremented": return count - 1;
    case "reset": return action.to;
    default: { const x: never = action; return x; }
  }
}
const steps: CounterAction[] = [{ type: "incremented" }, { type: "incremented" }, { type: "decremented" }, { type: "reset", to: 10 }, { type: "incremented" }];
console.log(steps.reduce(counterReducer, 0));
```

**Output:**

```text
11
```

2. It returns the **same** object, so React sees no change (`Object.is`) and doesn't re-render; the mutation also corrupts the previous state. Return `{ ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] }`.

</details>

## 36. Context: Passing Data Deeply

![Context lets a parent provide a value that any component below it can read with useContext, skipping the components in between; the nearest provider wins](images/react/04-context.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** passing a prop through five layers of components that don't use it is tedious ("prop drilling"). **Context** lets a parent **provide** a value to its whole subtree, and any component inside can **read** it directly with `useContext`, however deep. Typical uses: the current theme, the logged-in user, the language, a router. Components read the value from the **nearest** provider above them.

**Words to know:**

- **Context:** a way to pass a value deep down the tree without props, created with `createContext(defaultValue)`.
- **Provider:** the component that supplies a value to its subtree. In React 19 you render the context itself: `<ThemeContext value="dark">…</ThemeContext>` (older code: `<ThemeContext.Provider value=…>`).
- **`useContext(Context)`:** reads the value from the nearest provider above; returns the **default value** if there's none.
- **`use(Context)`:** React 19's `use` can also read context and, unlike hooks, may be called inside conditions and loops.
- **Default value:** what `useContext` returns with no provider above; often `null`, or a sensible fallback.
- **Nearest provider wins:** providers can be nested; a deeper provider overrides an outer one for its subtree.
- **Re-render on change:** when a provider's `value` changes (compared with `Object.is`), **every** component that reads that context re-renders, even if it only uses part of the value.
- **Context splitting:** using several smaller contexts (e.g. state and dispatch, or user and theme) so a change only re-renders the components that read that part.
- **Prop drilling:** passing props through components that don't need them, just to reach a deep child.

**Everyday picture.** **Building-wide Wi-Fi.** Instead of running a cable from the router through every room to reach your desk (prop drilling), the router broadcasts and any device in range just connects (useContext). A repeater on one floor (a nested provider) gives that floor its own network.

**How a context value is found, traced:**

```text
<ThemeContext value="dark">             ← provider A
  <Page>
    <Sidebar>
      <Button />                         useContext(ThemeContext) → walks up → finds A → "dark"
    </Sidebar>
    <ThemeContext value="light">         ← provider B
      <Footer><Button /></Footer>        → finds B first → "light"
    </ThemeContext>
  </Page>
</ThemeContext>
<Button /> outside everything             → no provider → the default value
```

**When to use context:** genuinely global or widely used values (theme, user, locale, feature flags, a dependency like an API client), and to pair with a reducer as an app-level store (Section [37](#37-scaling-up-with-reducer-and-context)). **When not:** to avoid passing props two or three levels (that's fine, and explicit), or before trying composition (Section [25](#25-composition-children-slots-and-layout-components)); and not for fast-changing values read by many components (every reader re-renders), where a store with selectors fits better (Section [55](#55-global-state-build-a-store-then-zustand-redux-toolkit-and-jotai)).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Reading context in a component that isn't inside the provider, then wondering why it's the default.
- ❌ Passing a new object as `value` on every render (`value={{ user, logout }}`), re-rendering every reader each time; memoise it (Section [45](#45-memo-usememo-usecallback-and-the-react-compiler)) or split contexts.
- ❌ One giant "AppContext" holding everything.
- ❌ Using context for state only one subtree needs.

**Used in real software:** React Router, TanStack Query, Redux's `Provider`, styled-components themes and internationalisation libraries (react-intl, i18next) all pass their objects down through context.

### Code

**From scratch: the drilling problem.** Without context, `level` must be passed through every heading component explicitly:

```tsx
import { createContext, useContext, use, useState } from "react";
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";

function DrilledHeading({ level, children }: { level: number; children: string }) {
  const Tag = `h${level}` as "h1";
  return <Tag>{children}</Tag>;
}
function DrilledSection({ level, children }: { level: number; children: (level: number) => ReactNode }) {
  return <section>{children(level)}</section>;
}
console.log(render(
  <DrilledSection level={1}>{(l) => <><DrilledHeading level={l}>Menu</DrilledHeading>
    <DrilledSection level={l + 1}>{(l2) => <DrilledHeading level={l2}>Teas</DrilledHeading>}</DrilledSection></>}</DrilledSection>,
).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<section><h1>Menu</h1><section><h2>Teas</h2></section></section>
```

It works, but every layer has to know about `level`. (`` `h${level}` as "h1" `` builds a tag name string; the cast tells TypeScript it's a valid tag.)

**The React way: each `Section` provides its level + 1; `Heading` reads it:**

```tsx
const LevelContext = createContext(0);

function Section({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const level = useContext(LevelContext);
  return <section><LevelContext value={level + 1}>{children}</LevelContext></section>;
}
function Heading({ children }: { children: string }) {
  const level = useContext(LevelContext);
  const Tag = `h${Math.min(level, 6)}` as "h1";
  return <Tag>{children}</Tag>;
}
console.log(render(
  <Section>
    <Heading>Menu</Heading>
    <Section>
      <Heading>Teas</Heading>
      <Section><Heading>Masala chai</Heading></Section>
    </Section>
  </Section>,
).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<section><h1>Menu</h1><section><h2>Teas</h2><section><h3>Masala chai</h3></section></section></section>
```

No component passes `level` explicitly; each `Section` reads the level from above and provides one deeper. This is react.dev's own example of context's power.

**Theme and user, nested providers and the default value:**

```tsx
type User = { name: string } | null;
const ThemeContext = createContext<"light" | "dark">("light");
const UserContext = createContext<User>(null);

function Button({ children }: { children: string }) {
  const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
  return <button className={`btn-${theme}`}>{children}</button>;
}
function Greeting() {
  const user = useContext(UserContext);
  return <p>{user ? `Hi, ${user.name}` : "Please log in"}</p>;
}
function App() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState<"light" | "dark">("dark");
  return (
    <ThemeContext value={theme}>
      <UserContext value={{ name: "Asha" }}>
        <Greeting />
        <Button>Order</Button>
        <ThemeContext value="light"><Button>Light island</Button></ThemeContext>
        <button onClick={() => setTheme(theme === "dark" ? "light" : "dark")}>toggle</button>
      </UserContext>
    </ThemeContext>
  );
}
const app = render(<><App /><Greeting /></>);
console.log(app.container.innerHTML);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("toggle"));
console.log("after toggle:", screen.getByText("Order").className);
```

**Output:**

```text
<p>Hi, Asha</p><button class="btn-dark">Order</button><button class="btn-light">Light island</button><button>toggle</button><p>Please log in</p>
after toggle: btn-light
```

The second `Greeting` sits outside every provider, so it gets the default `null`. The "Light island" button reads its nearest provider.

**Every reader re-renders when the value changes,** even readers that don't use the part that changed:

```tsx
const renders: Record<string, number> = {};
const AppState = createContext({ user: "Asha", cartCount: 0 });
function UserBadge() { renders.UserBadge = (renders.UserBadge ?? 0) + 1; return <span>{useContext(AppState).user}</span>; }
function CartBadge() { renders.CartBadge = (renders.CartBadge ?? 0) + 1; return <span>{useContext(AppState).cartCount}</span>; }
function Store() {
  const [cartCount, setCartCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <AppState value={{ user: "Asha", cartCount }}>
      <UserBadge /><CartBadge />
      <button onClick={() => setCartCount((c) => c + 1)}>add</button>
    </AppState>
  );
}
render(<Store />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("add"));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("add"));
console.log(renders, "← UserBadge re-rendered although the user never changed");
```

**Output:**

```text
{ UserBadge: 3, CartBadge: 3 } ← UserBadge re-rendered although the user never changed
```

Splitting into `UserContext` and `CartContext` (or a store with selectors) limits re-renders to the components that need the changed value.

**`use(Context)` may be called conditionally** (React 19), unlike `useContext`:

```tsx
function Price({ showCurrency }: { showCurrency: boolean }) {
  if (!showCurrency) return <span>180</span>;
  const theme = use(ThemeContext);                      // OK after an early return
  return <span className={theme}>₹180</span>;
}
console.log(render(<ThemeContext value="dark"><Price showCurrency /><Price showCurrency={false} /></ThemeContext>).container.innerHTML);
```

**Output:**

```text
<span class="dark">₹180</span><span>180</span>
```

### Practice

1. Create a `LocaleContext` (`"en-IN"` by default) and a `Price({ paise })` component that formats with `Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency", currency: "INR" })`. Render one price inside a provider for `"en-US"` and one outside.
2. A provider renders `<AuthContext value={{ user, login, logout }}>`. Why might every reader re-render on unrelated parent renders, and how do you fix it?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
const LocaleContext = createContext("en-IN");
function PriceTag({ paise }: { paise: number }) {
  const locale = useContext(LocaleContext);
  return <span>{new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }).format(paise / 100)} </span>;
}
console.log(render(<><LocaleContext value="en-US"><PriceTag paise={18499950} /></LocaleContext><PriceTag paise={18499950} /></>).container.textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
₹184,999.50 ₹1,84,999.50
```

1. Inside the provider, US grouping (thousands: 184,999.50); outside, the default `"en-IN"` uses Indian lakh grouping (1,84,999.50). Same component, different context value.
2. `{ user, login, logout }` is a **new object** every time the provider's component renders, so `Object.is` says the value changed and all readers re-render. Wrap the value in `useMemo` (and the functions in `useCallback`), let the React Compiler memoise it, or split state and functions into separate contexts.

</details>

## 37. Scaling Up with Reducer and Context

![A provider component owns state with useReducer and puts state and dispatch into two contexts; any component below reads tasks or dispatches actions through small custom hooks](images/react/37-reducer-context.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** combine the two previous sections and you get a small app-wide store with no library: a **provider component** holds state with `useReducer`, and provides **`state`** and **`dispatch`** through **two contexts**. Any component in the tree can read the state or dispatch actions, without prop drilling. Wrap the lookups in small **custom hooks** (`useTasks()`, `useTasksDispatch()`) so components never touch the contexts directly.

**Words to know:**

- **Provider component:** your own component (`TasksProvider`) that owns state and renders the context providers around `children`.
- **State context / dispatch context:** two separate contexts; `dispatch` never changes identity, so components that only dispatch don't re-render when state changes.
- **Accessor hooks:** tiny custom hooks such as `useTasks()` that call `useContext` and throw a helpful error when used outside the provider.
- **Store:** a single object holding app state plus a way to update it; reducer + context is a do-it-yourself store.
- **Colocation:** keeping the reducer, contexts, provider and hooks in one file (`TasksContext.tsx`).

**Everyday picture.** A **restaurant kitchen ticket rail**. The kitchen (provider) owns the orders (state). Any waiter can read the rail (state context) or clip a new ticket on it (dispatch context). Waiters don't carry orders from table to table to reach the kitchen; they all use the same rail.

**The structure, traced:**

```text
TasksContext.tsx
  tasksReducer(tasks, action)                      pure logic (Section 35)
  TasksContext, TasksDispatchContext               createContext(null)
  TasksProvider({ children }):
     const [tasks, dispatch] = useReducer(tasksReducer, initialTasks)
     return <TasksContext value={tasks}><TasksDispatchContext value={dispatch}>{children}</…></…>
  useTasks()         → useContext(TasksContext)   (throws if null)
  useTasksDispatch() → useContext(TasksDispatchContext)
App:  <TasksProvider><AddTask /><TaskList /></TasksProvider>
AddTask: dispatch({ type: "added", … })   TaskList: const tasks = useTasks()
```

**When to use it:** small to medium apps whose shared state changes at human speed (a cart, settings, a task list). **When not:** state that changes very often and is read by many components (every reader re-renders), server data (use TanStack Query, Section [52](#52-server-state-with-tanstack-query)), or large apps where a store library's selectors and devtools pay off (Section [55](#55-global-state-build-a-store-then-zustand-redux-toolkit-and-jotai)).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Putting `state` and `dispatch` in one object `value={{ state, dispatch }}` (a new object every render).
- ❌ Accessor hooks that silently return `null` outside the provider; throw a clear error instead.
- ❌ One store for everything, including server data and form drafts.

**Used in real software:** many small production apps use exactly this; it's also how libraries are built inside (React Router keeps its router state in context; Redux's `Provider` passes the store through context).

### Code

```tsx
import { createContext, useContext, useReducer } from "react";
import type { Dispatch, ReactNode } from "react";

export type Task = { id: number; text: string; done: boolean };
export type Action = { type: "added"; id: number; text: string } | { type: "toggled"; id: number } | { type: "deleted"; id: number };

function tasksReducer(tasks: Task[], action: Action): Task[] {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "added": return [...tasks, { id: action.id, text: action.text, done: false }];
    case "toggled": return tasks.map((t) => (t.id === action.id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t));
    case "deleted": return tasks.filter((t) => t.id !== action.id);
  }
}

const TasksContext = createContext<Task[] | null>(null);
const TasksDispatchContext = createContext<Dispatch<Action> | null>(null);

export function TasksProvider({ children, initial = [] }: { children: ReactNode; initial?: Task[] }) {
  const [tasks, dispatch] = useReducer(tasksReducer, initial);
  return (
    <TasksContext value={tasks}>
      <TasksDispatchContext value={dispatch}>{children}</TasksDispatchContext>
    </TasksContext>
  );
}

export function useTasks() {
  const tasks = useContext(TasksContext);
  if (tasks === null) throw new Error("useTasks must be used inside <TasksProvider>");
  return tasks;
}
export function useTasksDispatch() {
  const dispatch = useContext(TasksDispatchContext);
  if (dispatch === null) throw new Error("useTasksDispatch must be used inside <TasksProvider>");
  return dispatch;
}
```

The whole store lives in one file. Every exported piece is small; components only ever see `TasksProvider`, `useTasks` and `useTasksDispatch`.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";
import { TasksProvider, useTasks, useTasksDispatch } from "./TasksContext.tsx";

const renders = { AddTask: 0, TaskList: 0 };
let nextId = 3;
function AddTask() {
  renders.AddTask++;
  const dispatch = useTasksDispatch();
  const [text, setText] = useState("");
  return <><input aria-label="task" value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)} />
    <button onClick={() => { dispatch({ type: "added", id: nextId++, text }); setText(""); }}>Add</button></>;
}
function TaskList() {
  renders.TaskList++;
  const tasks = useTasks();
  const dispatch = useTasksDispatch();
  return <ul>{tasks.map((t) => <li key={t.id} onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "toggled", id: t.id })}>{t.done ? "☑" : "☐"} {t.text}</li>)}</ul>;
}
render(
  <TasksProvider initial={[{ id: 1, text: "Boil water", done: false }, { id: 2, text: "Add tea", done: false }]}>
    <h1>Day plan</h1>
    <AddTask />
    <TaskList />
  </TasksProvider>,
);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/Boil water/));
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("task"), { target: { value: "Strain" } });
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Add"));
console.log(screen.getAllByRole("listitem").map((li) => li.textContent));
console.log("renders:", renders);
```

**Output:**

```text
[ '☑ Boil water', '☐ Add tea', '☐ Strain' ]
renders: { AddTask: 3, TaskList: 3 }
```

`AddTask` re-rendered only for its own typing (its `text` state) and the clear after adding; it never re-rendered because the task list changed, since it reads only the dispatch context, whose value never changes. `TaskList` re-rendered on each change to the tasks.

**Outside the provider, the accessor hook explains the mistake:**

```tsx
function Orphan() { useTasks(); return null; }
render(<Orphan />);
```

**Output:**

```text
Error: useTasks must be used inside <TasksProvider>
```

### Practice

1. Add a `cleared-done` action (remove all finished tasks) and a "Clear done" button inside `AddTask`. Which files change?
2. Why does `AddTask` not re-render when a task is toggled?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. `TasksContext.tsx` (one more case in `Action` and the reducer; TypeScript's `switch` coverage helps) and the component with the button, which dispatches `{ type: "cleared-done" }`. No component in between changes: that's the point of the store.
2. It only reads `TasksDispatchContext`, and `dispatch` from `useReducer` keeps the same identity for the component's whole life, so that context's value never changes. Its parent (`TasksProvider`) re-renders, but `AddTask` was created by the **grandparent** as part of `children`, so it isn't re-rendered just because the provider re-rendered.

</details>

## 38. Custom Hooks: Reusing Stateful Logic

![A custom hook is a function starting with use that calls other hooks; two components calling useOnlineStatus share the logic but each gets its own independent state](images/react/38-custom-hooks.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** when two components need the same stateful logic (track online status, fetch some data, debounce a value, read and write `localStorage`), move it into a function whose name starts with **`use`** and which calls other hooks. That's a **custom hook**. Components call it like a built-in hook. Custom hooks share **logic**, not **state**: each component that calls `useCounter()` gets its own counter.

**Words to know:**

- **Custom hook:** a JavaScript function whose name starts with `use` and that calls other hooks (`useState`, `useEffect`, other custom hooks).
- **`use` prefix rule:** the name tells React's linter to apply the Rules of Hooks inside it and to its callers; a function that calls no hooks shouldn't start with `use`.
- **Sharing logic vs sharing state:** each call to a hook creates independent state; to share state itself, lift it up or use context.
- **Hook API design:** what the hook returns: a value (`isOnline`), a tuple (`[value, setValue]` like `useState`) or an object (`{ data, error, status }`).
- **`renderHook`:** Testing Library's helper to test a hook by rendering a tiny component that calls it; `result.current` holds the latest return value.
- **Abstraction:** hiding details behind a well-named interface; custom hooks let components say *what* they need (`useOnlineStatus()`) instead of *how* to get it.
- **Debounce:** wait until a value has stopped changing for some time before using it.

**Everyday picture.** A **recipe card** for masala chai. Every kitchen that follows it makes its own pot (separate state); the card just shares the method (logic). Giving the recipe a clear name ("masala chai") is like naming a hook `useOnlineStatus` instead of leaving twenty lines of effects in every component.

**Extracting a hook, traced:**

```text
StatusBar:   const [isOnline, setIsOnline] = useState(true); useEffect(subscribe to online/offline events …)
SaveButton:  the SAME 10 lines again
extract  →   function useOnlineStatus() { const [isOnline, set…] = useState(true); useEffect(…); return isOnline; }
StatusBar:   const isOnline = useOnlineStatus();        SaveButton: const isOnline = useOnlineStatus();
each component still has its own useState inside the hook; both subscribe separately; both update on the event
```

**When to write a custom hook:** the same hook logic appears in two places; a component's effect is long and has a nameable purpose; you want to test the logic separately. **When not:** for a single `useState` with no logic (indirection without benefit); for code that doesn't call hooks (make it a normal function).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Naming a non-hook function `useSomething` (or a hook without `use`, which hides Rules-of-Hooks violations from the linter).
- ❌ Expecting two components using the same hook to share state.
- ❌ Hooks that "do everything" (`useApp()`); keep each focused on one concern.
- ❌ Returning new objects or functions every render that consumers put in dependency arrays (memoise them or let the Compiler do it).

**Used in real software:** most libraries are delivered as custom hooks: `useQuery` (TanStack Query), `useForm` (React Hook Form), `useNavigate` (React Router), `useStore` (Zustand); every codebase also grows its own (`useDebounce`, `useMediaQuery`, `useLocalStorage`).

### Code

**Extracting `useOnlineStatus`:** two components share the logic; each has its own state and subscription:

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { render, renderHook, screen, act } from "@testing-library/react";

function useOnlineStatus() {
  const [isOnline, setIsOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine);
  useEffect(() => {
    const on = () => setIsOnline(true), off = () => setIsOnline(false);
    window.addEventListener("online", on);
    window.addEventListener("offline", off);
    return () => { window.removeEventListener("online", on); window.removeEventListener("offline", off); };
  }, []);
  return isOnline;
}
function StatusBar() { return <h3>{useOnlineStatus() ? "✅ Online" : "❌ Disconnected"}</h3>; }
function SaveButton() { const online = useOnlineStatus(); return <button disabled={!online}>{online ? "Save progress" : "Reconnecting…"}</button>; }

render(<><StatusBar /><SaveButton /></>);
console.log(screen.getByRole("heading").textContent, "|", screen.getByRole("button").textContent);
await act(async () => { window.dispatchEvent(new Event("offline")); });
console.log(screen.getByRole("heading").textContent, "|", screen.getByRole("button").textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
✅ Online | Save progress
❌ Disconnected | Reconnecting…
```

**Hooks share logic, not state:** two counters from the same hook are independent:

```tsx
function useCounter(start = 0) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(start);
  return { count, increment: () => setCount((c) => c + 1) };
}
const a = renderHook(() => useCounter());
const b = renderHook(() => useCounter(10));
act(() => { a.result.current.increment(); a.result.current.increment(); });
console.log("a:", a.result.current.count, "| b:", b.result.current.count);
```

**Output:**

```text
a: 2 | b: 10
```

`renderHook` renders a hidden test component that calls the hook; `result.current` is whatever the hook returned on the latest render, and `act` applies the updates.

**`useDebouncedValue`:** returns a value only after it has stopped changing for `delay` ms (useful for search boxes):

```tsx
function useDebouncedValue<T>(value: T, delay: number): T {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(id);                     // a new value cancels the pending update
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}
const d = renderHook(({ v }) => useDebouncedValue(v, 30), { initialProps: { v: "c" } });
for (const v of ["ch", "cha", "chai"]) d.rerender({ v });
console.log("immediately:", d.result.current);
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 60)));
console.log("after 60 ms:", d.result.current);
```

**Output:**

```text
immediately: c
after 60 ms: chai
```

**`useFetch`:** the effect from Section [34](#34-fetching-data-in-effects-loading-errors-race-conditions-and-abortcontroller) packaged as a reusable hook:

```tsx
import { createServer } from "node:http";

type FetchState<T> = { status: "loading" } | { status: "error"; error: string } | { status: "success"; data: T };
function useFetch<T>(url: string): FetchState<T> {
  const [state, setState] = useState<FetchState<T>>({ status: "loading" });
  useEffect(() => {
    let ignore = false;
    const controller = new AbortController();
    setState({ status: "loading" });
    fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then((r) => { if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${r.status}`); return r.json() as Promise<T>; })
      .then((data) => { if (!ignore) setState({ status: "success", data }); })
      .catch((e: Error) => { if (!ignore && e.name !== "AbortError") setState({ status: "error", error: e.message }); });
    return () => { ignore = true; controller.abort(); };
  }, [url]);
  return state;
}
const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  if (req.url === "/menu") res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "application/json" }).end('["Masala chai","Samosa"]');
  else res.writeHead(404).end();
});
await new Promise<void>((r) => server.listen(4403, r));

function Menu({ url }: { url: string }) {
  const state = useFetch<string[]>(url);
  if (state.status === "loading") return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (state.status === "error") return <p>Error: {state.error}</p>;
  return <p>{state.data.join(", ")}</p>;
}
render(<><Menu url="http://localhost:4403/menu" /><Menu url="http://localhost:4403/nope" /></>);
await screen.findByText(/Samosa/);
await screen.findByText(/Error/);
console.log(screen.getAllByRole("paragraph").map((p) => p.textContent));
server.close();
```

**Output:**

```text
[ 'Masala chai, Samosa', 'Error: HTTP 404' ]
```

### Practice

1. Write `useLocalStorage(key, initial)` that works like `useState` but reads the initial value from `localStorage` and saves every change.
2. Write `useToggle(initial = false)` returning `[value, toggle]`, and test it with `renderHook`.

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
function useLocalStorage<T>(key: string, initial: T) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState<T>(() => {
    const saved = localStorage.getItem(key);
    return saved !== null ? (JSON.parse(saved) as T) : initial;
  });
  useEffect(() => { localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value)); }, [key, value]);
  return [value, setValue] as const;
}
const first = renderHook(() => useLocalStorage("cart", [] as string[]));
act(() => first.result.current[1](["chai"]));
first.unmount();
const second = renderHook(() => useLocalStorage("cart", [] as string[]));   // a "new page load"
console.log("restored:", second.result.current[0], "| stored text:", localStorage.getItem("cart"));

function useToggle(initial = false) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(initial);
  return [on, () => setOn((v) => !v)] as const;
}
const t = renderHook(() => useToggle());
act(() => t.result.current[1]());
console.log("toggled:", t.result.current[0]);
```

**Output:**

```text
restored: [ 'chai' ] | stored text: ["chai"]
toggled: true
```

1. A lazy initializer reads storage once; an effect saves on change. `as const` makes the return a readonly tuple so callers get exact types. (Real apps also listen to the `storage` event to sync between tabs, Section [40](#40-more-hooks-uselayouteffect-useid-usesyncexternalstore-useimperativehandle-and-ref-as-a-prop).)
2. The toggle uses an updater, so calling it twice in one event toggles twice.

</details>
