## 60. Streaming SSR with Suspense

![Streaming SSR: the server sends the page shell with Suspense fallbacks immediately, keeps the connection open, and streams each slow section's HTML plus a tiny script that swaps it into place as soon as its data is ready](images/react/60-streaming.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** with plain SSR the server can't send anything until **all** data for the page has loaded, so one slow query delays the whole page. **Streaming SSR** sends the page **shell** right away, with Suspense **fallbacks** (skeletons) where slow parts go, keeps the connection open, and sends each slow part's HTML when its data is ready, with a tiny inline script that swaps it into place. The user sees useful content sooner, and React can hydrate each part as it arrives.

**Words to know:**

- **Streaming:** sending a response in pieces (**chunks**) over one open connection instead of all at once.
- **Shell:** the parts of the page outside any pending Suspense boundary (layout, header, fallbacks); sent first.
- **`renderToPipeableStream` (Node) / `renderToReadableStream` (web streams):** React's streaming server APIs.
- **`onShellReady` / `onAllReady`:** callbacks: the shell can be sent / everything is rendered (bots and static generation wait for `onAllReady`).
- **Suspense boundary on the server:** where React can pause; a component that's waiting for data (it **suspends**) is replaced by its boundary's fallback in the shell.
- **`use(promise)`:** reads a promise's value during render, suspending until it resolves (works on the server and the client).
- **Out-of-order streaming:** each boundary's HTML is sent as soon as it's ready, in any order, inside a hidden `<div>`, then moved into place by an inline script (React's `$RC` "reveal completed" function).
- **Chunked transfer encoding:** the HTTP mechanism that lets a server send a response in pieces without knowing its total length.
- **Selective hydration:** hydrating each streamed part independently; parts the user clicks on are hydrated first.
- **Time to first byte vs time to content:** streaming makes the first byte (and the shell) arrive early even when some data is slow.

**Everyday picture.** A **restaurant serving courses as they're ready** instead of holding the whole table's food until the slowest dish is done. The table is laid immediately (the shell), with a "coming soon" card where the slow dish goes (the fallback); each dish is brought out and put in its place the moment it's ready.

**One streamed page, traced:**

```text
<Layout>
  <h1>Chai Point</h1>                          fast
  <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading reviews…</p>}>
    <Reviews />                                 needs a 50 ms database query
  </Suspense>
</Layout>
t=0 ms   server renders → Reviews suspends → sends the shell: <h1>…</h1> <!--$?--><template id="B:0"></template><p>Loading reviews…</p><!--/$-->
         the browser paints the heading and the skeleton immediately
t=50 ms  data ready → server renders Reviews → sends <div hidden id="S:0"><ul>…reviews…</ul></div>
         plus <script>$RC("B:0","S:0")</script> → the script swaps the hidden content in place of the fallback
         response ends
```

**When to stream:** any server-rendered page with slow, independent parts (recommendations, reviews, personalised widgets). **When not:** when the slow part is needed for the page to make sense (then wait for it, or fetch it faster); for crawlers that don't run scripts, frameworks wait for `onAllReady` and send complete HTML.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ One Suspense boundary around the whole page (nothing streams early).
- ❌ Fetching data in effects in server-rendered components (effects don't run on the server; the HTML has only spinners).
- ❌ Creating a new promise on every render for `use()` (it suspends forever); create it once, outside render or in a cache.
- ❌ Buffering proxies or compression settings that hold back chunks (the page arrives all at once anyway).

**Used in real software:** Next.js App Router streams by default with `loading.tsx` and Suspense; React Router framework mode streams deferred loader data; Shopify Hydrogen and many e-commerce sites stream product recommendations.

### Code

**Streaming for real:** the server-side render is captured chunk by chunk with timestamps, showing the shell first and the slow part later:

```tsx
import { Suspense, use } from "react";
import { renderToPipeableStream } from "react-dom/server";
import { Writable } from "node:stream";

const reviewsPromise = new Promise<string[]>((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve(["Best chai in Pune!", "Perfect ginger kick"]), 50));
function Reviews() {
  const reviews = use(reviewsPromise);                                 // suspends until the "database" answers
  return <ul>{reviews.map((r) => <li key={r}>{r}</li>)}</ul>;
}
function Page() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Chai Point</h1>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading reviews…</p>}><Reviews /></Suspense>
    </main>
  );
}

const started = Date.now();
const chunks: { at: number; html: string }[] = [];
await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
  const sink = new Writable({
    write(chunk, _enc, done) { chunks.push({ at: Date.now() - started, html: chunk.toString() }); done(); },
    final(done) { resolve(); done(); },
  });
  const { pipe } = renderToPipeableStream(<Page />, {
    onShellReady() { console.log("onShellReady after", Date.now() - started < 30 ? "< 30 ms" : "≥ 30 ms"); pipe(sink); },
    onAllReady() { console.log("onAllReady after", Date.now() - started >= 45 ? "≥ 45 ms (waited for the reviews)" : "< 45 ms"); },
  });
});
for (const [i, c] of chunks.entries()) {
  const readable = c.html.replace(/<script>.*?<\/script>/gs, "<script>…</script>").replace(/<style>.*?<\/style>/gs, "");
  console.log(`chunk ${i + 1} (${c.at < 30 ? "early" : "later"}):`, readable.slice(0, 260));
}
```

**Output:**

```text
onShellReady after < 30 ms
onAllReady after ≥ 45 ms (waited for the reviews)
chunk 1 (early): <main><h1>Chai Point</h1><!--$?--><template id="B:0"></template><p>Loading reviews…</p><!--/$--></main><script>…</script>
chunk 2 (later): <div hidden id="S:0"><ul><li>Best chai in Pune!</li><li>Perfect ginger kick</li></ul></div><script>…</script>
```

The first chunk is the shell: the heading and the fallback, marked with `<!--$?-->` and an empty `<template id="B:0">` placeholder. The later chunk carries the reviews inside `<div hidden id="S:0">` plus a small script (shown as `<script>…</script>`) that moves them into the placeholder's place and removes the fallback. Timings are printed as "early/later" because exact milliseconds vary.

**The same kind of page rendered without streaming** (`renderToString`) can't wait for data: a part whose promise is still pending is rendered as its fallback, and the client would have to render it later:

```tsx
import { renderToString } from "react-dom/server";
const slowPromise = new Promise<string[]>((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve(["Lovely"]), 50));
function SlowReviews() { return <ul>{use(slowPromise).map((r) => <li key={r}>{r}</li>)}</ul>; }
const html = renderToString(<main><h1>Chai Point</h1><Suspense fallback={<p>Loading reviews…</p>}><SlowReviews /></Suspense></main>);
console.log(html.replace(/<!--.*?-->/g, "").replace(/data-msg="([^"]{0,60})[^"]*"/s, 'data-msg="$1…"').replace(/ data-cstck="[^"]*"/s, ' data-cstck="…"'));
await slowPromise;
```

**Output:**

```text
<main><h1>Chai Point</h1><template data-msg="Switched to client rendering because the server rendering ab…" data-cstck="…"></template><p>Loading reviews…</p></main>
```

`renderToString` doesn't wait for Suspense data; it renders fallbacks for parts that are still suspended. In development it also leaves a `<template>` with a `data-msg` explaining why that boundary will switch to client rendering and a `data-cstck` component stack (both shortened here; the full message names `renderToString` and suggests the streaming APIs). (A promise that has **already** resolved, like `reviewsPromise` above by now, would render immediately, because React remembers settled promises.) Streaming APIs and `prerender` are the ones that wait.

### Practice

1. A product page has a fast product summary, slow reviews (800 ms) and slow recommendations (1.2 s). Where do you put Suspense boundaries, and in what order does HTML arrive?
2. Why must `reviewsPromise` above be created outside the component?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. Two separate boundaries, one around reviews and one around recommendations (not one around both). The shell (summary + two skeletons) arrives at once; reviews stream at ~800 ms, recommendations at ~1.2 s, each replacing its own fallback.
2. `use()` suspends until the promise resolves, then React renders the component again. If the component created a **new** promise on every render, the retry would get a fresh, pending promise and suspend again forever. Create promises once: outside render, in a cache, in a loader, or (in Server Components) by awaiting data on the server.

</details>

## 61. React Server Components: How They Work

![React Server Components run only on the server and send a serialized description of the UI (the RSC payload) instead of their code; Client Components marked 'use client' are sent as JavaScript and hydrate; server components can render client components and pass them serializable props](images/react/06-server-client.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** **React Server Components (RSC)** are components that run **only on the server** (at build time or per request). They can be `async`, read databases and files directly, and their code is **never sent to the browser**. What the browser receives is the **RSC payload**: a compact description of the rendered UI, with "holes" for **Client Components** (marked with `"use client"`), which are normal interactive React components sent as JavaScript. **Server Functions** (`"use server"`) let client code call server code like a function.

**Words to know:**

- **Server Component:** the default kind of component in an RSC framework; runs on the server, may be `async`, can't use state, effects or browser APIs; its code isn't in the client bundle.
- **Client Component:** a component in a file starting with `"use client"` (and everything it imports); rendered on the server for the first HTML, then hydrated and interactive in the browser.
- **`"use client"` directive:** marks a module as a boundary: from here down, components are client components.
- **RSC payload (Flight format):** the serialized tree a Server Component render produces: elements, text, and **client references** (pointers to client component modules), streamed to the browser.
- **Client reference:** an entry such as `I[69819,["…chunk.js"],"LikeButton"]`: "load this module from these chunks and use its `LikeButton` export here".
- **Serializable props:** props passed from a Server to a Client Component must be serializable (strings, numbers, plain objects, arrays, Dates, promises, JSX); not functions (except Server Functions) or class instances.
- **Server Function (`"use server"`):** an async function that runs on the server but can be called from the client (as a form action or directly); the client gets a reference id, not the code. Formerly called "Server Actions" when used with forms.
- **Bundle size benefit:** libraries used only in Server Components (a markdown parser, a date library, a database client) add **zero** bytes to the client JavaScript.
- **Composition rule:** Server Components can render Client Components and pass Server Components to them as `children`; Client Components can't import Server Components (but can receive them as props).
- **RSC framework:** React defines RSC, but you need a bundler/framework integration to use it: Next.js App Router, React Router (RSC support is still marked unstable), Waku, Parcel.

**Everyday picture.** A **restaurant that sends finished dishes plus a few DIY kits**. Most dishes are cooked in the kitchen (Server Components): you get the food, not the recipe or the stove. A few items need finishing at the table, like a sizzling plate you season yourself (Client Components): those come as a kit with instructions (JavaScript). The waiter can also take requests back to the kitchen (Server Functions).

**What travels to the browser, traced** for a page that lists teas (server) with a like button (client):

```text
app/teas/page.tsx (Server Component)     reads the database, renders <ul> of teas, each with <LikeButton name=… />
LikeButton.tsx ("use client")            useState for likes

RSC payload lines (real ones are shown in the code below):
  1e:I[69819,["/_next/static/chunks/…js"],"LikeButton"]        ← client reference: which module and export
  9:["$","ul",null,{"children":[["$","li","1",{"children":["Masala chai"," ₹",180," ",["$","$L1e",null,{"name":"Masala chai"}]]}],…]}]
        ← the server-rendered tree; "$L1e" marks where the LikeButton client component goes, with its props
  c:{"id":"406a…","bound":null}                               ← a Server Function reference (the form's action)
the database code, getTeas() and the list rendering logic: NOT in the browser bundle
```

**When to use Server Components:** data fetching and rendering of mostly static content, keeping secrets and heavy libraries on the server, reducing client JavaScript. **When to use Client Components:** anything interactive: state, effects, event handlers, browser APIs, context providers that hold state. Keep `"use client"` boundaries **low** in the tree (wrap just the interactive leaf).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ `"use client"` at the top of every file (loses all RSC benefits).
- ❌ Passing functions or class instances from a Server to a Client Component as props (not serializable).
- ❌ Importing server-only code (database clients, secrets) into a client component; mark such modules with `import "server-only"`.
- ❌ Treating Server Functions as private: each one is a **public HTTP endpoint**; always check authentication and validate input inside it (React Router 8.4's notes say the same).
- ❌ Running an outdated React/Next version: in December 2025 a critical vulnerability in RSC's Server Function handling (CVE-2025-55182, "React2Shell") allowed remote code execution; React 19.0.1/19.1.2/19.2.1 and later fix it (`javascript.md`, [Frontend Security](javascript.md#35-frontend-security-xss-csrf-csp-prototype-pollution-and-the-supply-chain)).

**Used in real software:** Next.js App Router (stable since Next.js 13.4, May 2023) is the main RSC implementation; React Router has RSC support marked unstable, and smaller frameworks such as Waku and Parcel's RSC integration exist.

### Code

These files form a minimal Next.js 16 App Router app. `page.tsx` is a Server Component (async, reads "the database"); `LikeButton.tsx` is a Client Component:

```js
{ "name": "chai-rsc", "private": true, "type": "module" }
```

```tsx
import type { NextConfig } from "next";
const nextConfig: NextConfig = { cacheComponents: true, partialPrefetching: true };
export default nextConfig;
```

```tsx
const TABLE = "chai_server_only_table_7f3";            // a marker string we can search the bundles for
let teas = [{ id: 1, name: "Masala chai", price: 180 }, { id: 2, name: "Ginger chai", price: 160 }];
export async function getTeas() {                         // pretend database query
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50));
  return teas.map((t) => ({ ...t, table: TABLE }));
}
export async function addTea(name: string) { teas = [...teas, { id: teas.length + 1, name, price: 150 }]; }
```

```tsx
export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return <html lang="en"><body><header>Chai Point</header>{children}</body></html>;
}
```

```tsx
"use client";
import { useState } from "react";

export function LikeButton({ name }: { name: string }) {
  const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>♥ {name} {likes}</button>;
}
```

```tsx
"use server";
import { updateTag } from "next/cache";
import { addTea } from "../../lib/db";

export async function createTea(formData: FormData) {
  const name = String(formData.get("name") ?? "").trim();
  if (!name) return;                     // validate: this function is a public endpoint
  await addTea(name);
  updateTag("teas");                     // expire cached data tagged "teas"
}
```

```tsx
import { Suspense } from "react";
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from "next/cache";
import { connection } from "next/server";
import { getTeas } from "../../lib/db";
import { LikeButton } from "./LikeButton";
import { createTea } from "./actions";

async function TeaList() {
  "use cache";                            // cache this component's output
  cacheLife("hours");
  cacheTag("teas");
  const teas = await getTeas();          // a Server Component can await data directly
  return <ul>{teas.map((t) => <li key={t.id}>{t.name} ₹{t.price} <LikeButton name={t.name} /></li>)}</ul>;
}
async function RequestTime() {
  await connection();                     // opt into request-time rendering
  return <p>Rendered at request time, year {new Date().getFullYear()}</p>;
}
export default function TeasPage() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Teas</h1>
      <TeaList />
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading…</p>}><RequestTime /></Suspense>
      <form action={createTea}><input name="name" aria-label="name" /><button>Add tea</button></form>
    </main>
  );
}
```

```tsx
export default function Home() { return <h1>Welcome</h1>; }
```

**Build, start, and look at what the browser receives:** the HTML, and the RSC payload that Next.js embeds in it for hydration:

```text
import json, re, sys
html = open(sys.argv[1]).read()
payload = "".join(json.loads(c)[1] for c in re.findall(r"self\.__next_f\.push\((\[1,.*?\])\)</script>", html, re.S))
for line in payload.split("\n"):
    if "LikeButton" in line or '"ul"' in line or '"bound"' in line:
        print(line[:200])
```

```bash
export NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1
npx next build > build.log 2>&1 || { tail -30 build.log; exit 1; }
npx next start -p 4501 > start.log 2>&1 &
for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:4501/ && break; sleep 0.5; done
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4501/teas > teas.html
echo "--- visible HTML (scripts removed):"
python3 -c "import re;h=open('teas.html').read();h=re.sub(r'<script.*?</script>|<link[^>]*>|<meta[^>]*>','',h,flags=re.S);print(re.sub(r'<head>.*?</head>','<head>…</head>',h,flags=re.S))"
echo "--- RSC payload lines (first copy):"
python3 show-payload.py teas.html | head -3
echo "--- where does each module's code end up?"
echo "server-only marker in client chunks: $(cat .next/static/chunks/*.js | grep -o chai_server_only_table_7f3 | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
echo "server-only marker in server build:  $(grep -rlo chai_server_only_table_7f3 .next/server | wc -l | tr -d ' ') file(s)"
echo "LikeButton's ♥ in client chunks:     $(cat .next/static/chunks/*.js | grep -o '♥' | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
lsof -ti tcp:4501 | xargs kill            # stop the server listening on port 4501
```

**Output:**

```text
--- visible HTML (scripts removed):
<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en"><head>…</head><body><div hidden=""><!--$--><!--/$--></div><header>Chai Point</header><!--&--><!--&--><main><h1>Teas</h1><ul><li>Masala chai<!-- --> ₹<!-- -->180<!-- --> <button>♥ <!-- -->Masala chai<!-- --> <!-- -->0</button></li><li>Ginger chai<!-- --> ₹<!-- -->160<!-- --> <button>♥ <!-- -->Ginger chai<!-- --> <!-- -->0</button></li></ul><!--$?--><template id="B:0"></template><p>Loading…</p><!--/$--><form action="" encType="multipart/form-data" method="POST"><input type="hidden" name="$ACTION_ID_40b2ec262d71c73d084802f2e41e239a91be829c19"/><input aria-label="name" name="name"/><button>Add tea</button></form></main><!--$--><!--/$--><!--/&--><!--/&--><div hidden id="S:0"><p>Rendered at request time, year <!-- -->2026</p></div></body></html>
--- RSC payload lines (first copy):
c:{"id":"40b2ec262d71c73d084802f2e41e239a91be829c19","bound":null}
1e:I[26456,["$2","$1d"],"LikeButton"]
9:["$","ul",null,{"children":[["$","li","1",{"children":["Masala chai"," ₹",180," ",["$","$L1e",null,{"name":"Masala chai"}]]}],["$","li","2",{"children":["Ginger chai"," ₹",160," ",["$","$L1e",null,{
--- where does each module's code end up?
server-only marker in client chunks: 0
server-only marker in server build:  2 file(s)
LikeButton's ♥ in client chunks:     1
```

What this shows, line by line:

- The **HTML** already contains the rendered list (good for first paint and SEO), the fallback `<p>Loading…</p>` with a `<template id="B:0">` placeholder, and, later in the same response, the streamed `<div hidden id="S:0">` with the request-time part. The form posts to a hidden `$ACTION_ID_…` field: that's the Server Function reference.
- The **RSC payload** has a client reference for `LikeButton` (module id, chunk file, export name), the `ul` tree with `"$L…"` placeholders where `LikeButton` goes and its serializable props `{"name":"Masala chai"}`, and the Server Function as `{"id":"…","bound":null}`.
- The **client JavaScript** contains the `LikeButton` code (its ♥ is there), but the marker string from `lib/db.ts` appears **only in the server build**: the database module, `getTeas` and the list rendering never reach the browser. (String literals survive minification, which is why a marker string, not a comment, is the honest test.)

### Practice

1. A Server Component wants to pass `onSelect={(id) => …}` to a Client Component. Why does Next.js refuse, and what are the options?
2. Which of these can be Server Components: (a) a blog post body rendered from Markdown; (b) a search box with suggestions; (c) a page that reads `cookies()` to greet the user; (d) a theme provider that toggles dark mode?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. Functions can't be serialized into the RSC payload (the client only receives data). Options: move the handler into the Client Component itself; pass a **Server Function** (`"use server"`), which is serialized as a reference; or lift the interactive part entirely into a Client Component.
2. (a) Yes (the Markdown library stays on the server); (c) yes (cookies are read on the server; the page becomes dynamic); (b) and (d) need state and events, so Client Components (the theme provider can still wrap Server Component `children`).

</details>

## 62. Next.js App Router: Layouts, Server Functions and Caching

![The Next.js app directory: folders are URL segments; layout.tsx wraps its pages and persists across navigation; page.tsx is the route's UI; loading.tsx and error.tsx add Suspense and error boundaries; route.ts handles API requests; proxy.ts runs before requests](images/react/62-nextjs.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** **Next.js** is the most used React framework. In its **App Router**, the folder structure under `app/` **is** the URL structure: `app/teas/[id]/page.tsx` serves `/teas/42`. Special files add behaviour: `layout.tsx` (shared UI that stays mounted while you navigate), `loading.tsx` (a Suspense fallback), `error.tsx` (an error boundary), `route.ts` (an API endpoint). Pages are Server Components by default; mutations use **Server Functions**; and in Next.js 16 caching is explicit with **Cache Components** (`"use cache"`, `cacheLife`, `cacheTag`, `updateTag`).

**Words to know:**

- **App Router:** Next.js's router based on the `app/` directory and React Server Components (the older `pages/` directory is the **Pages Router**).
- **Route segment / dynamic segment:** each folder is a URL segment; `[id]` is dynamic (`params.id`), `[...slug]` catches all.
- **`page.tsx`:** the UI for a route; receives `params` and `searchParams` (both promises in Next.js 15+, so you `await` them).
- **`layout.tsx`:** wraps the pages below it; preserved across navigations (state and DOM stay).
- **`loading.tsx` / `error.tsx` / `not-found.tsx`:** automatic Suspense fallback / error boundary (a Client Component) / 404 UI for a segment.
- **`route.ts` (Route Handler):** exports `GET`, `POST`… functions that return web `Response`s: an API endpoint inside the app.
- **`proxy.ts`:** code that runs before matching requests (redirects, rewrites, auth checks); renamed from `middleware.ts` in Next.js 16.
- **Cache Components:** Next.js 16's caching model (enabled with `cacheComponents: true`; default for new apps from 16.4 and planned as the default in Next.js 17): everything is dynamic unless you mark it cached with `"use cache"`; static parts are prerendered as a shell (partial prerendering).
- **`"use cache"` + `cacheLife` + `cacheTag`:** cache a component's or function's result, for how long, with which tags.
- **`updateTag(tag)` / `revalidateTag(tag)`:** expire cached entries with a tag immediately (read-your-own-writes after a Server Function) / in the background.
- **`connection()`:** marks the rest of a component as request-time (dynamic) rendering.
- **Turbopack:** Next.js's Rust-based bundler, the default for `next dev` and `next build` since Next.js 16.
- **`next/link` / `next/image`:** client-side navigation with prefetching / automatic image optimisation.

**Everyday picture.** A **department store floor plan**. The building's entrance and escalators (root layout) are the same on every floor; each department (a route segment) has its own signage (nested layout); every shelf location (page) is found by walking the aisles in order (the folder path). A "back in 5 minutes" sign (`loading.tsx`) appears while a shelf is restocked, and the security desk at the door (`proxy.ts`) checks people before they enter.

**A request to `/teas` in this section's app, traced:**

```text
build time:  TeaList ("use cache", cacheLife hours) is prerendered into a static shell; RequestTime calls connection() → dynamic
             build output marks /teas as ◐ Partial Prerender, revalidate 1h, expire 1d
request:     the static shell (header, h1, cached list, fallback) is sent immediately
             RequestTime renders now and streams into its Suspense slot
user submits the form → createTea Server Function (POST to the same URL with the action id)
             → updateTag("teas") expires the cached list → Next re-renders and sends a fresh RSC payload
             → the list updates in place; LikeButton's client state survives (same component, same position)
```

**When to use Next.js:** products that need SEO, server rendering, a backend in the same project, and the RSC model; Vercel hosting is the smoothest but it also runs on Node servers, Docker and other platforms through adapters. **When not:** a client-only internal tool (Vite is simpler, Section [6](#6-setting-up-node-npm-vite-and-how-these-examples-run)); teams wanting a lighter framework (React Router framework mode, TanStack Start, Astro for content).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Adding `"use client"` to `page.tsx` to make a hook work (turns the whole page into client code); extract the interactive bit instead.
- ❌ Forgetting that `params` is a promise (`const { id } = await params`).
- ❌ Expecting data to be cached automatically (with Cache Components nothing is cached unless you say `"use cache"`).
- ❌ Doing authorisation only in `proxy.ts` (check inside Server Functions and data access too).
- ❌ Using `revalidateTag` when the user must see their own change immediately (use `updateTag`).

**Used in real software:** Next.js is the most widely used React framework and the one react.dev lists first among full-stack frameworks; its App Router was the first production implementation of Server Components.

### Code

The app from Section [61](#61-react-server-components-how-they-work), plus a dynamic route, a route handler, a `loading.tsx` and a `proxy.ts`:

```bash
npx next start -p 4502 > start.log 2>&1 &
for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:4502/ && break; sleep 0.5; done
echo "--- GET /api/teas:"; curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4502/api/teas; echo
echo "--- GET /menu (proxy.ts):"; curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} → %{redirect_url}\n" http://127.0.0.1:4502/menu
echo "--- GET /teas/99:"; curl -s -o page99.html -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:4502/teas/99; grep -o '<meta name="robots" content="noindex"/>' page99.html | sed 's/^/ + /'
echo "--- in Chrome:"; node e2e.mjs
lsof -ti tcp:4502 | xargs kill            # stop the server listening on port 4502
```

**Output:**

```text
Route (app)           Revalidate  Expire
┌ ○ /
├ ○ /_not-found
├ ƒ /api/teas
├ ○ /teas                     1h      1d
└   /teas/[id]
  └ ◐ /teas/[id]
ƒ Proxy (Middleware)
○  (Static)             prerendered as static content
◐  (Partial Prerender)  prerendered as static HTML with dynamic server-streamed content
ƒ  (Dynamic)            server-rendered on demand
--- GET /api/teas:
[{"id":1,"name":"Masala chai","price":180},{"id":2,"name":"Ginger chai","price":160}]
--- GET /menu (proxy.ts):
307 → http://127.0.0.1:4502/teas
--- GET /teas/99:
200 + <meta name="robots" content="noindex"/>
--- in Chrome:
after the Server Function: Masala chai ₹180 ♥ Masala chai 1 | Ginger chai ₹160 ♥ Ginger chai 0 | Lemon tea ₹150 ♥ Lemon tea 0
client navigation to: /teas/2 | heading: Ginger chai
```

Reading the results:

- **Route table:** `/`, `/_not-found` and `/teas` are static (○); `/teas` is static because everything on it is inside the cached `TeaList`, and it shows the cache lifetime from `cacheLife("hours")` (revalidate after 1 hour, expire after 1 day). `/teas/[id]` is a partial prerender (◐): its shell (navigation plus the `loading.tsx` fallback) is static and the tea itself streams in per request. The route handler and the proxy run on demand (ƒ).
- **`proxy.ts`** redirected `/menu` to `/teas` with a 307.
- **`/teas/99` returned status 200**, not 404, but with `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` and the not-found UI. Because the page streams, the 200 status and the shell were already sent before `notFound()` ran inside the streamed part; Next.js adds the `noindex` tag so search engines still drop the page. If a real 404 status matters (for APIs or crawlers), check existence before anything streams, for example in `proxy.ts` or a route handler.
- **In Chrome**, the Server Function added "Lemon tea" and `updateTag` refreshed the cached list immediately, while the `LikeButton` the user had clicked kept its count of 1; clicking a `Link` navigated client-side to `/teas/2`.

### Practice

1. Where would you put a "Back to menu" header shared by every page under `/teas`, so it stays mounted while navigating between teas?
2. After an admin edits a price in a Server Function, regular visitors may see the old price for a few seconds, which is acceptable; but the admin must see the new price at once. Which cache API fits?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. In `app/teas/layout.tsx`: it wraps `app/teas/page.tsx` and `app/teas/[id]/page.tsx`, and layouts are preserved across navigations within their segment.
2. `updateTag("teas")` inside the Server Function: it expires the tagged cache immediately, so the response to the admin's own action is rendered with fresh data (read-your-own-writes). `revalidateTag` would refresh in the background (stale-while-revalidate), fine for changes made elsewhere.

</details>

## 63. Transitions: useTransition, useDeferredValue, Activity and ViewTransition

![Urgent updates (typing) render immediately; transitions mark slower updates as interruptible so typing stays responsive; useDeferredValue shows the old value while the new one renders in the background; Activity hides UI while keeping its state; ViewTransition animates changes made in transitions](images/react/63-transitions.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** some updates are **urgent** (the letter you just typed must appear now) and some can **wait** (re-filtering 10,000 products). **`useTransition`** lets you mark an update as a **transition**: React renders it in the background, interruptibly, and keeps the old UI responsive meanwhile, telling you via `isPending`. **`useDeferredValue`** gives you a version of a value that "lags behind" during heavy renders. **`<Activity>`** (React 19.2) hides part of the UI while **keeping its state**, and **`<ViewTransition>`** (React 19.3) animates changes made in transitions with the browser's View Transitions API.

**Words to know:**

- **Urgent update:** typing, clicking, pressing: users expect immediate feedback; rendered synchronously.
- **Transition (non-urgent update):** an update that can be interrupted and doesn't need to show instantly (filtering, switching tabs, navigation).
- **`useTransition()`:** returns `[isPending, startTransition]`; updates inside `startTransition(() => …)` are transitions; `isPending` is true until they commit. Since React 19 the function can be `async` (an **action**, Section [53](#53-react-19-forms-actions-useactionstate-useformstatus-and-useoptimistic)).
- **`startTransition` (standalone):** the same, without `isPending`, usable outside components.
- **`useDeferredValue(value)`:** returns the previous value during urgent renders and re-renders with the new value in the background; ideal when you don't control the state update (a prop).
- **Stale UI indicator:** dimming content while `isPending` or while `value !== deferredValue`.
- **`<Activity mode="visible" | "hidden">`:** hides its children without unmounting them: state and DOM are kept, effects are cleaned up while hidden and set up again when visible, and hidden content can pre-render at low priority.
- **View Transitions API:** a browser feature (`document.startViewTransition`) that animates between two DOM states with CSS.
- **`<ViewTransition>`:** React 19.3's component that triggers view transitions for its children when they change **inside a transition** (or a deferred value, or a Suspense reveal); `addTransitionType(type)` labels a transition so CSS can animate differently (e.g. "forward" vs "back").
- **Transitions render independently (React 19.3):** a slow transition no longer holds up unrelated transitions.

**Everyday picture.** A **waiter taking a big order** while customers keep calling for water. Water requests (typing) are served immediately; the big order (the filtered list) is prepared in the background and can be restarted if the customer changes their mind. `Activity` is putting a half-eaten meal under a cover when someone steps out: the plate isn't thrown away, it's just not on the table.

**Typing in a filter box, traced:**

```text
without transitions: keystroke → setQuery("c") → filter + render 10,000 rows (200 ms) → the input shows "c" only after 200 ms ⇒ laggy typing
with useTransition:
  keystroke → setInput("c") (urgent: the input updates now)
            → startTransition(() => setQuery("c"))   (background render of the list)
  next keystroke "ch" arrives mid-render → React ABANDONS the "c" list render, starts "ch" ⇒ typing stays smooth
  isPending = true while the list is behind → dim the old list
```

**When to use which:** `useTransition` when you own the state update (tab switches, filters, navigation); `useDeferredValue` when you receive the value (a prop or a hook's result); `Activity` for tabs, drawers and back-navigation where state should survive hiding; `ViewTransition` for animating between UI states. **When not:** for controlled input values themselves (the text in an input must update urgently); as a fix for slow code that could simply be faster (memoise, virtualise).

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Wrapping the input's own `setValue` in `startTransition` (typing becomes laggy and can lose characters).
- ❌ Expecting a transition to make a slow component faster (it keeps the UI responsive; the work is the same).
- ❌ Using `Activity` for things that must stop completely (effects are cleaned up, but the DOM and memory stay).
- ❌ Expecting `<ViewTransition>` to animate urgent updates (only transitions, deferred values and Suspense reveals trigger it).

**Used in real software:** routers (React Router, Next.js) wrap navigations in transitions so the old page stays visible and interactive while the next one loads; search UIs use deferred values; Next.js uses `Activity` to keep previously visited pages' state, and its 16.2 `transitionTypes` prop on `Link` feeds `ViewTransition`.

### Code

**`useTransition`: the input updates urgently; the slow list renders as a transition** (`isPending` is visible in between):

```tsx
import { useState, useTransition, useDeferredValue, Activity, memo, useEffect } from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent, act } from "@testing-library/react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";

const ITEMS = Array.from({ length: 2000 }, (_, i) => `Order #${i + 1}`);
const busy = (ms: number) => { const t = performance.now(); while (performance.now() - t < ms) {} };
const SlowList = memo(function SlowList({ query }: { query: string }) {
  busy(30);                                                              // pretend this render is expensive
  const shown = ITEMS.filter((item) => item.includes(query)).slice(0, 3);
  return <ul aria-label="results">{shown.map((s) => <li key={s}>{s}</li>)}</ul>;
});

function Search() {
  const [input, setInput] = useState("");
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  return (
    <>
      <input aria-label="search" value={input} onChange={(e) => {
        setInput(e.target.value);                                        // urgent
        startTransition(() => setQuery(e.target.value));                 // can wait
      }} />
      <div style={{ opacity: isPending ? 0.5 : 1 }} data-pending={isPending}><SlowList query={query} /></div>
    </>
  );
}
// Testing Library wraps its events in act(), which finishes transitions at once; so this example runs React
// the way a browser does and types with a plain DOM event.
(globalThis as any).IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = false;
function typeInto(input: HTMLInputElement, value: string) {
  Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype, "value")!.set!.call(input, value);   // like a keystroke
  input.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", { bubbles: true }));
}
const searchRoot = document.body.appendChild(document.createElement("div"));
createRoot(searchRoot).render(<Search />);
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100));
const pendingAttr = () => searchRoot.querySelector("[data-pending]")!.getAttribute("data-pending");
const listText = () => [...searchRoot.querySelectorAll("li")].map((li) => li.textContent).join(", ");
typeInto(searchRoot.querySelector("input")!, "#19");
await Promise.resolve();
console.log("right after typing → input:", searchRoot.querySelector("input")!.value, "| pending:", pendingAttr(), "| list still shows:", listText());
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 200));
console.log("after the transition → pending:", pendingAttr(), "| list:", listText());
```

**Output:**

```text
right after typing → input: #19 | pending: true | list still shows: Order #1, Order #2, Order #3
after the transition → pending: false | list: Order #19, Order #190, Order #191
```

Immediately after the keystroke, the input already shows `#19` while the list still shows the **old** results with `isPending = true` (so it's dimmed). Once the background render finished, the list switched to the new results.

**`useDeferredValue`:** the component receives the value as a prop and defers the expensive part itself:

```tsx
function Results({ query }: { query: string }) {
  const deferred = useDeferredValue(query);
  const isStale = query !== deferred;
  return <div data-stale={isStale}><p>showing results for "{deferred}"</p><SlowList query={deferred} /></div>;
}
function DeferredSearch() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  return <><input aria-label="q2" value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} /><Results query={query} /></>;
}
const deferredRoot = document.body.appendChild(document.createElement("div"));
createRoot(deferredRoot).render(<DeferredSearch />);
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100));
const shownText = () => `${deferredRoot.querySelector("p")!.textContent} | stale: ${deferredRoot.querySelector("[data-stale]")!.getAttribute("data-stale")}`;
typeInto(deferredRoot.querySelector("input")!, "#7");
await Promise.resolve();
console.log("during:", shownText(), "| input already shows:", deferredRoot.querySelector("input")!.value);
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 200));
console.log("after: ", shownText());
(globalThis as any).IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
```

**Output:**

```text
during: showing results for "" | stale: true | input already shows: #7
after:  showing results for "#7" | stale: false
```

**`<Activity>`: hide a tab without losing its state.** A draft typed in the hidden tab survives; the tab's effect is cleaned up while hidden:

```tsx
function Composer() {
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState("");
  useEffect(() => { console.log("  composer effect: start"); return () => console.log("  composer effect: cleanup"); }, []);
  return <textarea aria-label="draft" value={draft} onChange={(e) => setDraft(e.target.value)} />;
}
function Tabs({ useActivity }: { useActivity: boolean }) {
  const [tab, setTab] = useState<"write" | "preview">("write");
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setTab(tab === "write" ? "preview" : "write")}>switch</button>
      {useActivity
        ? <Activity mode={tab === "write" ? "visible" : "hidden"}><Composer /></Activity>
        : tab === "write" && <Composer />}
    </>
  );
}
for (const useActivity of [false, true]) {
  console.log(useActivity ? "with <Activity>:" : "with conditional rendering:");
  const v = render(<Tabs useActivity={useActivity} />);
  fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("draft"), { target: { value: "Dear Chai Point," } });
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("switch"));
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("switch"));
  console.log(`  draft after switching away and back: "${(screen.getByLabelText("draft") as HTMLTextAreaElement).value}"`);
  v.unmount();
}
```

**Output:**

```text
with conditional rendering:
  composer effect: start
  composer effect: cleanup
  composer effect: start
  draft after switching away and back: ""
  composer effect: cleanup
with <Activity>:
  composer effect: start
  composer effect: cleanup
  composer effect: start
  draft after switching away and back: "Dear Chai Point,"
  composer effect: cleanup
```

Both versions clean up the effect when the tab is hidden, but only `Activity` kept the typed draft (it hid the DOM with `display: none` instead of unmounting the component).

**`<ViewTransition>` in a real browser.** jsdom has no View Transitions API, so this runs in Chrome; the browser's `startViewTransition` is wrapped to log each call:

```tsx
import { ViewTransition, startTransition, addTransitionType, useState } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";

const original = document.startViewTransition.bind(document);
(document as any).startViewTransition = (arg: any) => {
  console.log("document.startViewTransition called, types:", JSON.stringify(arg?.types ?? []));
  return original(arg);
};
function Card() {
  const [big, setBig] = useState(false);
  return (
    <>
      <button id="transition" onClick={() => startTransition(() => { addTransitionType("grow"); setBig(!big); })}>toggle (transition)</button>
      <button id="urgent" onClick={() => setBig(!big)}>toggle (urgent)</button>
      <ViewTransition><div style={{ width: big ? 300 : 100 }}>{big ? "big" : "small"}</div></ViewTransition>
    </>
  );
}
createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!).render(<Card />);
setTimeout(() => { console.log("click: transition"); document.getElementById("transition")!.click(); }, 100);
setTimeout(() => { console.log("click: urgent"); document.getElementById("urgent")!.click(); }, 800);
setTimeout(() => console.log("final text:", document.querySelector("#root div")!.textContent), 1400);
```

```js
import { chromium } from "@playwright/test";
const browser = await chromium.launch({ channel: "chrome" });
const page = await browser.newPage();
page.on("console", (message) => console.log(message.text()));
await page.setContent('<div id="root"></div>');
await page.addScriptTag({ path: process.argv[2] });
await page.waitForTimeout(1700);
await browser.close();
```

```bash
npx esbuild vt.tsx --bundle --outfile=vt.js --jsx=automatic --define:process.env.NODE_ENV='"production"' --log-level=warning
node run-in-chrome.mjs vt.js
```

**Output:**

```text
click: transition
document.startViewTransition called, types: ["grow"]
click: urgent
final text: small
```

The update inside `startTransition` started a browser view transition (labelled with the type `grow`, which CSS can target with `:active-view-transition-type(grow)`); the urgent update changed the DOM instantly with no animation. Styling the animation is plain CSS on the `::view-transition-*` pseudo-elements.

### Practice

1. A tab bar switches between three heavy tabs; clicking a tab freezes the UI for 300 ms. Which tool, and where does the call go?
2. Why shouldn't you write `startTransition(() => setInputValue(e.target.value))` for a controlled input?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. `useTransition`: `onClick={() => startTransition(() => setTab(next))}`. The current tab stays interactive (and can show `isPending`), and a second click interrupts the first render. Wrapping the tabs in `<Activity>` additionally keeps each tab's state and lets React pre-render hidden tabs at low priority.
2. The input's value must update immediately or the field lags behind the keyboard; transitions can be delayed and interrupted. Keep the input state urgent, and put only the expensive derived update (the query that drives the list) in a transition, or use `useDeferredValue` on it.

</details>

## 64. Real-Time and Streaming UIs: WebSockets, SSE and AI Chat

![Three ways to get data pushed to the UI: WebSockets (two-way, long-lived), Server-Sent Events (server to client over HTTP), and streamed fetch responses read chunk by chunk, which is how AI chat interfaces show tokens as they're generated](images/react/64-realtime.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** some UIs must update without the user asking: chat messages, live prices, notifications, and AI answers that appear word by word. **WebSockets** keep a two-way connection open; **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** let the server push a stream of events over normal HTTP; and a **streamed fetch response** can be read piece by piece. In React you connect in an **effect** (with cleanup to disconnect), and append incoming data with **updater functions**. AI chat UIs stream tokens with exactly these tools, often through a library such as the Vercel AI SDK's `useChat`.

**Words to know:**

- **Polling:** asking the server "anything new?" every few seconds (simple, wasteful, delayed).
- **WebSocket:** a long-lived, two-way connection (`new WebSocket("wss://…")`) for messages in both directions with low latency.
- **Server-Sent Events (SSE):** a one-way stream from server to client over HTTP (`Content-Type: text/event-stream`), with lines like `data: {…}` separated by blank lines; the browser's `EventSource` reconnects automatically.
- **Streaming response / `ReadableStream`:** a `fetch` response body read chunk by chunk with `response.body.getReader()` and a `TextDecoder`.
- **Token streaming:** LLM APIs send their answer as small pieces of text (tokens) as they're generated; showing them immediately makes waiting feel shorter.
- **Backpressure / buffering:** handling data that arrives faster than you can process it (batch updates rather than one state update per tiny chunk if needed).
- **Reconnect with backoff:** retrying a dropped connection after increasing delays (1 s, 2 s, 4 s…).
- **`AbortController` for streams:** cancels a streaming fetch (a "Stop generating" button).
- **Vercel AI SDK (`ai`, `@ai-sdk/react`):** a TypeScript toolkit for LLM apps; `useChat` manages messages, streaming status and sending, using a **UI message stream** protocol over SSE. Version 7 (June 2026) is current.
- **Optimistic message:** showing the user's message instantly before the server confirms (Section [53](#53-react-19-forms-actions-useactionstate-useformstatus-and-useoptimistic)).
- **Auto-scroll:** keeping the newest message in view (a ref + `scrollIntoView` after updates).

**Everyday picture.** **Three ways to get news**: phoning the newsroom every five minutes (polling); a walkie-talkie both of you can talk on at any time (WebSocket); and a radio station broadcasting to you (SSE). A streamed AI answer is a live radio commentary: you hear the sentences as they're spoken instead of waiting for the full report.

**A streamed AI answer, traced:**

```text
user sends "What is masala chai?" → add { role: "user" } message (optimistic) and an empty assistant message
POST /api/chat → the server calls the LLM with stream: true → forwards each token as an SSE line: data: {"delta":"Masala "}
client reads chunks → parses lines → setMessages(m => update the last message's text += delta) → React re-renders each token
user clicks Stop → controller.abort() → the reader throws AbortError → keep the partial text, status "stopped"
stream ends → status "ready" → enable the input again
```

**Which transport when:** SSE for server → client streams (notifications, AI tokens, progress), because it's plain HTTP and works through proxies; WebSockets for genuinely two-way, chatty traffic (multiplayer, collaborative editing, live chat at scale); polling only when updates are rare and real-time doesn't matter. **When not:** don't hold a WebSocket open on every page for data that changes once an hour.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Connecting in the component body (a new connection every render). ✅ An effect with cleanup.
- ❌ `setMessages([...messages, msg])` in a socket handler (stale closure: messages get lost). ✅ `setMessages(m => [...m, msg])`.
- ❌ Not handling disconnects and reconnection.
- ❌ Calling an LLM API directly from the browser with your API key (anyone can steal it). ✅ Call your own server route, which holds the key.
- ❌ Rendering model output as HTML with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` without sanitising (an XSS hole; see `javascript.md`, [Frontend Security](javascript.md#35-frontend-security-xss-csrf-csp-prototype-pollution-and-the-supply-chain)).

**Used in real software:** ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini stream their answers over SSE-style responses; Slack and Discord use WebSockets; trading apps stream prices; the Vercel AI SDK, assistant-ui and CopilotKit package streaming chat UIs for React (`llm-engineering.md` covers the server side).

### Code

**From scratch: a streaming chat with a stop button.** A local server streams an answer word by word as SSE; the React component reads the stream with `fetch` and appends each piece with an updater function:

```tsx
import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { render, screen, fireEvent, act } from "@testing-library/react";

const server = createServer(async (req, res) => {
  let body = ""; for await (const chunk of req) body += chunk;
  const { question } = JSON.parse(body);
  res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "text/event-stream", "Cache-Control": "no-cache" });
  const answer = `You asked "${question}". Masala chai is black tea simmered with milk, sugar and spices like cardamom and ginger.`;
  for (const word of answer.split(" ")) {
    if (res.destroyed) return;                                           // the client stopped listening
    res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify({ delta: word + " " })}\n\n`);    // one SSE event per word
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 8));
  }
  res.end("data: [DONE]\n\n");
});
await new Promise<void>((r) => server.listen(4430, r));

type Msg = { role: "user" | "assistant"; text: string };
function Chat() {
  const [messages, setMessages] = useState<Msg[]>([]);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState<"ready" | "streaming" | "stopped">("ready");
  const controllerRef = useRef<AbortController | null>(null);

  async function send(question: string) {
    setMessages((m) => [...m, { role: "user", text: question }, { role: "assistant", text: "" }]);
    setStatus("streaming");
    const controller = new AbortController();
    controllerRef.current = controller;
    try {
      const response = await fetch("http://localhost:4430/api/chat", { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ question }), signal: controller.signal });
      const reader = response.body!.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader();
      let buffer = "";
      while (true) {
        const { value, done } = await reader.read();
        if (done) break;
        buffer += value;
        const events = buffer.split("\n\n");                               // SSE events end with a blank line
        buffer = events.pop()!;                                            // keep an incomplete event for later
        for (const event of events) {
          const data = event.replace(/^data: /, "");
          if (data === "[DONE]") continue;
          const { delta } = JSON.parse(data);
          setMessages((m) => m.with(-1, { ...m.at(-1)!, text: m.at(-1)!.text + delta }));   // updater: never stale
        }
      }
      setStatus("ready");
    } catch (e) {
      if ((e as Error).name === "AbortError") setStatus("stopped"); else throw e;
    }
  }
  return (
    <>
      <ul>{messages.map((m, i) => <li key={i}>{m.role}: {m.text}</li>)}</ul>
      <p role="status">{status}</p>
      <button onClick={() => send("What is masala chai?")} disabled={status === "streaming"}>Ask</button>
      <button onClick={() => controllerRef.current?.abort()} disabled={status !== "streaming"}>Stop</button>
    </>
  );
}
render(<Chat />);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Ask"));
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 60)));
console.log("mid-stream:", screen.getAllByRole("listitem")[1].textContent!.split(" ").length - 1, "words so far | status:", screen.getByRole("status").textContent);
await screen.findByText("ready", undefined, { timeout: 3000 });
console.log("complete:", screen.getAllByRole("listitem")[1].textContent);
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Ask"));
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 40)));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Stop"));
await screen.findByText("stopped");
console.log("stopped early:", screen.getAllByRole("listitem")[3].textContent!.length < screen.getAllByRole("listitem")[1].textContent!.length, "| status:", screen.getByRole("status").textContent);
server.close();
```

**Output:**

```text
mid-stream: 6 words so far | status: streaming
complete: assistant: You asked "What is masala chai?". Masala chai is black tea simmered with milk, sugar and spices like cardamom and ginger. 
stopped early: true | status: stopped
```

`m.with(-1, …)` replaces the last message with an updated copy (negative indexes count from the end), so each token creates a new array as React expects. Exact word counts mid-stream vary with timing, so only "some words so far" matters.

**WebSockets: a live order feed** with a `ws` server; the component connects in an effect and closes the socket in the cleanup. In a browser you'd use the built-in `WebSocket`; here the `ws` package's client, which has the same `onmessage`/`close()` API, stands in for it, because Node's built-in client can't share event classes with the simulated page:

```tsx
import { WebSocketServer, WebSocket as WsClient } from "ws";

const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: 4431 });
wss.on("connection", (socket) => {
  console.log("  server: client connected");
  let n = 0;
  const timer = setInterval(() => socket.send(JSON.stringify({ order: 90312 + n++, item: n % 2 ? "Masala chai" : "Samosa" })), 10);
  socket.on("close", () => { clearInterval(timer); console.log("  server: client disconnected"); });
});

function LiveOrders() {
  const [orders, setOrders] = useState<{ order: number; item: string }[]>([]);
  useEffect(() => {
    const socket = new WsClient("ws://localhost:4431");                                               // browser: new WebSocket(…)
    socket.onmessage = (event) => setOrders((o) => [JSON.parse(String(event.data)), ...o].slice(0, 3));   // newest first, keep 3
    return () => socket.close();                                                                        // disconnect on unmount
  }, []);
  return <ul>{orders.map((o) => <li key={o.order}>#{o.order} {o.item}</li>)}</ul>;
}
const live = render(<LiveOrders />);
await act(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 80)));
console.log("latest orders:", screen.getAllByRole("listitem").length, "shown, newest first:", screen.getAllByRole("listitem")[0].textContent!.startsWith("#"));
live.unmount();
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50));
wss.close();
```

**Output:**

```text
  server: client connected
latest orders: 3 shown, newest first: true
  server: client disconnected
```

**The library way: `useChat` from the Vercel AI SDK 7.** The server side here uses the SDK's own stream helpers to send a fake answer (no LLM or API key needed); in a real app the route would call a model with `streamText` and return its UI message stream:

```tsx
import { createUIMessageStream, pipeUIMessageStreamToResponse, DefaultChatTransport } from "ai";
import { useChat } from "@ai-sdk/react";

const aiServer = createServer(async (req, res) => {
  let body = ""; for await (const chunk of req) body += chunk;
  const question = JSON.parse(body).messages.at(-1).parts.find((p: { type: string }) => p.type === "text").text;
  const stream = createUIMessageStream({
    execute: async ({ writer }) => {
      writer.write({ type: "text-start", id: "answer" });
      for (const word of `You asked: ${question} Masala chai is spiced milk tea.`.split(" ")) {
        writer.write({ type: "text-delta", id: "answer", delta: word + " " });
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 5));
      }
      writer.write({ type: "text-end", id: "answer" });
    },
  });
  pipeUIMessageStreamToResponse({ response: res, stream });              // SSE in the AI SDK's UI message format
});
await new Promise<void>((r) => aiServer.listen(4432, r));

function AiChat() {
  const { messages, sendMessage, status } = useChat({ transport: new DefaultChatTransport({ api: "http://localhost:4432/api/chat" }) });
  const [input, setInput] = useState("");
  return (
    <>
      <ul>{messages.map((m) => <li key={m.id}>{m.role}: {m.parts.map((p) => (p.type === "text" ? p.text : "")).join("")}</li>)}</ul>
      <p data-testid="status">{status}</p>
      <form onSubmit={(e) => { e.preventDefault(); sendMessage({ text: input }); setInput(""); }}>
        <input aria-label="message" value={input} onChange={(e) => setInput(e.target.value)} />
        <button disabled={status !== "ready"}>Send</button>
      </form>
    </>
  );
}
render(<AiChat />);
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText("message"), { target: { value: "What is masala chai?" } });
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText("Send"));
await screen.findByText(/spiced milk tea/, undefined, { timeout: 3000 });
await screen.findByText("ready");
console.log(screen.getAllByRole("listitem").map((li) => li.textContent));
aiServer.close();
```

**Output:**

```text
[
  'user: What is masala chai?',
  'assistant: You asked: What is masala chai? Masala chai is spiced milk tea. '
]
```

`useChat` handled the message list, the streaming status (`submitted` → `streaming` → `ready`) and parsing the stream; each message is made of **parts** (text, tool calls, reasoning, files), which is how AI chat UIs render rich answers. Swapping the fake stream for a real model changes only the server.

### Practice

1. A chat component does `socket.onmessage = (e) => setMessages([...messages, JSON.parse(e.data)])` inside `useEffect(…, [])`. Users report only the last message ever shows. Why, and what's the fix?
2. Why should the browser call your `/api/chat` route rather than the LLM provider's API directly?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

1. The handler was created in the first render and captured `messages = []` forever (a stale closure), so each message replaces the list with `[newMessage]`. Use the updater form: `setMessages((m) => [...m, JSON.parse(e.data)])`.
2. The provider API needs your secret API key; anything sent to the browser can be read by users. Your server route keeps the key secret and can also enforce authentication, rate limits, input validation and logging.

</details>

## 65. Internationalisation: Translations, Plurals, Dates, Numbers and Right-to-Left Layouts

![Internationalisation: UI text comes from translation files by key, plurals follow each language's rules, numbers, currencies and dates are formatted with Intl for the user's locale, and right-to-left languages flip the layout with the dir attribute and logical CSS](images/react/65-i18n.svg)

### Theory

> **In simple words:** **internationalisation (i18n)** means building the app so it can work in any language and region; **localisation (l10n)** is actually adapting it for one (translating text, formatting money and dates the local way). In React you stop writing text directly in components and look it up by **key** from translation files, let each language's **plural rules** pick the right sentence, format numbers, currencies and dates with the browser's built-in **`Intl`** APIs, and support **right-to-left** languages such as Arabic and Urdu.

**Words to know:**

- **Internationalisation (i18n) / localisation (l10n):** making software adaptable to languages and regions / adapting it to one ("i18n" = i + 18 letters + n).
- **Locale:** a language plus regional conventions, written as a tag like `en-IN` (English, India), `hi-IN` (Hindi, India), `ar-EG` (Arabic, Egypt).
- **Translation key / message catalogue:** a stable identifier (`"cart.items"`) mapped to the text in each language, usually stored in one JSON file per locale.
- **Interpolation:** inserting values into a message: `"Hello, {{name}}"`.
- **Plural rules:** languages differ in how many plural forms they have (English: one/other; Arabic: zero/one/two/few/many/other); `Intl.PluralRules` tells you which form a number needs.
- **`Intl` APIs:** built-in JavaScript formatters: `NumberFormat` (numbers, currencies, percentages), `DateTimeFormat` (dates and times, with time zones), `RelativeTimeFormat` ("3 days ago"), `ListFormat` ("tea, coffee and juice"), `PluralRules`, `Collator` (locale-aware sorting).
- **ICU message format:** a standard syntax for messages with plurals and selections (`{count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}`), used by FormatJS/react-intl.
- **i18next / react-i18next:** a popular i18n library and its React binding (`useTranslation()` returns a `t` function).
- **RTL (right-to-left):** scripts written from right to left (Arabic, Hebrew, Urdu, Persian); the page sets `dir="rtl"` and the layout mirrors.
- **Logical CSS properties:** `margin-inline-start`, `padding-inline-end`, `inset-inline-start` instead of left/right, so layouts flip automatically for RTL.
- **Time zone:** the region whose clock rules apply (`Asia/Kolkata`); the same instant shows different local times, and server and client may disagree (a hydration risk, Section [59](#59-hydration-and-hydration-mismatches)).
- **Pseudo-localisation:** replacing text with accented, longer versions ("[Ǻđđ ŧǿ ƈȧřŧ]") during testing to find untranslated strings and layouts that break with longer text.

**Everyday picture.** A **restaurant chain opening in new countries**. The kitchen and recipes (components) stay the same; the menu text is translated (catalogues), prices are written the local way (₹1,84,999.50 in India, $184,999.50 in the US), dates on receipts follow local order, and in some countries the menu is read right to left, so the whole layout is mirrored.

**Formatting one value for different locales, traced:**

```text
amount 184999.5 in INR
  en-IN → ₹1,84,999.50      (Indian lakh grouping: 1,84,999)
  en-US → ₹184,999.50       (thousands grouping)
  de-DE → 184.999,50 ₹      (dot for thousands, comma for decimals, symbol after)
plural for "item" with count 1 / 5:
  en: one → "1 item", other → "5 items"
  ar: needs zero/one/two/few/many/other → six different sentences
```

**When to internationalise:** any product with users in more than one language or region, or likely to be; and even in a one-language app, always format numbers, money and dates with `Intl` rather than by hand. **When not:** a short-lived internal tool for one team can hard-code text, but should still use `Intl` for formatting.

**Common mistakes:**

- ❌ Building sentences by concatenation (`"You have " + n + " items"`): word order and plurals differ by language. ✅ Whole messages with placeholders.
- ❌ `count === 1 ? "item" : "items"` (wrong for many languages). ✅ Plural rules.
- ❌ Formatting money with `toFixed(2)` and a hard-coded "₹". ✅ `Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency", currency })`.
- ❌ Using `left`/`right` in CSS for things that should mirror. ✅ Logical properties.
- ❌ Rendering dates with the server's time zone and re-rendering with the user's on the client (hydration mismatch); pass an explicit time zone, or render client-only (Section [69](#69-whats-new-20222026-react-18-to-193-and-the-ecosystem) shows `browser()`).

**Used in real software:** Airbnb, Booking.com and most global products ship dozens of locales; react-i18next and FormatJS (react-intl) are the most used React i18n libraries; Next.js supports locale-based routing; translation platforms (Crowdin, Lokalise, Phrase) sync catalogues with code.

### Code

**From scratch: the built-in `Intl` formatters** cover numbers, money, dates, relative times, lists and plural rules for any locale:

```tsx
const amount = 184999.5;
for (const locale of ["en-IN", "en-US", "de-DE"]) {
  console.log(locale.padEnd(6), new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }).format(amount));
}
const instant = new Date("2026-10-17T14:30:00Z");
console.log("Kolkata:", new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-IN", { dateStyle: "medium", timeStyle: "short", timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata" }).format(instant));
console.log("New York:", new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "medium", timeStyle: "short", timeZone: "America/New_York" }).format(instant));
console.log(new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat("en", { numeric: "auto" }).format(-1, "day"), "|", new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat("hi", { numeric: "auto" }).format(-1, "day"));
console.log(new Intl.ListFormat("en", { type: "conjunction" }).format(["chai", "samosa", "jalebi"]));
console.log("en plural forms for 0, 1, 5:", [0, 1, 5].map((n) => new Intl.PluralRules("en").select(n)).join(", "));
console.log("ar plural forms for 0, 1, 2, 3, 11, 100:", [0, 1, 2, 3, 11, 100].map((n) => new Intl.PluralRules("ar").select(n)).join(", "));
```

**Output:**

```text
en-IN  ₹1,84,999.50
en-US  ₹184,999.50
de-DE  184.999,50 ₹
Kolkata: 17 Oct 2026, 8:00 pm
New York: Oct 17, 2026, 10:30 AM
yesterday | कल
chai, samosa, and jalebi
en plural forms for 0, 1, 5: other, one, other
ar plural forms for 0, 1, 2, 3, 11, 100: zero, one, two, few, many, other
```

The same instant is 8:00 pm in Kolkata and 10:30 am in New York. Arabic needs six plural forms, which is why `n === 1 ? … : …` can't work in general.

**From scratch: a tiny translation function** with interpolation and plural rules:

```tsx
type Catalogue = Record<string, string | Record<string, string>>;
const catalogues: Record<string, Catalogue> = {
  en: { greeting: "Hello, {name}!", items: { one: "{count} item in your cart", other: "{count} items in your cart" } },
  hi: { greeting: "नमस्ते, {name}!", items: { one: "आपकी टोकरी में {count} वस्तु है", other: "आपकी टोकरी में {count} वस्तुएँ हैं" } },
};
function translate(locale: string, key: string, values: Record<string, string | number> = {}) {
  let message = catalogues[locale][key];
  if (typeof message === "object") message = message[new Intl.PluralRules(locale).select(Number(values.count))] ?? message.other;
  return message.replace(/\{(\w+)\}/g, (_, name) => String(values[name]));
}
for (const locale of ["en", "hi"]) {
  console.log(translate(locale, "greeting", { name: "Asha" }), "|", translate(locale, "items", { count: 1 }), "|", translate(locale, "items", { count: 3 }));
}
```

**Output:**

```text
Hello, Asha! | 1 item in your cart | 3 items in your cart
नमस्ते, Asha! | आपकी टोकरी में 1 वस्तु है | आपकी टोकरी में 3 वस्तुएँ हैं
```

**The library way: react-i18next.** Translations are loaded once; components call `useTranslation()`; plurals use the `_one`/`_other` key suffixes, and changing the language re-renders every translated component:

```tsx
import i18n from "i18next";
import { initReactI18next, useTranslation } from "react-i18next";
import { render, screen, fireEvent, act } from "@testing-library/react";

await i18n.use(initReactI18next).init({
  lng: "en",
  fallbackLng: "en",
  interpolation: { escapeValue: false },                     // React already escapes text
  resources: {
    en: { translation: { title: "Your cart", items_one: "{{count}} item", items_other: "{{count}} items", total: "Total: {{amount}}" } },
    hi: { translation: { title: "आपकी टोकरी", items_one: "{{count}} वस्तु", items_other: "{{count}} वस्तुएँ", total: "कुल: {{amount}}" } },
  },
});

function Cart({ count, amount }: { count: number; amount: number }) {
  const { t, i18n: instance } = useTranslation();
  const money = new Intl.NumberFormat(instance.language === "hi" ? "hi-IN" : "en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }).format(amount);
  return (
    <section lang={instance.language}>
      <h2>{t("title")}</h2>
      <p>{t("items", { count })} · {t("total", { amount: money })}</p>
      <button onClick={() => instance.changeLanguage(instance.language === "en" ? "hi" : "en")}>हिन्दी / English</button>
    </section>
  );
}
render(<Cart count={3} amount={1849.5} />);
console.log(screen.getByRole("heading").textContent, "|", screen.getByText(/item/).textContent);
await act(async () => { fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button")); });
console.log(screen.getByRole("heading").textContent, "|", screen.getByText(/कुल/).textContent);
```

**Output:**

```text
Your cart | 3 items · Total: ₹1,849.50
आपकी टोकरी | 3 वस्तुएँ · कुल: ₹1,849.50
```

`escapeValue: false` is safe here because React escapes all text it renders (Section [8](#8-jsx-markup-inside-javascript-and-what-it-compiles-to)); escaping twice would show `&amp;` on screen.

**Right-to-left layouts: `dir` plus logical CSS properties.** The same card is rendered in English and Arabic and screenshotted in Chrome; `margin-inline-start` and `border-inline-start` flip automatically:

```tsx
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from "react-dom/server";
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

function Notice({ dir, lang, title, body }: { dir: "ltr" | "rtl"; lang: string; title: string; body: string }) {
  return (
    <article dir={dir} lang={lang} className="notice">
      <span className="badge">●</span>
      <div><h3>{title}</h3><p>{body}</p></div>
    </article>
  );
}
const css = `body{font-family:system-ui,sans-serif;margin:0;padding:16px;background:#f1f5f9;display:grid;gap:12px}
.notice{display:flex;gap:12px;align-items:flex-start;background:#fff;border-radius:12px;padding:14px 18px;border-inline-start:6px solid #2563eb;width:460px}
.badge{color:#2563eb;font-size:20px;margin-inline-end:4px}h3{margin:0 0 4px;font-size:17px;color:#0f172a}p{margin:0;color:#475569;font-size:14px}`;
const page = renderToStaticMarkup(<>
  <Notice dir="ltr" lang="en" title="Order confirmed" body="Your masala chai will arrive in 20 minutes." />
  <Notice dir="rtl" lang="ar" title="تم تأكيد الطلب" body="سيصل شاي الماسالا خلال ٢٠ دقيقة." />
</>);
writeFileSync("rtl.html", `<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8"><style>${css}</style>${page}`);
console.log(page.replace(/<\/article>/g, "</article>\n"));
```

**Output:**

```text
<article dir="ltr" lang="en" class="notice"><span class="badge">●</span><div><h3>Order confirmed</h3><p>Your masala chai will arrive in 20 minutes.</p></div></article>
<article dir="rtl" lang="ar" class="notice"><span class="badge">●</span><div><h3>تم تأكيد الطلب</h3><p>سيصل شاي الماسالا خلال ٢٠ دقيقة.</p></div></article>
```

![Chrome's rendering of the code above: the English card has its blue border and badge on the left; the Arabic card mirrors them to the right, with no extra CSS](images/react/65-rtl-screenshot.png)

The Arabic card puts its border, badge and text on the right because the CSS uses `*-inline-start`/`*-inline-end`, which follow the writing direction set by `dir`.

### Practice

1. Format `1234567.891` as a percentage-free plain number for `en-IN`, `en-US` and `fr-FR`, with at most 2 decimals. What differs?
2. Why is `t("hello") + ", " + name + "!"` a bad message design, and what's better?

<details>
<summary><b>Answer</b></summary>

```tsx
for (const locale of ["en-IN", "en-US", "fr-FR"]) console.log(locale, new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { maximumFractionDigits: 2 }).format(1234567.891));
```

**Output:**

```text
en-IN 12,34,567.89
en-US 1,234,567.89
fr-FR 1 234 567,89
```

1. Grouping (12,34,567 in India; 1,234,567 in the US) and the separators: French uses a narrow non-breaking space for thousands and a comma for decimals.
2. Translators can't reorder the parts, and some languages put the name first or need different punctuation. Use one whole message with a placeholder: `t("greeting", { name })` with `"greeting": "Hello, {{name}}!"` (and `"नमस्ते, {{name}}!"` etc.).

</details>
